text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- The Jacksonville Jaguars are getting closer and closer to Week 1, and we are starting to get more of an idea of who will be on the field when Sept. 13 arrives,

The Jaguars dealt with their fair share of injuries over the course of training camp, but nothing overly serious. Patrick Mekari and Zach Durfee will start the year on the injured reserve/resignated to return list before joining the 53-man roster, while the Jaguars have four players (Jared Bartlett, Garrett DiGiorgio, Parker Hughes, and Sam Mustipher) on the season-ending injured reserve.

Otherwise, the only notable injuries the Jaguars had coming out of camp came down to four key players: wide receivers Brian Thomas Jr. (shoulder) and Jakobi Meyers (wrist), offensive lineman Cole Van Lanen (knee), and running back LeQuint Allen.

Jaguars head coach Liam Coen provided updates on all four on Wednesday as the Jaguars start preparing for Week 1, and we break down what it all means below.

Brian Thomas Jr. and Jakobi Meyers

The Jaguars' talented pair of receivers each dealt with minor injuries at the end of camp that never seemed overly serious, though it did keep both out of the final days of camp. Meyers sustained a wrist injury before the second preseason game against the Carolina Panthers, while Thomas had a shoulder injury pop up after catching a touchdown in joint practices against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers.

Thomas was present at the last day of training camp a week ago, going through individual drills in an red non-contact jersey. That alone seemed like a good enough sign that he would be good to go for Week 1 against the Cleveland Browns, something Coen noted would be the case the day Thomas injured his shoulder.

Both Thomas and Meyers were at practice Wednesday, with neither wearing a non-contact jersey or appearing to have any limitations in the two periods open to the media during individual drills. All signs point to them being ready to roll when the Jaguars take the field in 11 days.

“Yeah, they'll be good. Jakobi should be going today. He went yesterday," Jaguars head coach Liam Coen said before Wednesday's practice. "Was limited in terms of catching it a little bit. And then B.T. was full go yesterday. No issues.”

Cole Van Lanen

It remains to be seen if the Jaguars will have veteran offensive tackle Cole Van Lanen active in Week 1, though it does appear he is on a good track toward an earlier return than many may have anticipated. Van Lanen was activated off the Active/PUP list toward the end of camp and began to start taking reps in practice, and Coen has already said how he practices in the lead-up to Week 1 will determine whether he plays vs. the Browns.

If Van Lanen does play, it can be expected for him to be in the starting lineup at right tackle. Or perhaps the Jaguars have Van Lanen serve as the swing tackle at the very start of the season until he is 100%. Either way, his trajectory will impact what the offensive line looks like on the active game day roster. Coen seemed optimistic about his chances ahead of practice.

"I know Cole’s looked good. I know he's looked really good. I know he’s got some confidence," Coen said on Wednesday.

"The preseason game the other night he did one-on-ones against some of the defensive players, and he felt really good doing that. So, I'm hopeful. You always want them to be able to go, but you also have to, all right, it's a long year, a lot of football to play, and make sure that you're putting both the player and our team in the best position."

LeQuint Allen Jr.

One of the most important injuries the Jaguars have been facing over the last few weeks is at the running back spot. Bhayshul Tuten and Chris Rodriguez Jr. get most of the coverage when it comes to the running back rotation, but LeQuint Allen is one of the offense's most important players thanks to his ability to pass-protect.

Allen was set to serve as the Jaguars' top passing down back at the start of the season, but a soft-tissue injury in the middle of training camp sidelined him and has kept him sidelined since. The fact Allen was not placed on IR with a designation to return is a good sign that he will be available within the first month, but Week 1 might be a long-shot.

"LeQuint, look, we definitely miss the presence for sure. I mean, the physicality, the edge, the toughness, all that stuff. I'd be pleasantly surprised if he was ready to go, but I know that this guy has attacked it," Coen said.

So, what would that mean for the Jaguars at the running back position? The Jaguars' running back rotation would still be led by Tuten and Rodriguez when it came to the ground game, but Allen not being in the line-up would lead to quite the void on passing downs. Coen addressed that very role on Wednesday, noting that he has been impressed by different parts of Rodriguez's and Ammer Abdullah's traits in the passing game.

"I think that the backs have done a nice job of, like, okay, LeQuint, we know has been our third-down back pass protector. Who's going to fill that void and be able to do some of those things? I think all of them have been working at it," Coen said. "I think C-Rod's [RB Chris Rodriguez Jr.] done a great job in pass protection specifically. And then Ameer, I think, can help us in some of the pass game and things that we wanted to do with LeQuint as we go. I think he can kind of help fill that void as well."

All things considered, it seems like the Jaguars are getting more positive injury news than otherwise ahead of Week 1. The sky may have felt like it was falling at times in training camp, but they are in a good spot right now.

The biggest news of the NFL preseason from a University of Kansas perspective was undrafted rookie quarterback Jalon Daniels’ ascension to the No. 2 spot for the Tampa Bay Buccaneers.

Daniels, who started portions of six seasons at KU, including the entirety of 2024 and 2025, beat out veteran Jake Browning and second-year quarterback Connor Bazelak in order to back up Baker Mayfield. That’s a promising start to his career that suggests Daniels could stick around in the professional ranks for longer than most former KU quarterbacks.

Several past Jayhawks also survived Sunday’s roster cutdown deadline, while others have caught on with practice squads in the days since. Quite a few more were not so lucky and will be looking for new homes.

Dorance Armstrong, now an outside linebacker for the Washington Commanders, is the longest-tenured Jayhawk in the NFL. The veteran missed much of the 2025 season after suffering a torn ACL. He has been working his way back into action at practice but will not technically be on the Commanders’ 53-man roster due to a one-game suspension for violating the league’s personal conduct policy. The Athletic reported that Armstrong “kicked a police officer while being arrested during an incident in May 2025 in Frisco, Texas.”

Also technically absent from his team’s initial roster this season is running back Devin Neal of the New Orleans Saints. Neal received a fair bit of playing time and scored two touchdowns as a rookie but will miss the 2026 season due to a hamstring injury after being placed on season-ending injured reserve.

Austin Booker, now entering his third year, seems poised for a big role with the Chicago Bears after playing just nine snaps in one preseason game, according to Pro Football Focus. However, he is currently battling a groin injury.

Two former KU linemen, both recent NFL Draft selections, made the San Francisco 49ers’ 53-man roster. Dominick Puni has long been firmly ensconced as a starter at guard. Enrique Cruz Jr., a rookie fifth-rounder, saw extensive action with 156 snaps across three preseason contests.

The Seattle Seahawks had entered camp with three Jayhawks on the roster. Second-year guard Bryce Cabeldue earned a spot on the final 53, while second-year tackle Logan Brown returned to the practice squad; both received Super Bowl rings with the team last season. Sixth-round rookie wideout Emmanuel Henderson Jr., who caught four passes for 65 yards, returned four kicks and made a pair of tackles in the preseason, will join Brown on the practice squad.

Bangally Kamara, who initially made the Minnesota Vikings in the spring via a minicamp tryout, found his way onto their practice squad. Tommy Dunn and D.J. Withers had been reunited on the interior defensive line for the Dallas Cowboys, but now they’ve been split up as Dunn made the practice squad, while Withers was waived on Sunday.

Cobee Bryant, who was thrust into action as an undrafted rookie for the Atlanta Falcons as a rookie last year and recorded eight tackles with a pass breakup for the team this preseason, initially appeared to have made the Falcons’ practice squad but was released on Wednesday morning.

Other current free agents include wide receiver Luke Grimm (waived by Los Angeles Chargers with an injury settlement on Aug. 25), kicker Laith Marjan (cut by Pittsburgh Steelers on Aug. 23) and wideouts Quentin Skinner (released by Buffalo Bills on Saturday) and Levi Wentz (waived by Steelers on Saturday).

There's been plenty of frustration surrounding the status of Chicago Bears cornerback Kyler Gordon, who's been sidelined for the entirety of training camp and preseason with a calf injury that landed landed him on the physically unable to perform list to start the regular season.

Gordon has been injury prone since he was drafted in the second round of the 2022 NFL Draft, and he's yet to play an entire season in four years. Which is a shame considering he's among the NFL's best nickel cornerbacks when healthy.

With Gordon landing on the PUP list, he'll miss at least the first four games of the 2026 season, and he's eligible to return in Week 5 against the Green Bay Packers. But there are questions about it Gordon will even play this season. On Tuesday, general manager Ryan Poles sounded uncertain about Gordon's availability this season.

"I don’t know. I would hope so. I still have hope there," Poles said. "He’s going to have to continue to work hard and get back to playing football again. … Any time you have an injury and you’re coming back from something, there’s discomfort that you have to push through. And that’s what it comes down to. We haven’t been able to get over that hump and we’re not progressing as fast as we’d like. That’s really all I have to say about it."

One day later, a video showing Gordon training with NFL rehab specialist, the Foot Doctor, who's also worked with Bears cornerback Jaylon Johnson, defensive back Cam Lewis and running back D'Andre Swift.

With Gordon sidelined, it sounds like it'll come down to rookie Malik Muhammad, veteran Cam Lewis and newcomer Clark Phillips III at nickel. But the hope remains that Gordon can get healthy and back on the field, as it's been proven that the Bears defense has been better when he's out there.

title: Agent's Take: Cam Skattebo needs better advice as preseason antics wear thin for Giants
description:

The Giants surely wouldn't have paid Skattebo for any missed games for careless actions that could have been easily avoided.

text:
Cam Skattebo is attracting attention for the wrong reasons lately. The New York Giants running back reportedly ruffled some feathers at an Aug. 26 practice. Skattebo's late slide after catching a pass ignited a fight with defensive backs Jevon Holland and Greg Newsome, according to multiple New York reports. Holland and Newsome took exception because Skattebo came close to taking out their legs, even though the defense wasn't allowed to make hard contact with offensive players.

Coach John Harbaugh criticized Skattebo after the practice.

"Did you see that? Yeah, it's infectious," Harbaugh said. "It can be infectious the other way, an infectious disease type thing. We want it to be in a positive way."

Several days earlier, Skattebo ran over linebacker Zaire Barnes when defensive players weren't allowed to make hits.

Previously, Skattebo's failed attempt at his signature backflip, in which he landed awkwardly on his surgically repaired right ankle at Fanatics Fest in July, reportedly prompted Harbaugh and general manager Joe Schoen to speak with him about his actions. Another backflip performed in late May after hitting a home run at teammate Brian Burns' celebrity softball game was successful.

Skattebo's rookie season in 2025 was cut short because of the dislocated ankle, tibia and fibula fracture and deltoid ligament rupture he suffered in a Week 8 contest against the Philadelphia Eagles. He gained 401 yards on 101 carries with five touchdowns and caught 24 passes for 207 yards and another two scores in his eight games played.

When situations like these arise, an agent should provide counsel to their client. It's an agent's job to tell a client what he needs to hear, not what he wants to hear. That isn't always done. Some agents are reluctant to be candid for fear of being fired and instead become enablers.

The initial backflip created an opportunity to warn Skattebo about the risk he was taking, considering he hadn't completely recovered from a serious injury. Had there been a major setback that jeopardized or ended Skattebo's 2026 season, which fortunately didn't occur with either backflip, he would have landed on the Reserve/Non-Football Injury list (NFI).

Teams don't have to pay players on NFI during the season, but can elect to do so. The skill, injury and salary cap guarantees in NFL contracts aren't applicable to non-football injuries. Salary is considered fully guaranteed when all three of these guarantees exist, but it will be void for a laundry list of reasons.

As a 2025 fourth-round pick, the only guaranteed money in Skattebo's four-year rookie contract is his $1.07 million signing bonus. That's standard for players drafted in the fourth round and beyond. The rest of Skattebo contract consists of minimum base salaries, which is also the norm beginning in the fourth round. Skattebo's 2026 salary is $1.005 million. The Giants surely wouldn't have paid Skattebo for any missed games for careless actions that could have been easily avoided.

Skattebo has more than his health at risk

More importantly, games on NFI don't count towards an accrued season (a year of service for free agency), a credited season for benefits or a credited season for minimum salary. A player must have six or more regular-season games on the 53-man roster, injured reserve, or physically unable to perform list to qualify for an accrued season. For example, if Skattebo missed the 2026 season due to a setback from a backflip and completed his rookie contract, he would have three accrued seasons, making him a restricted free agent in 2029, since four accrued seasons are necessary to be an unrestricted free agent. These ramifications could have been conveyed to Skattebo.

Another point that could be stressed to Skattebo is that Harbaugh is the main power broker with the Giants, since he reports only to ownership rather than to Schoen. The idea would be to avoid doing things that could make a negative impression on Harbaugh, as he doesn't have a vested interest in Skattebo since he wasn't part of the decision to draft him.

Several players Harbaugh coached with the Baltimore Ravens signed with the Giants during free agency. A suggestion would be to ask Skattebo to gather intel from those players, particularly fullback Patrick Ricard, on how Harbaugh operates. All of Ricard's nine NFL seasons were with the Ravens, so he should be able to provide the most insight about Harbaugh. Based on this intel, Skattebo could begin to act accordingly.

Why Skattebo's margin for error is shrinking

The Giants signed running back Najee Harris, who is returning from a left Achilles tear that occurred with the Los Angeles Chargers three games into the 2025 regular season, a couple of weeks ago. There was plenty of media speculation that the signing of Harris was related to Skattebo. Harris is a bigger running back, listed at 6-foot-1 and 232 pounds, who fits Harbaugh's preference for physical, smash-mouth football.

If representing Skattebo, the Harris signing could have been used a pre-text to get information about Skattebo's training camp performance and a sense of how the addition could impact him. During my agent days, I would routinely check with front offices where I had clients, especially those who I thought were on the roster bubble, throughout the preseason for a progress report. Any useful information would be discussed with the client.

Harris was signed to an unsecured one-year deal at his $1.215 million league minimum salary. The contract includes an injury waiver for the left Achilles and a split of $615,000. Because of the split, any week Harris isn't on the 53-man roster, he will be paid at the lower amount. This will most likely apply if Harris is put on injured reserve. Skattebo doesn't have anything to worry about with Harris from a financial standpoint.

The signing may have been more of an indictment of Tyrone Tracy Jr., who was inconsistent during the preseason. There's a reason the Pittsburgh Steelers didn't pick up a $6.79 million fifth-year option despite Harris consistently rushing beyond 1,000 yards each season. He had such a soft free agent market in 2025 that he signed a one-year prove-it deal for $5.25 million with an additional $4 million in incentives.

The reports of Skattebo's skirmish with his defensive teammates would have prompted another call to the front office for their assessment of the incident. Any negative feedback certainly would have been shared with Skattebo.

Skattebo's comments about the Fanatics Fest backflip suggest he may not necessarily follow any candid advice he receives from his representation. "I'm just gonna keep being me, Skattebo said. "If they wanna say I'm braindead and I don't have no brain, then who cares? F**k it."

Agents rarely sever relationships with clients. It's typically the player firing his agent. Erik Burkhardt eventually dropped 2012 Heisman Trophy winner Johnny Manziel as a client. There is no comparison between Skattebo and Manziel. Skattebo's antics are benign, comparatively speaking.

text:
FLOWERY BRANCH, Ga. — After leading the league in scrimmage yards during the 2025 season, Atlanta Falcons running back Bijan Robinson has cemented his reputation across the NFL.

Robinson claimed the No. 3 spot in this year's NFL Top 100 list, a 59-spot jump from where he landed last year. He is the second Falcons player named in the NFL Top 100, joining wide receiver Drake London, who appeared at No. 66. Players' votes determine this ranking, indicating just how much respect Robinson has earned from his peers in his first three seasons.

THE BEST OF BIJAN

The Falcons signed Robinson to a three-year extension this offseason, and he is expected to be a focal point for the offense under new coordinator Tommy Rees. Each offseason, Robinson has worked to improve specific elements of his game. Before the 2025 season began, Robinson aimed to produce more explosive runs and long touchdowns. The results were historic. Robinson scored a 93-yard touchdown against the Los Angeles Rams in Week 17, the longest ever by a Falcons running back. He also had an 81-yard house call on a carry against the Buffalo Bills in Week 6. Three of the four longest plays of Robinson's career happened last season.

Under Rees and new head coach Kevin Stefanski, the Falcons are expected to evolve their offense. With Bill Callahan in place as the team's offensive line coach, Atlanta could incorporate more gap and power elements in its run scheme, which has been an outside-zone approach thus far in Robinson's time with the team. In addition to what he can do on the ground, Robinson has also developed as a receiver in his first three seasons. In 2026, he's excited by what he sees as a more diverse screen package from Rees.

"We've been doing the same kind of screen the past year, which has been effective," Robinson said. "I love us having to add more screens, and screens that can go across the play. There are just so many things that we can do with that scheme."

Since he entered the league as the No. 8 overall pick in the 2023 NFL Draft, Robinson has forced more missed tackles than any other player. According to Next Gen Stats, he has made a defender miss 243 times, which puts him just ahead of Derrick Henry, who has 231 missed tackles forced.

text:
What are Guardian Caps? What to know about NFL's concussion-reducing helmet originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia

New helmet protection is sweeping the National Football League .

The NFL announced before the 2024 season that Guardian Caps could be worn by players during regular-season games, a first for the league.

Advertisement

Ahead of Week 8 that season, Miami Dolphins quarterback Tua Tagovailoa made headlines for saying he will not wear the protective gear after returning from another concussion. But a number of other players have started wearing them, and the Guardian Caps have a new, sleeker design for this season.

Here's what to know about Guardian Caps entering the 2026 NFL season:

What are Guardian Caps?

Guardian Caps are soft shell covers on top of helmets that provide extra cushioning and enhanced safety for head-to-head contact.

For 2026, the NFL has approved use of a new Guardian Cap — teams can choose between the Guardian Cap NXT and the Guardian Cap NXT 2.0. The new caps have an "external energy-absorbing layer designed to help reduce impact forces, no interference with helmet fit, vision or mobility and a new sleek surface for customization and team branding."

Advertisement

See the comparison here:

When did the NFL start using Guardian Caps?

The NFL started allowing Guardian Cap usage during the 2022 training camp before making it mandated for some position groups in 2023. That then rolled over to regular-season and postseason practices, and more positions have since been added to the mandate.

For 2026, Guardian Caps are mandatory for all contact practices for all positions except quarterbacks, kickers and punters. They are still optional for games, but at least 25 players wore them in 2025.

Are Guardian Caps required for NFL players?

Guardian Caps are required for all positional groups during practices, except for quarterbacks, kickers and punters. Wide receivers and defensive backs were the last position group added to the mandatory list for 2026 after other groups were required to wear it in prior years.

Advertisement

Guardian Caps remain optional for all players in the regular season.

Are Guardian Caps allowed during regular-season NFL games?

Yes, the NFL authorized their use during regular-season games entering the 2024 season.

After a year of data, the league found that the 2024 season saw the fewest concussions since tracking began nine years earlier. The league was more strict with checking on players in 2025, as there were a record 538 in-game concussion evaluations and 26 medical timeouts.

What are the impacts of wearing a Guardian Cap?

text:
Jonathon Brooks, the Carolina Panthers running back fans love to fantasize about, gave his supporters a scare earlier this week.

On Tuesday, Brooks was held out of team drills with what coach Dave Canales called “general soreness.” Then on Wednesday, the Panthers again held Brooks out of team drills without the actual injury being specified -- they aren’t required to do that until next week, when the NFL’s injury reporting kicks in for Week 1.

But on Wednesday, in his last media availability of the week, Canales issued a positive update on Brooks.

“I’m very optimistic he’ll be available for Week 1,” Canales said.

That would be good news for the Panthers, who have been using AJ Dillon as their top running back this week with usual No. 1 back Chuba Hubbard out with a hamstring injury, No. 2 Brooks out with “general soreness” and No. 3 Trevor Etienne (ankle) out for at least a month.

The veteran Dillon was at one point considered a question mark to make the team; now he looks like a real possibility to get some touches against the Chicago Bears in the season opener Sept. 13 in Charlotte.

However, Canales has now said Brooks and Hubbard both should be available against the Bears.

Brooks, in particular, Panthers fans have dreamed about for years. He was the team’s second-round draft pick in 2024, but has been limited to playing in only three of a possible 34 games in his first two seasons due to two separate ACL tears suffered in his football career. He missed all of last season due to the second one, but has been playing this preseason, where he scored his first NFL touchdown.

T-Mac puts on weight, feels stronger

Panthers wide receiver Tetairoa McMillan said he has gained about 20 pounds this offseason but hasn’t lost any speed. He will play at roughly 220 pounds this season.

“He kind of was just a man on a mission to get stronger, to be able to feel that power in his game,” said Canales, whose Panthers practice again Thursday before taking Friday through Sunday off before ramping up for the Bears game starting on Labor Day. “That really is a part of his game that needed to be addressed, he really wanted to do that and he attacked it. … He’s been great at the line of scrimmage, rugged to the ball, and he’s still got all the same stuff.”

McMillan also accepted his NFL Rookie of the Year award Wednesday from the Pro Football Writers Association, the voice of the professional journalists who cover the NFL. In McMillan’s rookie year, he quickly established himself as Bryce Young’s No. 1 target and finished the season with 70 catches for 1,014 yards and seven touchdowns. However, when asked to rate himself about two-thirds of the way through last season, he gave himself a C+.

McMillan said this season his primary goal is to “win a playoff game.” When asked when the last-second home loss to the L.A. Rams in January had stopped being painful, McMillan said: “I feel like it’s still here. I think I can speak for the rest of the team when I say that as well.”

text:
Reporters crowded the press conference room at the Washington Commanders facility waiting for head coach Dan Quinn and general manager Adam Peters to speak about the team's initial 53-man roster.

Most of them only wanted to ask about one position group, though, and it's the same one the fan base has had since Laremy Tunsil was ruled out for the foreseeable future with a torn triceps: what's going on with the offensive line, and what is the team doing to fix it?

"We had no idea that was coming," Peters joked when asked about the offensive line on the first question.

The group's structure was a talking point throughout camp. Nick Allegretti -- the team's top option at center -- missed most of August with a calf strain. That, along with Tunsil's injury, forced the Commanders to shuffle around the players available to them. Brandon Coleman was moved to tackle, and Julian Good-Jones spent most of the time at center. When Sam Cosmi got sick during the joint practice with the Baltimore Ravens, Good-Jones moved to guard, and draft pick Matt Gulbin played center.

Despite all the movement up front and some formidable opponents appearing early on the schedule, the coaches and offensive linemen remain confident in their ability.

"To have this combination of guys going that way, yeah, [there's] a lot of confidence," Quinn said.

It's worth pointing out that Washington's current mashup of offensive linemen was not the plan the team had in mind. In a perfect world, Tunsil would remain the left tackle, Allegretti would have been on the field for most of camp and the duo of Sam Cosmi and Josh Conerly would have continued building their chemistry together on the right side. The only position that would have been undecided was left guard, but the team felt like it was in a good spot with either Coleman or Chris Paul.

But Tunsil's injury changed all that. The team likes what it has with Coleman at tackle, but that move affected the depth at guard. The uncertainty at guard put a brighter spotlight on the center position, which was already going through some flux with Allegretti's injury.

That's a lot of uncertainty for a position at which Commanders need to be solid this season, but the team is looking at the situation with optimism.

"I'm excited about what we got," Cosmi said following Tuesday's practice. "We can prove everybody wrong, I don't really care about everyone else, to be honest with you. I care about the guys in that room and our ability and what we can do."

Though it is not ideal to move Coleman to tackle and reduce the depth at guard, the Commanders consider themselves fortunate to have the ability to do so. Coleman was the Commanders' starting left tackle during their NFC Championship run and held his own against some quality competition. During their matchup against the Cleveland Browns, Myles Garrett did not record a single stat -- tackle, sack or otherwise -- with Coleman rotating in at left tackle alongside Cornelius Lucas. He was relegated to a backup role once the team traded for Tunsil, but the team feels like he has made progress in both maturity and skill over the past year.

"I think you've seen a young man grow here," Blough said of Coleman. "I think he has demonstrated everything that we're looking for to protect that side for us."

Still, questions have surrounded the position, and the concerns reached high points during the preseason game against the Detroit Lions and joint practice against the Baltimore Ravens. However, as with most things in the preseason, context matters. Teams don't put together comprehensive game plans for preseason opponents, and not all the starting offensive line was on the field for bigger evaluation opportunities.

That doesn't mean the offensive linemen who were on the field get an excuse for not playing well, but it is worth pointing out that Cosmi's illness required more shuffling to an offensive line that had already experienced changes.

"I think it's a huge misconception because I know how much we work," Conerly said. "There's only been so much put out there of the five being out there at once."

Fortunately for the Commanders, it appears that things are beginning to settle on the offensive line. Cosmi is back, which helps stabilize the interior, and Allegretti has returned to practice to take his spot as the starting center. He said in the locker room that he felt good in the days leading up to his return to the field, and that continued into this week. He understands the attention surrounding him and the position, particularly with him being sidelined, but he is not shying away from it. He appreciates the trust the team has placed in him and respects their decision to be cautious with his injury.

"I think I missed more practices in this training camp than I have in my entire career combined," Allegretti said. "So, [I was] trusting that process that we need to be right for September, not August."

Assuming things stay as they are, the Commanders have about 10 days with their offensive line together to get ready for their Week 1 matchup against the Philadelphia Eagles, which has an interior manned by Jalen Carter and Jordan Davis. It's a daunting task for a season-opening opponent, but the Commanders believe there is enough time for Allegretti to get himself ready.

"Not having Nick for most of camp was something we had to work through, but we have a ton of confidence in him," Peters said. "And he's played, I think, 3,000-some-odd snaps in this league. And he's played good football for us before. He went through the whole offseason, so we're really confident. He's not a guy that needs a ton of reps, especially from a mental standpoint."

And, for what it's worth, the Commanders' offensive linemen aren't in panic mode. They're focused on relying on each other to succeed, and they feel good about their odds.

"We're gonna try to be the best five guys on that football field," Cosmi said. "I think, from a relationship from a relationship standpoint, from a communication standpoint, we just have a great group of guys ... I'm excited to go to battle with that versus Philly."

text:
Carolina Panthers running back Jonathon Brooks has been sidelined for the first two practices following the NFL cut-down deadline. But coach Dave Canales doesn't seem too concerned about the third-year running back's status for the Week 1 matchup against the Chicago Bears on Sunday, Sept. 13.

"I'm very optimistic he'll be available for Week 1," Canales said Wednesday.

Brooks has been dealing with "soreness," Canales said Tuesday, but the coach wouldn't specify the location of his current discomfort. Brooks, who is coming off back-to-back ACL surgeries in his right knee, participated in the entire training camp and two preseason games this summer with little issue.

During the first preseason work of his career, Brooks produced 23 rushing yards on eight carries (2.7 yards per carry) and caught one pass for nine yards. He played 17 total preseason snaps, which were his first in-game reps since retearing his right ACL against the Philadelphia Eagles in December 2024 during his rookie season. Brooks, the 46th overall pick in the 2024 NFL draft, initially tore his right ACL while playing for the Texas Longhorns during his final college season in 2023.

Brooks' status is notable considering the injury history within the running back rotation. Veteran starter Chuba Hubbard's 2025 campaign was spoiled by a lingering calf injury, and he spent the bulk of this year's preseason with a hamstring injury. Hubbard, though, returned to practice on Tuesday and worked again on Wednesday.

Brooks is expected to be a key cog in the running back rotation opposite Hubbard this season. Hubbard will be the primary option in the backfield, but Brooks can carve out a larger role with his ability to catch the ball out of the backfield. Hubbard and Brooks can form a tandem similar to last year's duo of Hubbard and Rico Dowdle, who signed with the Pittsburgh Steelers this offseason.

title: Falcons GM Ian Cunningham calls decision to keep four QBs 'a little bit of an insurance policy'
description:
The Falcons haven’t announced a starting quarterback and also have Cooper Rush and undrafted rookie Jack Strand on their 53-man roster at the position.
The turnovers by Tagovailoa may have played a role in Falcons first-year coach Kevin Stefanski waiting to select a regular-season starter.
If Penix starts at Pittsburgh, plays well and shows he is fully recovered from his injury, the Falcons could adjust their 53-man roster and proceed with three quarterbacks.
The decision to carry four quarterbacks left the team with only Bijan Robinson and Brian Robinson at running back.
“I feel like that’s a little bit of the roster gymnastics, right?” Cunningham said.
text:
FLOWERY BRANCH, Ga. -- Atlanta Falcons general manager Ian Cunningham said Wednesday the decision to open the season with four quarterbacks on the 53-man roster was “a little bit of an insurance policy.”

The injury histories and performances of the top two quarterbacks, Michael Penix Jr. and Tua Tagovailoa, made that necessary for the Falcons, who open the season at Pittsburgh on Sept. 13.

The Falcons haven’t announced a starting quarterback and also have Cooper Rush and undrafted rookie Jack Strand on their 53-man roster at the position. When Tagovailoa was slowed at the start of training camp by lower back tightness, the Falcons signed Rush, and Strand had an unexpected opportunity to work with the first-team offense.

“What it did show, it wasn’t too big for him, you know, to come in and do what he did early on,” Cunningham said of Strand before adding the rookie from Division II Minnesota State-Moorhead “showed the ability to just progress and get better ever since.”

Penix did not play in a preseason game as he continued his recovery from a left knee injury which ended his 2025 season. He was cleared to join team drills for the first time last week but was held out of the Falcons' final preseason game at Miami on Friday night.

Tagovailoa, who has a history of concussions, led a touchdown drive but lost a fumbled snap in Atlanta's 17-12 win over the Dolphins. It was Tagovailoa's second fumbled snap in three preseason games -- one from the shotgun and one under center.

The turnovers by Tagovailoa may have played a role in Falcons first-year coach Kevin Stefanski waiting to select a regular-season starter. The return to Miami last week provided a reminder that Tagovailoa was benched for the final three games of his sixth season with the Dolphins last season after he set a career high with 15 interceptions.

Cunningham confirmed on Wednesday there has been no decision on a starter.

The Falcons were 3-6 in Penix's nine starts last season as he completed 60.1% of his passes with nine touchdowns and three interceptions. In two seasons, the 2024 first-round draft pick has 12 touchdown passes with six interceptions.

If Penix starts at Pittsburgh, plays well and shows he is fully recovered from his injury, the Falcons could adjust their 53-man roster and proceed with three quarterbacks.

The decision to carry four quarterbacks left the team with only Bijan Robinson and Brian Robinson at running back. Tyler Goodson is on the 16-player practice squad as the third running back.

“I feel like that’s a little bit of the roster gymnastics, right?” Cunningham said. “It’s four quarterbacks and two running backs. You have to sacrifice at some position. ... And it will probably change throughout the season. Just because we start with this 53 now, it may not be the same 53 that it is, you know, Week 18."

title: Kalshi Stops Its Sports Injury Betting Markets at CFTC's Request - Sportico.com
description:
Kalshi removed betting markets tied to athlete injury durations from its app on Tuesday.
Critics warn injury bets commoditize sensitive medical information, put health care providers at greater risk of harassment and are vulnerable to manipulation.
Kalshi pared back injury betting for much of the summer, and for a while, injury markets tied to Nabers and tennis star Carlos Alcaraz were the only ones visible in Kalshi’s app.
The company appeared to embrace injury betting again in recent weeks by rolling out a wide variety of NFL “player availability” markets.
Kalshi has not said how it will resolve the injury markets it took down from its app that were already live.
text:
Kalshi removed betting markets tied to athlete injury durations from its app on Tuesday. The prediction market company’s federal regulator, the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC), asked it to do so, a source at the agency told Sportico.

As Sportico previously reported, the prediction market company has facilitated at least hundreds of thousands of dollars in wagers connected to player health in 2026, capitalizing on the uncertain statuses of marquee stars like Luka Dončić, Anthony Edwards and Malik Nabers as it collected fees from those bets.

Critics warn injury bets commoditize sensitive medical information, put health care providers at greater risk of harassment and are vulnerable to manipulation.

Kalshi pared back injury betting for much of the summer, and for a while, injury markets tied to Nabers and tennis star Carlos Alcaraz were the only ones visible in Kalshi’s app. The company appeared to embrace injury betting again in recent weeks by rolling out a wide variety of NFL “player availability” markets. Now, the bets have come to a complete stop.

The NFL, one of the few major sports leagues without a prediction market partnership, has expressed concern toward some of the bets Kalshi has offered or proposed, including the injury markets and a plan to allow bets on weather delays. NFL communications director Tim Schlittner told Sportico in an email that the league “made it crystal clear we do not approve of these markets.”

The CFTC declined to comment. Kalshi did not respond to a request for comment.

Unwritten rules

The CFTC does not yet possess specific rules for sports, having only embraced exchange betting on the subject during President Donald Trump’s second term.

The CFTC did propose rules for sports event contracts in June, specifically writing that its preliminary belief is that companies shouldn’t let people bet on markets directly related to injuries. The proposal did not immediately deter Kalshi, which continued to offer those wagers for months before hitting the brakes this week.

In its proposal, the CFTC says injury bets likely “create perverse financial incentives,” raise “public interest concerns about the confidentiality of medical information” and do not provide sufficient manipulation resistance. Yet in practice, the CFTC has not spoken out on the record about Kalshi’s offerings specifically.

The process for listing bets on CFTC exchanges is typically straightforward.

CFTC-registered companies inform the agency of the types of bets they think they might offer, and if the CFTC doesn’t express opposition, the firms list the bets to customers. This process is known as self-certification.

In the details

The titles for Kalshi’s player health markets began with explicit references to injuries. The company self-certified market rules with the headlines “INJURYRETURN” and “NFLINJURYRETURN,” and used those rules for markets such as “Anthony Edwards: Next Game Played” and “Malik Nabers: Next Game Played.”

While the NFL player participation markets from the past couple of weeks were underpinned by rules titled “ATHLETE EVENT,” the “ATHLETE EVENT” filing similarly stipulates that markets resolve to “no” if an athlete is injured for the game in question.

Kalshi has not said how it will resolve the injury markets it took down from its app that were already live. Precedent suggests the markets will pay out based on “fair market value,” meaning the latest odds before the markets disappeared, though the company did not confirm this when Sportico reached out.

Users of Kalshi’s official Discord channel were taken aback by the development.

“So what happens to these positions? can’t even find it in my portfolio now,” wrote one commenter, to which another replied, “Pray for payout.”

Kalshi is believed to be the only CFTC-registered prediction market that has facilitated injury bets. Polymarket’s U.S. exchange self-certified similar markets last month but withdrew the propositions before putting them in its app.

title: Gators in the NFL: Historic Draft Class Heads Into Week 1 - WRUF 98.1 FM
description:
Kickoff for the NFL season is just one week away, and nine players from last season’s Florida football team are set to represent the Gators across the league.
For the first time in school history, Florida football had a player selected in every round of the NFL draft.
Florida has had a pick in every NFL draft since 1967, the longest streak of any SEC program.
On Day 3 of the NFL draft, the Gators special teams unit didn’t disappoint, with kicker Trey Smack and punter Tommy Doman being selected.
Undrafted rookies J. Michael Sturdivant and long snapper Rocco Underwood cap off the group of Gators rookies that made an NFL roster.
text:
Kickoff for the NFL season is just one week away, and nine players from last season’s Florida football team are set to represent the Gators across the league. Throughout OTAs, training camp and the preseason, Florida’s rookies put their skills on display and earned spots on NFL rosters.

For the first time in school history, Florida football had a player selected in every round of the NFL draft. Florida has had a pick in every NFL draft since 1967, the longest streak of any SEC program.

Defensive tackle Caleb Banks was the first Gator taken off the board. Selected No. 18 overall by the Minnesota Vikings, Banks joins a stacked defensive line that finished fourth in total sacks last season.

Preseason action was rocky for Banks, as he recorded just four tackles across 50 preseason snaps. This small sample size hasn’t diminished the confidence that defensive coordinator Brain Flores has in the team’s first-round pick. Banks enters the season as the top nose tackle on the depth chart with hopes of staying healthy after a foot injury limited him to just three games in 2025.

Former AP All-American and first-team All SEC center Jake Slaughter was taken at pick No. 63 by the Los Angeles Chargers after he spent his entire collegiate career with the Gators, starting every game the last two seasons.

His first NFL start is coming quicker than anybody anticipated. Chargers center Tyler Biadasz suffered damage to his ACL in training camp, moving Slaughter up the depth chart. Playing under coach Jim Harbaugh on an offensive line that is finally healthy, Slaughter slides into a great system for him to grow throughout his rookie season.

Slaughter wasn’t the only Florida offensive lineman drafted. Offensive tackle Austin Barber was taken by the Cleveland Browns in round three. Barber started all 12 games last season, recording 750 snaps and earning a PFF run block grade of 82.2.

Barber is listed as a backup to open the season, but his success in the run game has potential for a Browns offense that ranked in the bottom five in yards per carry in 2025.

Flipping back to the defensive side of the ball, cornerback Devin Moore and defensive end George Gumbs Jr. were drafted in rounds four and five, respectively.

Moore joins a Cowboys team with four former Gators and Super Bowl aspirations. Unfortunately for Moore, the Cowboys placed him on injured reserve with an undisclosed injury and he won’t be eligible to return to action until at least Week 5.

Gumbs showcased his athleticism in the preseason, recording a sack in the Colts preseason opener. The Colts have a lot of depth on their defensive front, so don’t expect Gumbs to see much action in the season opener.

On Day 3 of the NFL draft, the Gators special teams unit didn’t disappoint, with kicker Trey Smack and punter Tommy Doman being selected.

Smack was the first kicker selected, marking the fourth time in the modern draft era that the Gators produced the No. 1 kicker in the draft. Smack has made an immediate impact for the Packers, finishing 9-for-9 on field goals including a 59 yard bomb across three preseason games. He is slated to start in Week 1.

Tommy Doman is also listed as a Week 1 starter. Doman was selected in the seventh round by the Bills, but may not see the field much if Josh Allen leads Buffalo to another top-five scoring season.

Undrafted rookies J. Michael Sturdivant and long snapper Rocco Underwood cap off the group of Gators rookies that made an NFL roster. Sturdivant joins Trey Smack III in Green Bay while Underwood heads up north to play with the Eagles.

Here is a list of the draft selections for every Gators rookie in 2026:

Round 1 (Pick 18): Caleb Banks (DT) – Minnesota Vikings

Round 2 (Pick 63): Jake Slaughter (C) – Los Angeles Chargers

Round 3 (Pick 86): Austin Barber (OT) – Cleveland Browns

Round 4 (Pick 114): Devin Moore (CB) – Dallas Cowboys

Round 5 (Pick 156): George Gumbs Jr. (EDGE) – Indianapolis Colts

Round 6 (Pick 216): Trey Smack (K) – Green Bay Packers

Round 7 (Pick 239): Tommy Doman (P) – Buffalo Bills

MONZA, Italy — Isack Hadjar will miss the 2026 Italian Grand Prix, marking his second consecutive race weekend that he’s been sidelined due to an injury.

News broke ahead of the Dutch Grand Prix, the first race after summer break, that Hadjar suffered a wrist injury during the summer break. Liam Lawson was promoted from Racing Bulls to fill the vacant Red Bull seat, while Yuki Tsunoda, the teams’ reserve driver, re-joined the grid as he competed for Racing Bulls.

The same driver line-ups will remain for the Italian GP weekend, both teams confirmed.

Red Bull said Hadjar is making “encouraging progress” in his recovery and it “is closely monitoring his rehabilitation and will take no unnecessary risks with his return to competition and wishes him a speedy recovery.”

While Hadjar continues to recover from his injury, this provides key opportunities for Lawson and Tsunoda to make their cases for being on the grid. Lawson finished the Dutch GP seventh, which looked like the maximum for Red Bull that day, while Tsunoda brought home 11th place for Racing Bulls, just shy of points.

Tsunoda’s main goal remains returning to F1 full-time, though he did say during media day at Zandvoort that he doesn’t want to not be racing. He managed to stay close to teammate Arvid Lindblad’s times, but Monza will be more power-sensitive than Zandvoort, introducing a new challenge to Tsunoda in this new regulation era.

Lawson, meanwhile, has been making a strong case during his Racing Bulls chapter and proved to be solid in the new Red Bull machinery — a stark contrast to the races he did in Red Bull colours last season.

text:
The Commanders need solid play from Brandon Coleman: The young tackle pencils in as Washington's blindside protector with Laremy Tunsil out.

The Lions will rely upon secondary contributors on both sides: Center Juice Scruggs and safety Avonte Maddox will play sneakily significant roles for Detroit, especially early in the season.

With the 2026 NFL preseason wrapped up, the roster cutdown deadline having passed and the calendar turning to September, teams are all systems go on getting set for the regular season. Besides the return of fully meaningful football itself, the best part about a new year is a fresh slate for all 32 organizations.

However, a glut of teams have already been knocked down from full strength in the health department. Indeed, numerous clubs will have to navigate multi-week or even season-ending losses suffered in training camp or the preseason, already putting them a bit behind the eight ball. Also complicating the picture are players who have been suspended or placed on the Commissioner’s Exempt List, with several stars set to be out for months on end.

In the wake of absences, the 10 players below carry extra — and perhaps unexpected — magnitude in driving their team’s 2026 outcome.

T Brandon Coleman, Washington Commanders

The Commanders are hopeful for a rebound campaign after a dismal 2025 season that saw them finish 5-12 after reaching the NFC championship the year before. Unfortunately for Washington, the team is already without elite tackle Laremy Tunsil, who suffered a torn triceps in early August.

There’s no easy fix for losing the sixth-most valuable tackle by PFF Wins Above Replacement since 2022, but Coleman will look to fill Tunsil’s void. The former third-round pick has played 1,240 career snaps at left tackle over his two pro seasons, producing a 62.9 overall PFF grade in his career. Perhaps encouraging is that Coleman looked better in the preseason, notching a 76.3 PFF pass-blocking grade — a performance the Commanders will need over a larger sample if they want to return to glory.

S Xavier Woods, ChicagoBears

The Bears entered the second season of the Ben Johnson era with improved aspirations after making the NFC divisional round in 2025. However, Chicago has endured a slew of defensive injuries, including losing free-agent addition Coby Bryant for most of the year with a knee issue.

Consequently, the Bears signed Woods, who is poised to step into a starting role next to first-round pick Dillon Thieneman. The 31-year-old veteran sported a 65.5 overall PFF grade across 526 snaps with the Titans last year, although he was effective in coverage. Indeed, Woods’ 70.3 PFF coverage grade sat in the 83rd percentile. Woods will look to keep that consistency after a down 2024 season in Carolina, especially on a Bears defense with lots of question marks.

S Avonte Maddox, Detroit Lions

The Lions’ quest for redemption after missing the playoffs has already endured numerous roadblocks. A quintessential part of that is having both Kerby Joseph (knee) and Brian Branch (Achilles) still working their way back from season-ending injuries in 2025 and landing on the physically unable to perform list.

With both starting safeties out for at least the first four games of 2026, players like Maddox become that much more important. The former Eagle turned heads in reserve work for Detroit last year, generating a 79.1 overall PFF grade over 342 snaps. Impressively, Maddox notched a 75.0-plus grade in both coverage and run defense while primarily operating as the team’s true free safety. If he can sustain that level of play, it will go a long way for Detroit’s battered defense.

EDGE Princely Umanmielen, Carolina Panthers

The Panthers have been victimized by injury arguably more than any other team before the season has begun, losing both starting tackles for the initial weeks of the year as well as second-year edge defender Nic Scourton due to a torn ACL. Now, players like Umanmielen will be asked to do even more.

A third-round pick in 2025, Umanmielen had a tough time acclimating in his rookie campaign. Over 235 snaps, he posted just a 49.5 overall PFF grade. Umanmielen’s PFF pass-rush and run-defense grades both fell below the 24th percentile as well. Down Scourton and his 37 pressures, Umanmielen will be tasked with offering complementary pass-rush next to big-ticket addition Jaelan Phillips.

EDGE Samson Ebukam, Atlanta Falcons

The start to a new league year hasn’t been especially kind to the Falcons either. On top of enduring a quarterback debate, Atlanta has lost second-year pass-rushers Jalon Walker (torn ACL) and James Pearce Jr. (suspension) for at least half of 2026.

The Falcons’ depth at edge defender is considerably thinner, which has elevated names like Ebukam. The former Ram, 49er and Colt joined the franchise on a one-year deal this offseason as projected depth but could see a lion’s share of starting snaps. Ebukam’s 60.1 PFF pass-rush grade and 10.2% pass-rush win rate were both in no better than the 36th percentile last year as he returned from an Achilles tear, but the Falcons will hope to see more of his pre-injury self.

C Juice Scruggs, Detroit Lions

Detroit’s defense has been especially besieged by injury in recent seasons, but its offense also endured a big blow when starting center Cade Mays fractured a bone in his wrist during training camp. With Mays out for at least the first four weeks of the year, Scruggs could step up to fill his absence.

Acquired by the Lions this offseason in the deal for running back David Montgomery, Scruggs has occupied all three interior offensive line slots throughout his pro career, but he only played center in 2024. That season happened to be his best as a pro with a 63.5 overall PFF grade, which placed 17th among qualified centers. Scruggs will look to bounce back in a new ecosystem after a trying 2025 saw him earn a 40.5 PFF run-blocking grade and let up 11 pressures on 202 opportunities.

EDGE Dani Dennis-Sutton, Green Bay Packers

When the Packers picked Dennis-Sutton in the fourth round, the team figured it had landed a high-upside depth piece during his rookie season. But with Micah Parsons expected to miss the first six weeks of 2026 while recovering from an ACL tear, Dennis-Sutton could be thrown into the spotlight sooner than projected.

Dennis-Sutton was consistently excellent throughout a four-year stint at Penn State, earning at least a 75.0 PFF pass-rush grade every season while compiling 147 total pressures. He transferred that talent in his first taste of the preseason, collecting five pressures on 22 pass-rushing snaps against the Cardinals. Down Parsons in an edge defender room without many proven talents, Dennis-Sutton looms as an X-factor on a Packers defensive line facing initial questions.

RB MarShawn Lloyd, Green Bay Packers

On top of Parsons starting the year on the PUP list, Green Bay also confronts the loss of Josh Jacobs. The Pro Bowl running back was placed on the Commissioner’s Exempt List stemming from an offseason domestic violence dispute, and his return date (or potential suspension length) is unknown.

With Jacobs’ status up in the air, the Packers figure to turn to Lloyd in their backfield. The former third-round pick has been devastated by injury to start his career, appearing on just 10 regular-season offensive snaps through two pro seasons. Lloyd looked solid with a 72.2 PFF rushing grade in his final preseason contest, and his efficacy and health should define how well the Packers’ offense fares in the first few weeks of 2026.

EDGE Jonah Elliss, DenverBroncos

The Broncos return the nucleus of their stingy defense in 2025, including a defensive line that’s one of the foremost in the league. However, standout edge defender Jonathon Cooper is out for an undetermined amount of time after also being placed on the Commissioner’s Exempt List.

Sans Cooper and his 176 pressures since 2023, the Broncos will have to turn to their front-four depth, which includes Elliss. The 2024 third-round pick has appeared on 811 snaps as a pro, amassing 44 pressures and 29 stops in the process as a backup. If Elliss can improve upon his 61.8 PFF pass-rush grade as a second-year player, it would help offset the loss of Cooper and John Franklin-Myers along Denver’s defensive line.

WR Devaughn Vele, New Orleans Saints

The Saints have warranted major anticipation this season, largely courtesy of a strong offseason. At the center of that is eighth overall pick Jordyn Tyson, although the touted rookie will now miss a considerable portion of the year due to a hamstring injury.

title: Christopher Nowinski, PhD's Post - LinkedIn

Our new JAMA Network Open study shows that autopsy proven #CTE is associated with worse objectively measured cognitive function.
Our study identified limitations related to the NFL Concussion Settlement’s testing program.
Many players who had cognitive impairment on standardized testing, and were ultimately confirmed to have CTE at autopsy, did not meet the settlement's criteria for cognitive impairment.
As a result, the current BAP testing program is likely suboptimal in the identification of former players deserving of support.
Hopefully these findings will inform revisions to the BAP testing program to better align with clinical care standards in order to maximize support to the players in need.
text: Our new JAMA Network Open study shows that autopsy proven #CTE is associated with worse objectively measured cognitive function. Of those with CTE, 63% had impaired memory test performance. Cognitive impairments were more common in high stage CTE (Figure 3). Led by Boston University School of Medicine PhD student Anna Aaronson, this study provides a window into the types and frequency of objectively defined cognitive impairments that can result from CTE. #Neuropsychological evaluation remains a cornerstone to the accurate diagnosis of neurodegenerative diseases, making this a timely study to our efforts to diagnose CTE during life. 🚨There is more to the story🚨 To accomplish our primary objective of characterizing the cognitive profile of CTE, we examined 33 National Football League (NFL) players who were diagnosed with CTE at autopsy and completed the NFL Concussion Settlement’s testing program during life known as the baseline assessment program (BAP). This testing program involves standard paper and pencil neuropsychological testing that is used to inform if players should be compensated for neurological problems related to their football play. Read about it here: https://lnkd.in/gj8Qc-4a The program has been criticized for requiring overly strict and prescriptive algorithms for making cognitive diagnoses and associated determinations of whether NFL players should receive compensation and support for their neurological problems. Our study identified limitations related to the NFL Concussion Settlement’s testing program. Many players who had cognitive impairment on standardized testing, and were ultimately confirmed to have CTE at autopsy, did not meet the settlement's criteria for cognitive impairment. Seven participants had advanced CTE (stage 3 or 4). Six showed cognitive impairment on testing, yet all seven received the BAP's lowest impairment rating (Level 0) and thus would not come close to qualifying for a monetary award (Level 1.5 is needed). The settlement's diagnostic algorithm differs from the clinical standards typically used to diagnose cognitive disorders. As a result, the current BAP testing program is likely suboptimal in the identification of former players deserving of support. Hopefully these findings will inform revisions to the BAP testing program to better align with clinical care standards in order to maximize support to the players in need. Link: https://lnkd.in/gqebfgM2 Thanks to all co-authors, particularly the Boston University CTE Center research staff and the team of #neuropsychologists who came together across many different institutions: Sophia Nosek, Bobak Abdolmohammadi, Jadeynne Hadley, Jacob Labonte, Madeline Uretsky Resnick, MS, Sydney Mosaheb, MS, Caroline Altaras, PhD, Sarah Banks, William Barr, Ph.D., ABPP, Kristen Dams-O'Connor, PhD, Gabrielle Hromas, Jennifer Wethe, PhD, ABPP-CN, Robert Stern

title: Intriguing QB Target Should Have Vikings' Attention With J.J. McCarthy Injury Expected to Linger
description:
Kyler Murray, Carson Wentz, J.J. McCarthy and Max Brosmer made for a crowded quarterback room.
On the other hand, McCarthy is dealing with a complicated and controversial injury.
Now, with depth on the active roster suddenly lacking, recently released quarterback Joe Milton III could be exactly what the Vikings are looking for.
J.J. McCarthy's injury makes timing right for a QB addition McCarthy sat out the Vikings' final preseason game against the Denver Broncos with an ankle injury that he sustained against the Baltimore Ravens in Week 2 of the preseason.
The injury was made to sound minor, with McCarthy opting to sit out due to discomfort.
text:
The Minnesota Vikings announced their initial 53-man roster on Sunday, and the biggest surprise from the list was how the team included four quarterbacks, while it is normal to carry two or three into a season. Kyler Murray, Carson Wentz, J.J. McCarthy and Max Brosmer made for a crowded quarterback room.

Things have changed since then. Brosmer was released on Monday, and after clearing waivers was predictably signed to the Vikings' practice squad. On the other hand, McCarthy is dealing with a complicated and controversial injury.

Now, with depth on the active roster suddenly lacking, recently released quarterback Joe Milton III could be exactly what the Vikings are looking for.

J.J. McCarthy's injury makes timing right for a QB addition

McCarthy sat out the Vikings' final preseason game against the Denver Broncos with an ankle injury that he sustained against the Baltimore Ravens in Week 2 of the preseason. The injury was made to sound minor, with McCarthy opting to sit out due to discomfort.

Now, McCarthy's injury has escalated to the point where ESPN's Adam Schefter talked about the situation during Monday's appearance on "The Pat McAfee Show." The NFL insider stated that McCarthy could miss multiple weeks. If that is the case, he is a candidate to be placed on the short-term injured reserve to start the season.

If Brosmer is on the practice squad and McCarthy is on short-term IR, Minnesota could search for a quality QB3 to put on the 53-man roster. And Milton is a great fit.

Milton is a third-year quarterback who was a sixth-round pick in 2024. During his rookie year with the New England Patriots, he gained national attention when he entered their regular season finale against the Buffalo Bills and was ultra-impressive.

In that game against Buffalo, he completed 22 of his 29 pass attempts for 241 yards and a touchdown. He also showed his athleticism and elusiveness by scrambling 10 times for 16 yards and another touchdown.

After the season, the Patriots traded Milton and a seventh-round pick to the Dallas Cowboys in exchange for a fifth-round pick. He immediately became Dak Prescott's backup but struggled to recreate his success in New England, going 15-for-24 for 183 yards, one touchdown, and two interceptions in four games while adding 50 yards on five rushing attempts.

Why Milton fits with the Vikings

If the Vikings are interested in adding a high-potential backup to evaluate while McCarthy is out of action, Milton is an interesting option. A six-foot-five, 236-pound quarterback is already impressive, but seeing what he did as a rookie in New England shows the potential he has to become a solid player for Minnesota if given the opportunity.

Milton offers a skill set that is completely different from Wentz's. A veteran who prefers being in the pocket, Wentz is an old-school quarterback, while Milton fits more of what the modern NFL wants from a passer.

There is some irony in how Dallas chose to go with Sam Howell as their backup quarterback for Prescott this year and opted to cut Milton. Vikings fans will remember the draft-day trade that sent Howell to the Vikings to potentially back up McCarthy last season, but he was traded to the Eagles when the experiment didn't work out.

text:
CLEVELAND, OHIO (TheOBR.com) -

Good morning, Cleveland Browns fans!

THE DAILY BLOVIATION

I'm a numbers guy. I like data. In college, I specialized in digital and satellite communications, wrestling ones and zeros from background static using math and statistics.

I don't remember a damn bit of it now.

I thought it was cool back then, though, which may explain why I spent so many Saturday nights date-less. I spent a little too much time trying to figure out Fourier Transforms, but not quite enough, so I sort of stumbled through grad school lacking in top-flight engineering and social skills both. I liked engineering, but I really liked beer and chasing girls, too. I wasn't very good at either.

At any rate, I noticed this morning that The Athletic ran a story noting how exceptional it was for five teams out of the 32 to have four quarterbacks on their roster or cleverly stashed away on a four-game IR.

Atlanta, Pittsburgh, Philadelphia and Minnesota have four rostered. Cleveland gets an asterisk: three on the 53 and Dillon Gabriel on IR designated to return, which is four bodies in the building and one of them legally unavailable until Week 5. League-wide, teams are averaging 2.75 quarterbacks. That used to be two and a clipboard.

It seems to me like more and more teams are stashing away quarterbacks and we might have a developing trend here. If I can spot a developing trend before anyone else, that allows me to get ahead of the curve and play the Polymarkets or something. Or write a bloviation about it. So, I got a little over-excited at the idea of writing about this developing trend.

So, I added up the number of quarterbacks on injured reserve over the past ten years, courtesy of Sportrac.

Here it is:

2016 14

2017 17

2018 10

2019 18

2020 9

2021 16

2022 11

2023 13

2024 11

2025 15

The only one under double digits was 2020, when QBs who came down with COVID weren't designated as IR. There are already four this year, including Dillon Gabriel

So, these are a lot of injured quarterbacks, but not a real trend of increasing injuries pushing teams to increase the number of quarterbacks on the roster.

In all situations where four are being rostered, per the Athletic, there's generally a quality consideration. The Browns' four quarterbacks are all unproven, or proven to not be that good. The Falcons still haven't really figured out who the starter will be, and Jack Strand was good enough they wanted to keep him. The Steelers are led by a brittle social security-eligible geezer, and they like Will Howard and Drew Allar enough to keep them. Plus, Mason Rudolph is needed because his thoroughly punchable face brings in 15-yard Unsportsmanlike Conduct penalties. The Vikings count, too, but I don't know a lot about that situation because it reminds me of the Browns, which I find frightening. Interestingly, another that kept four was the Eagles because they liked fifth-rounder Cole Payton.

So, overall, we have a trend of quarterbacks on the roster generally increasing, but no hard evidence that IR designations are spiking to explain it.

As a result, I have two theories. One, there are fewer quarterbacks that teams can trust, so they keep more rolls of the dice available to them. That certainly seems to be the case in Cleveland. Or they're rostering a youngster like Strand or Taylen Green because quarterback is complicated to play these days and they need time to develop them.

This seems more the case for me. As the NFL gets more and more passing-oriented, the job gets harder and harder. Quarterbacks need to be not only strong of arm and fleet of foot, but they also need to diagnose a play like a supercomputer and act on the developing play in split seconds. It takes a long time to nurture those skills, so teams are finding them harder to locate and requiring more time to develop.

Hence, more quarterbacks on the rosters as time goes on.

That's my theory, and I feel good about it. Now, if only there were a way to turn that knowledge into money. Then again, I figured creating a media outlet to cover the sure-to-be-exciting on-field exploits of the sure-to-be-successful Cleveland Browns was a nifty career move.

Maybe I'm not the right guy to ask about stuff like this.

Have a good one! GO BROWNS!

text:
By Adam Cooke

With the NFL season rapidly approaching, professional football will boast red and yellow from coast to coast. 23 former Terps are officially set to suit up for the 2026 regular season, which kicks off next week. From all-time greats to recent graduates, here is where you can find the location of all Maryland alumni in the NFL this year.

Welcome home, Stefon (and more)

All-time Maryland great Stefon Diggs returns to the DMV. The wide receiver joined the Washington Commanders, the fifth team of his career, on a one-year, $8 million contract.

The 32-year-old enters his 12th NFL season after one year in New England. Diggs tallied 1,013 yards in the regular season and contributed to the Patriots’ Super Bowl appearance. He was released in March with two years left on his deal.

Joining Diggs in the national capital is Chig Okonkwo, who had a productive four-year stint with the Titans. He signed with the Commanders in free agency. The 2022 Maryland graduate enters a three-year contract as Washington’s top tight end.

Bowie product Nick Cross also signed with Washington in March. He started at safety in every game for Indianapolis over the past two years, recording three interceptions in the 2024 season.

Defensive tackle Byron Cowart made four tackles in a preseason loss to Baltimore. The 2019 graduate was named to the Commanders’ practice squad.

The recent graduates

Jalen Huskey was Maryland’s sole pick in the 2026 NFL Draft. He signed with the Jaguars as a third-round pick and was named to the 53-man roster. The rookie will likely earn limited minutes behind Jacksonville’s current veterans at safety.

Huskey graduated from College Park this past spring. The Frederick, Maryland, native transferred to College Park after playing for Bowling Green in his first two collegiate seasons, and he was a second team All-Big Ten selection in his junior season.

Additionally, 2026 alum Alan Herron was selected to New Orleans’ practice squad. The Saints signed the undrafted offensive lineman in April, after he was selected as honorable mention all-Big Ten as a senior.

Potential starters

DJ Moore benefited from great quarterback play in his final year with the Chicago Bears and now teams up with an even greater one in Josh Allen in Buffalo. After claiming the NFC North with the Bears, he was traded to the Bills in March. He enters his first year of a four-year, $110 million extension.

Former Terp and 2023 first-round pick Deonte Banks continues to shine with the New York Giants. Banks has

made 35 starts across 45 appearances in his first three seasons, and he will compete for a secondary cornerback spot.

Jordan Phillips made 34 tackles on the defensive line during his rookie season in Miami. The Dolphins selected Phillips in the fifth round in 2025, and he played in 16 of 17 games.

Offensive lineman Spencer Anderson enters year four in Pittsburgh. He appeared in every game for the Steelers over the past two seasons, making seven starts in his 2025 campaign.

DJ Glaze has appeared in every game, starting all but three, for the Raiders after being selected in the third round in 2024. Whether it’s Kirk Cousins or Fernando Mendoza who gets the nod in Las Vegas, Glaze will be a valuable part of the protection crew.

Defensive end Sam Okuayinonu is set to begin his third season in the Bay Area. Okuayinonu made 15 appearances with the 49ers last season and started in 12 of them, and he has 74 tackles over his young career.

Tarheeb Still battled a minor injury in the summer, but returned to Chargers practice in mid-August. He started 13 games at cornerback last season and will continue battling for an established starting role.

Chad Ryland remains Arizona’s kicker in his third year with the team and fourth overall in the league. Ryland was selected by the Patriots in 2023 and has made 69 field goals over three seasons.

Others who made the 53

Ty Johnson is entering his eighth year in the league, four of which have been spent in Buffalo. He rushed for three touchdowns last year and now enters the second year of a two-year contract.

Corey Bullock was picked up on waivers by the Panthers and was named to Carolina’s roster after being waived on Monday by Baltimore. The versatile offensive lineman appeared in 16 games with the Ravens last season.

Receiver Tai Felton made three catches across 17 games for the Vikings in his rookie season. He returns to Minneapolis as an athletic third or fourth wide receiver option.

Jeshaun Jones returned two punts in one appearance with the Vikings last season. The 2024 Maryland graduate and native Floridian enters year two in Minnesota.

Josh Woods, a 2018 graduate, was added to Atlanta’s 53-man roster on Monday. The linebacker signed a one-year contract to stay with the Falcons in July.

Dante Trader Jr. earned snaps in all 17 games for the Dolphins last season. Entering his sophomore campaign in Miami, he’s expected to receive more defensive snaps and compete for a starting role.

Jakorian Bennett was placed on the injured reserve with a knee injury and will miss at least four games. The cornerback appeared in 11 games in 2025, his first season with the Eagles, having spent his first two years in Las Vegas.

Practice squad additions

Tackle Gottlieb Ayedze signed with the Dolphins in June and was named to Miami’s practice squad. The Germantown native competed in the UFL this spring.

Former Terps center Josh Kaltenberger enters year two on the Chargers’ practice squad. He was signed as an undrafted free agent in 2025.

Not rostered

Darnell Savage Jr. appeared in games for four teams across seven years in the NFL. The Steelers picked up the safety in March then decided to release him in early August.

Ruben Hyppolite II, a 2025 graduate, was selected in the fourth round by Chicago and appeared in seven games. The Bears waived him with an injury designation on Sunday.

The 2026 season is slated to kick off on Sept. 9 in Seattle, as the defending champion Seattle Seahawks play host to the New England Patriots in a Super Bowl LX rematch. It’s an exciting new season for the 23 Maryland alumni who call the NFL their home.

text:
BOSTON —

Newly published research conducted at Boston University examined the cognitive symptoms of NFL players who were confirmed to have chronic traumatic encephalopathy after death and found that a common diagnostic test might underrate the severity of impairments suffered by players with CTE.

The study, which was published in JAMA Network Open, examined 33 NFL players who had taken a baseline test while they were alive and were later diagnosed with CTE through autopsies. According to a BU spokesperson, the Baseline Assessment Program was created as part of the NFL Concussion Settlement's testing program and consists of a standardized paper-and-pencil battery of neuropsychological tests.

According to the researchers, the comparison identified potential limitations for the testing program. Six of the participants who were found to have advanced CTE also showed a measurable cognitive impairment on testing but received the lowest impairment rating on the BAP.

The research concluded that differences between the scoring rules established by the settlement and clinical standards may contribute to "suboptimal identification of former players deserving of support."

"This is the largest study of its kind to directly link the amount of CTE pathology found at autopsy with objective cognitive testing during life," said Anna Aaronson, lead author and a PhD student at the Boston University CTE Center. "These findings provide an important roadmap for recognizing CTE in living patients."

"The BAP's diagnostic criteria might miss cases of cognitive impairment that are objectively measurable and associated with confirmed CTE pathology," said Michael Alosco, PhD, co-director of clinical research at the BU CTE Center. "This has important implications for former players seeking diagnosis and potential compensation through the NFL Concussion Settlement."
