text:
Teams across the league continue managing injuries and fine-tuning rosters as the regular season inches closer.

San Francisco 49ers running back Christian McCaffrey was back at practice Tuesday, while Chicago Bears general manager Ryan Poles addressed ongoing uncertainty surrounding cornerback Kyler Gordon's return.

New England Patriots running back TreVeyon Henderson remains sidelined while rehabilitating an ankle injury and when Pittsburgh Steelers Joey Porter Jr. was asked about whether or not he will play for the Steelers in Week 1, he responded, "I don't know."

Keep up with the latest news from around the league on Tuesday.

After weeks of speculation, San Francisco 49ers running back Christian McCaffrey is back on the field practicing. He was seen on a Tuesday afternoon making cuts and looking explosive during team drills, showing he's ready for the Week 1 opener.

McCaffrey missed more than two weeks of training camp while dealing with what was described as general "tightness." It’s unclear if the issue was related to the Achilles tendinitis that sidelined him in 2024 or simply a precaution for other injuries he’s dealt with over his career.

However, this should be an encouraging sign as he looks fully healthy heading into Australia, when the 49ers take on the Los Angeles Rams in Week 1.

McCaffrey is coming off the heaviest workload season of his career, accumulating a career-high 413 total touches. He logged 311 rushes for 1,202 yards and 10 touchdowns, while adding 102 receptions for 924 yards and seven touchdowns in the passing game.

If McCaffrey stays healthy, the 49ers offense could make serious noise in a competitive NFC West. The additions of Mike Evans and rookie De’Zhaun Stribling, alongside a healthy McCaffrey and Brock Purdy, make this offense one of the most intriguing units in the league.

Chicago Bears general manager Ryan Poles expressed uncertainty Tuesday regarding when defensive back Kyler Gordon will return to action as he continues to recover from a lingering calf injury. Gordon, who signed a three-year, $40 million contract extension in April 2025, has appeared in just five games since signing the deal and has been sidelined throughout the entire offseason.

When asked Tuesday if he envisions Gordon playing for Chicago during the upcoming 2026 season, Poles offered a guarded response.

"I don't know. I would hope so," Poles said to reporters Tuesday. "I still have hope there. He's going to have to continue to work hard and get back to playing."

Poles declined to provide specifics on Gordon's recovery process, confirming that the defensive back is working with team trainers while also consulting outside medical personnel.

"When people come back from injuries, there's different things that happen," Poles said. "Sometimes they return fast, sometimes they're slow. So it's really a timing thing and a healing thing and a confidence thing. Anytime you have an injury and you're coming back from something, there's discomfort that you have to push through, and that's what it comes down to. So we haven't been able to get over that hump, and we're not progressing as fast as we would like."

As Gordon remains on the reserve list, the Bears made additional roster moves Tuesday.

Chicago placed safety Coby Bryant and tight end Hayden Large on injured reserve, leaving open the flexibility to designate both for return later in the season. To fill those roster spots, the Bears signed defensive tackle James Lynch and linebacker Jack Sanborn to the active 53-man roster.

Pittsburgh Steelers cornerback Joey Porter Jr. returned to practice on Tuesday after dealing with a back injury, but remained noncommittal about whether he will play in the season opener without a new contract.

Entering the final year of his rookie contract, Porter addressed his Week 1 availability when asked if he would suit up against the Atlanta Falcons on Sept. 13.

"I don't know," Porter said. "I've got to talk to the front office and my agents about that one."

General manager Omar Khan stated Monday that the team wants Porter to remain with the franchise long-term, but Pittsburgh holds a long-standing policy of ceasing all contract negotiations once the regular season begins. While Porter acknowledged that navigating the business side has been difficult, he noted that teammates and coaches have offered support as he continues preparing.

"I could hope and think all day, but it’s really up to the front office and what they want to do with this team," Porter said. "So all I can do is just show up every day to work and be prepared."

New England Patriots running back TreVeyon Henderson hasn’t practiced in over a week due to an ankle injury suffered in training camp. It’s an injury that has flown under the radar, especially with Ashton Jeanty also grabbing headlines after suffering a scary ankle injury of his own.

Henderson returned to Patriots practice on Tuesday afternoon but has not yet been cleared for full participation, ESPN first reported. While he continues to rehab a right ankle injury on the side, he was seen walking normally in the locker room, but his Week 1 status is unclear.

He is coming off a productive rookie season in the Patriots offense. On just 180 carries, Henderson racked up 911 yards and nine touchdowns, while adding 35 receptions for 221 receiving yards and a score in the pass game.

If Henderson can’t suit up next Wednesday night against the Seattle Seahawks, Rhamondre Stevenson is expected to see a full workload. Even though Stevenson is already the featured back, he could turn into a true three-down workhorse early in the season.

title: Brian Gutekunst offers encouraging Micah Parsons update and more Packers observations
description:
Tight end Tucker Kraft returned to practice this summer around eight and a half months after his surgery.
The Packers signed the veteran tight end in part because Luke Musgrave (neck) is starting the season on the PUP list.
“He can kind of do everything you ask of a tight end.
The Packers traded for running back Kaleb Johnson from the Pittsburgh Steelers and tight end Mark Redman from the Los Angeles Rams.
The fourth-year tight end suffered a neck injury this offseason and missed all of camp.
text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. — Tuesday was an action-packed day full of newsy tidbits at Lambeau Field.

Let’s dive into the most notable things we learned, aside from what general manager Brian Gutekunst said about running back Josh Jacobs.

1. Micah Parsons might be on the field sooner than we thought.

Gutekunst said the Packers have a “pretty good idea” that Parsons will be “pretty close” to playing once his mandated four games on the physically unable to perform list are up. The Packers’ top edge rusher and best player overall tore his ACL last Dec. 14 and also suffered a meniscus injury that required surgery on Dec. 29.

“I’m going to be pretty cautious with that. We’ve got a big investment there,” Gutekunst said. “It’s really important to what we’re trying to do. To accomplish the goals we want to late in the year, he’s going to need to be at his best. So I want to make sure that that happens. But he’s eager. There’s a new rule this year where we can open their window to practice after the second game. I imagine when that time comes, there’s going to be some conversations about things … because he’s going to be really eager to get out there.”

The Packers typically have a nine-month, no-football rule for players rehabbing torn ACLs. Tight end Tucker Kraft returned to practice this summer around eight and a half months after his surgery. Parsons’ nine-month mark post-surgery is the Tuesday before Green Bay’s Week 4 visit to Tampa Bay, so practicing in Week 3 would also beat that timeline.

2. Jonnu Smith is a wise man at 31 years old, and he thinks he has plenty left in the tank.

The Packers signed the veteran tight end in part because Luke Musgrave (neck) is starting the season on the PUP list. Smith’s nine years in the league make him wise on the field, but he showed his smarts off it when he sat next to quarterback Jordan Love in his first team meeting.

“That’s a vet move,” said head coach Matt LaFleur, who was the Tennessee Titans’ offensive coordinator in 2018 when Smith was a second-year player for the Titans.

Smith may be on the wrong side of 30, but just two years ago, he caught 88 passes for 884 yards and eight touchdowns for the Miami Dolphins. LaFleur said Smith still runs well and at 6 feet, 3 inches and 248 pounds, Smith said his size advantages and catch-and-run ability benefit him out of the slot.

“He’s really versatile,” Gutekunst said. “He can kind of do everything you ask of a tight end. He can line up on the line of scrimmage. He can move. He can be one of the move guys in the backfield. Been a tremendous receiver in this league for a long time from the tight end position.”

After playing for the likes of former Steelers offensive coordinator Arthur Smith in Pittsburgh and former Dolphins head coach Mike McDaniel in Miami, Smith estimated he’s played in an iteration of the Shanahan/LaFleur/etc. offense seven out of his 10 years in the league and that will help him acclimate with less than two weeks until the season opener.

“I’ve got a lot of football left in me, man, a lot of football left in me,” Smith said. “I’m grateful for every snap because I know how dangerous this game can be. I’ve got a lot of ball left in me and I’m excited to show it, for sure.”

3. MarShawn Lloyd is eager for his turn in the spotlight.

The Packers’ new starting running back didn’t miss a practice this summer after playing in just one game over his first two years in the league. Finally equipped with a clean bill of health, Lloyd is primed to show off the explosiveness, speed and shiftiness that made the Packers keep faith in him.

“I’m ready to play as much as they want me to play,” Lloyd said. “I’m excited. It’s a dream come true playing for the Packers, so however much carries I get, however much they put me in the game, I’m ready to go.”

Lloyd averaged fewer than 10 carries per game and barely more than 10 in his final year at USC. He has only seven touches in the NFL since Green Bay drafted him in the third round two years ago. Lloyd said he hasn’t shouldered a significant load since high school, but he might have to now with Jacobs on the commissioner exempt list.

“You never in 100 years think something like this will happen,” Lloyd said. “You gotta be ready and the coaches have been able to help me to be ready.”

Despite the disturbing allegations against Jacobs, Lloyd threw his full support behind him.

“I don’t know what’s going on, but that’s my brother, so I just gotta stay on that forever,” Lloyd said. “He’s helped me when I was in the worst part of my life really, those last two years.”

4. Two other new guys will play important roles for the Packers’ offense.

The Packers traded for running back Kaleb Johnson from the Pittsburgh Steelers and tight end Mark Redman from the Los Angeles Rams.

Similar to Smith, Johnson is familiar with the Packers’ offense because he played for Arthur Smith in Pittsburgh last season as a rookie. Johnson also said there are similarities between Green Bay’s outside zone running game and what he ran at Iowa under Hawkeyes OC Tim Lester. LaFleur, who called Johnson “really good at the outside zone stuff,” said he’s talked to Lester about Johnson since Lester was a senior analyst for the Packers in 2023.

Lloyd said Johnson’s size — 6 feet, 1 inch and 224 pounds — impressed him. That frame might lend itself well to pass protection, a trait vital for backup running backs that Johnson touted when asked about his skill set.

Redman stands 6 feet, 5 inches and 258 pounds. He knows exactly what his role is, and it’s not to catch passes. Gutekunst said the Packers have been looking for a Y tight end who can move people in the run game and protect the quarterback.

“I’m an in-line tight end that’s going to block at the point of attack,” Redman said. “And that’s what I’m coming here to do. So just kind of embracing that role, just get dirty, and finish some blocks and stuff like that. I think I put it on tape in the preseason and that’s what I like to do. Hopefully that’s what they’ll use me for.”

Redman is also familiar with this system because he spent his rookie year last season on the Rams’ practice squad. Mike LaFleur was also the Rams’ offensive coordinator under Sean McVay.

“Got here and J.D. (tight ends coach John Dunn) started talking about the offense and I was like, ‘Wait, I know that play (and) I know that play,’” Redman said. “Obviously there’s going to be some new stuff … a lot of it’s carryover, so it’s pretty nice to be able to go out there and play Day 1.”

5. Defensive tackle Warren Brinson has a “good chance” to play in Week 1, Gutekunst said.

Brinson had a fantastic first couple weeks of camp before injuring his calf while warming up for the Packers’ second preseason game in Denver. He’s been out since and was the only player on the active roster not practicing on Tuesday.

The Packers used their two cutdown-day injured reserve spots on wide receiver Savion Williams and edge Collin Oliver. Williams has a high-ankle sprain and Gutekunst said he should be ready once his four-game window is up. Oliver was listed with a calf injury — Gutekunst said it’s an Achilles tendon issue — and the GM said Oliver should be ready even before his four games are up (he still has to wait until Week 5 to play).

Gutekunst also said that he expects Musgrave to play this season. The fourth-year tight end suffered a neck injury this offseason and missed all of camp.

Long snapper Matt Orzech practiced Tuesday for the first time this summer. He spent all of camp on the PUP list with a calf injury.

HENDERSON, Nev. -- Las Vegas Raiders running back Ashton Jeanty's status for the season opener against the Miami Dolphins is uncertain. But general manager John Spytek said the second-year player is in a "good spot" in his recovery from an ankle injury.

"I expect him to be back as quick as he can, maybe quicker than some people would expect," Spytek said Tuesday. "When that is, we'll see."

Jeanty did not practice Tuesday but he was seen on the side field alongside second-year wide receiver Dont'e Thornton Jr., who was placed on injured reserve. It was the first look of Jeanty since last Sunday, when he was helped off the indoor practice field by trainers after spraining his ankle.

Spytek said Jeanty has been working hard to return to play.

"It's hard to knock him down, and I think he attacks everything with a great mindset," Spytek said. "I don't think that this will be any different for him."

While Jeanty recovers, rookie running back Mike Washington Jr. is the Raiders' top running back. Spytek said Washington had a "great" preseason and that the staff has been excited about the progress the former Arkansas standout has made.

In three preseason games, Washington totaled 23 carries for 168 yards (7.3 per attempt). He had four carries for 10-plus yards.

"We have an expectation that he's going to help us win football games this year," Spytek said.

text:
As we approach the start of the NFL season, it's time for our annual ranking of the league's top 100 players. Which players do we project to be the best in 2026?

To create our list, we asked 12 NFL analysts and reporters -- Aaron Schatz, Ben Solak, Dan Graziano, Eric Moody, Field Yates, Jeff Legwold, Liz Loza, Matt Bowen, Mina Kimes, Mike Clay, Nick Wagoner and Seth Walder -- to rank players based on expected performance for the 2026 season. Their rankings are based on predicting potential greatness rather than past performance. We used those 12 sets of votes to come up with our consensus list.

The Eagles lead the pack in players included (eight) for the second straight year, and the Lions and 49ers are next up with six players each. The Jets, meanwhile, are the only team without a single representative. By position, quarterbacks dominated the list with 16 mentions. Edge rushers followed with 13.

Along with the top-100 ranking, our NFL Nation reporters weighed in on every player's outlook for the season, ESPN Research provided a stat to know and fantasy analyst Mike Clay projected 2026 stats. Here's our list, starting at No. 100 and working our way to No. 1.

Note: Commanders offensive tackle Laremy Tunsil was not considered for this exercise due to his recent triceps injury; again, this is predicting 2026 play. Rams defensive tackle Aaron Donald, who came out of retirement Sunday, also was not considered.

Jump to:

100-76 | 75-51 | 50-26 | 25-1

More on NFL Rank:

Execs and scouts name snubs

100. Sam Darnold

QB | Seahawks

Age: 29

2025 rank: NR

No quarterback has more wins over the past two seasons than Darnold, who has 31 with the Vikings and Seahawks. He'd be higher on this list if not for his league-high 20 turnovers in 2025, though he went the final four games without one. One reason Darnold could be better in 2026: This is the first time since 2020 that he returns to the same team as its unquestioned starter. -- Brady Henderson

Signature stat: Last season, Darnold went 14-3 as a starter with the Seahawks after finishing the 2024 season with a 14-3 record for the Vikings. Darnold joined Tom Brady (2003-04) as the only QBs to record back-to-back 14-win seasons.

2026 projections: 4,013 passing yards, 24 TDs, 12 INTs; 44 carries, 126 rushing yards, 1 TD

99. Jessie Bates III

S | Falcons

Age: 29

2025 rank: 62

One of the premier ball hawks in the NFL, Bates has 27 interceptions and 11 forced fumbles (fifth most among defensive backs) since he entered the league in 2018. He's the unquestioned leader of the Falcons' defense and could be part of one of the best 2026 safety duos alongside Xavier Watts (five interceptions as a rookie in 2025). -- Marc Raimondi

Signature stat: Bates' 27 interceptions over the past eight seasons is the third most in the NFL behind Kevin Byard and Justin Simmons (both 28).

2026 projections: 96 tackles, 6 PDs, 2 INTs, 1 FF

98. Antoine Winfield Jr.

S | Buccaneers

Age: 28

2025 rank: 85

The Bucs were really intentional about bringing in some new players on defense who fit their type of attitude and instinct. Having linebacker Alex Anzalone -- one of the best cover inside linebackers in the league -- patrolling the middle of the field will be a huge assist to Winfield. So will another year of experience for Winfield's fellow safety Tykee Smith, as well as a revamped pass rush with rookie Rueben Bain Jr. -- Jenna Laine

Signature stat: Winfield leads all safeties in forced fumbles (12) and fumble recoveries (10) since entering the league in 2020.

2026 projections: 95 tackles, 8 PDs, 2 sacks, 2 INTs, 1 FF

97. Jalen Hurts

QB | Eagles

Age: 28

2025 rank: 38

Hurts is coming off an up-and-down year and is now at the controls of a brand-new scheme designed by offensive coordinator Sean Mannion. Hurts has found ways to maneuver around obstacles in the past, though. He has a 57-25 record as a starting QB and ranks second to only Josh Allen in total touchdowns (138) since 2022. -- Tim McManus

Signature stat: Hurts recorded his fourth straight season with 30-plus combined passing and rushing touchdowns, the fourth-longest active streak behind Allen (six). That included his fewest rushing TDs (eight) since becoming the full-time starter in 2021.

2026 projections: 3,779 passing yards, 24 TDs, 12 INTs; 106 carries, 438 rushing yards, 9 TDs

96. Trevor Lawrence

QB | Jaguars

Age: 26

2025 rank: NR

It can't be coincidence that Liam Coen coached quarterback Baker Mayfield and Lawrence to their best seasons in back-to-back years. Unlike 2025, Lawrence isn't learning a new offense or changing his footwork. So, it shouldn't take half of the season for him to get rolling the way he did over the final eight games of 2025 (19 TD passes and five rushing TDs). -- Michael DiRocco

Signature stat: Lawrence set a franchise record with 38 total touchdowns last season. He also finished fifth in MVP voting, which was the highest finish ever by a Jaguar.

2026 projections: 3,932 passing yards, 25 TDs, 13 INTs; 73 carries, 335 rushing yards, 5 TDs

95. Rashawn Slater

OT | Chargers

Age: 27

2025 rank: NR

Slater missed all of last season with a ruptured patellar tendon in his left knee. Through training camp, he looks like the Pro Bowl version of himself at left tackle, but the true determination will be when the season starts. Slater has already missed practice time this offseason due to a flare-up, so it will be something to watch as he tries to reestablish himself as one of the best players at his position. -- Kris Rhim

Signature stat: In 2024, Slater finished 10th in run block win rate (78.6%) and 22nd in pass block win rate (90.7%) among qualifying tackles.

94. Jaycee Horn

CB | Panthers

Age: 26

2025 rank: NR

Horn will be more fluid in the defensive backfield in 2026. This summer, he has been used in the slot, which should take advantage of his blitzing ability. While he was sent at the quarterback just 16 times over the past two seasons, according to NFL Next Gen Stats, he created pressure on 25% of those opportunities (including two sacks and four QB hits). -- Mike Kaye

Signature stat: All five of Horn's interceptions last season came on passes at least 20 yards downfield, the most in the NFL.

2026 projections: 50 tackles, 10 PDs, 1 INT

93. DeVonta Smith

WR | Eagles

Age: 27

2025 rank: NR

Philadelphia is highly confident Smith can take his game to another level as the clear-cut No. 1 receiver after A.J. Brown's departure. A 100-catch season certainly seems within reach; he already came close with 95 catches for nearly 1,200 yards in 2022. -- Tim McManus

Signature stat: Smith is one of five players to win the Heisman Trophy, NCAA title and Super Bowl. The others are Tony Dorsett, Marcus Allen, Reggie Bush and Charles Woodson.

2026 projections: 91 receptions, 1,130 receiving yards, 6 TDs

92. Jack Campbell

LB | Lions

Age: 26

2025 rank: NR

Campbell is fresh off a first-team All-Pro season in 2025. So naturally, his confidence is at an "all-time high," according to coach Dan Campbell. Over the offseason, Campbell inked a four-year, $81 million extension. Defensive coordinator Kelvin Sheppard is now giving him more leeway to run the defense in Year 4. "You've got to earn it every year," Campbell told ESPN. "No matter what, it's just my mindset to try to get a little better every single year." -- Eric Woodyard

Signature stat: Campbell is one of five players with at least 375 tackles and four forced fumbles since entering the league in 2023, joining Zaire Franklin, Bobby Okereke, Patrick Queen and Germaine Pratt.

2026 projections: 156 tackles, 4 PDs, 3 sacks, 2 FFs, 1 INT

91. Kamari Lassiter

CB | Texans

Age: 23

2025 rank: NR

Lassiter would be the No. 1 cornerback on a lot of teams, but he just happens to share a defense with Derek Stingley Jr. Lassiter told ESPN recently that the "mental" aspect of his game has improved, which he believes should elevate him more going into Year 3. If he has another strong year, he should cash in a large extension during the 2027 offseason. -- DJ Bien-Aime

Signature stat: Lassiter has allowed a 52% completion rate in coverage over the past two seasons, fifth best by any defensive back with at least 1,000 coverage snaps in that span (per NFL Next Gen Stats).

2026 projections: 96 tackles, 20 PDs, 2 INTs

90. Darnell Wright

OT | Bears

Age: 25

2025 rank: NR

The Bears made Wright the highest-paid right tackle in NFL history (four years, $116 million) after he earned second-team All-Pro honors. "When you watch us on offense, we're certainly a little bit more right-handed than left-handed, and that is with him in mind," coach Ben Johnson said. "I think he's one of those tackles that's a powerful player and can displace guys off the line of scrimmage. ... He's proven that he can do that and carry the load, if you will, a lot of times in the running game on his back." -- Courtney Cronin

Signature stat: Wright's 95% pass block win rate was the fourth best among offensive tackles last season. He ranked 33rd among offensive tackles over the previous two seasons in that metric.

89. Colston Loveland

TE | Bears

Age: 22

2025 rank: NR

If his form continues, he'll not only go down as the best Bengals receiver ever but also make a strong case as an All-Decade player. -- Ben Baby

Signature stat: Chase has had 80-plus receptions and 1,000-plus receiving yards in all five seasons of his NFL career. He's the only player in NFL history to reach both of those marks in each of his first five seasons.

2026 projections: 120 receptions, 1,509 receiving yards, 11 TDs; 4 carries, 21 rushing yards

3. Lamar Jackson

QB | Ravens

Age: 29

2025 rank: 4

Jackson has an impressive track record when it comes to clicking in his first season of a new offensive system. He has won MVP the past two times the Ravens made a switch at offensive coordinator. With first-year playcaller Declan Doyle, Jackson is looking to bounce back from his first losing season (6-7). And he isn't showing any signs of his age. "I feel like he got faster," safety Kyle Hamilton said. -- Jamison Hensley

Signature stat: Jackson is one of seven quarterbacks in NFL history with three-plus seasons of at least 3,000 passing yards and 500 rushing yards. He currently has a 70% win percentage in the regular season, which is the third-best by any QB since 2019 (minimum of 40 starts) behind Patrick Mahomes (.752) and Josh Allen (.716).

2026 projections: 3,887 passing yards, 26 TDs, 10 INTs; 122 carries, 671 rushing yards, 4 TDs

2. Josh Allen

QB | Bills

Age: 30

2025 rank: 2

Allen is back for his ninth NFL season, armed with a new head coach (Joe Brady) who has worked closely with him since 2022 and a new No. 1 wide receiver (DJ Moore). In each of the past three seasons, Allen has scored at least 25 passing touchdowns and 10 rushing touchdowns. In NFL history, all other players combined have only two such seasons. "I know Josh Allen is the best football player in the world," Brady said. -- Alaina Getzenberg

Signature stat: Allen has finished top-five in MVP voting in each of the past four seasons, which is tied with Peyton Manning (2003 to 2006) for the second-longest streak over the past 40 years. Tom Brady leads in that category with five straight from 2013 to 2017.

2026 projections: 3,946 passing yards, 26 TDs, 12 INTs; 116 carries, 580 rushing yards, 12 TDs

1. Myles Garrett

Edge | Rams

Age: 30

2025 rank: 3

Garrett, the reigning DPOY, set an NFL record with 23 sacks last season. Now, he's entering his first season with the Rams as the first defender at No. 1 on this list since Aaron Donald in 2019. Stafford called going against Garrett in practice a chess match because "he affects every time you drop back to throw the football." "He's an alien," Rams safety Kam Curl said. "He can do whatever he wants to do, and the offense can't do anything about it." -- Sarah Barshop

Signature stat: Garrett's trade to the Rams marks the third time any player won DPOY and then played the next season with a different team. Dana Stubblefield (1997) and Deion Sanders (1994) were the other two, but both moved as free agents.

The Detroit Lions placed running back Isiah Pacheco on injured reserve with a back issue, the team announced Tuesday, sidelining him for at least four games.

The Lions signed Pacheco this offseason to replace the departed David Montgomery as Jahmyr Gibbs' backup. Jacob Saylors now projects to begin the campaign as Detroit's No. 2 running back.

Pacheco also dealt with an MCL sprain in training camp.

The 27-year-old spent the first four seasons of his career with the Kansas City Chiefs. He served as Kansas City's No. 1 running back in the first two years of his career, but his effectiveness waned in 2024 and 2025 as he dealt with injuries.

Pacheco rushed for 1,765 yards in 2022 and 2023, averaging 4.7 yards per attempt. He was an integral piece of Kansas City's back-to-back Super Bowl victories, adding 510 rushing yards in seven playoff games. However, Pacheco appeared in just 20 games over the last two seasons and rushed for 772 yards, averaging 3.8 yards per attempt.

The Chiefs drafted Pacheco in the seventh round in 2022.

Saylors, an undrafted free agent out of East Tennessee State in 2023, has just two career NFL rushing attempts under his belt.

text:
The San Francisco 49ers hoped to have Mike Evans back on the practice field this week. Their latest timetable for the veteran wide receiver isn't as encouraging.

49ers president of football operations and general manager John Lynch said the team hopes Evans, who is dealing with an adductor injury, will return to practice next week, according to David Lombardi of The San Francisco Standard on September 1.

Advertisement

Last week, Shanahan said Evans was dealing with a groin issue. Now, it's an adductor.

That represents a change from the timetable head coach Kyle Shanahan offered only a week earlier. On August 25, Shanahan said Evans was dealing with groin tightness and that San Francisco hoped to get him back "next week" — referring to the week beginning August 31. The 49ers' own website subsequently listed Evans among the players expected to return that week.

Evans has not made that return yet, and Lynch's latest projection pushes the target another week closer to San Francisco's September 10 season opener against the Los Angeles Rams in Melbourne, Australia.

There has been no indication that Evans aggravated the injury, so it would be premature to label the changed timeline a confirmed setback. But with Week 1 approaching, it's nevertheless a disappointing development for the 49ers and their new No. 1 receiver.

Advertisement

Here's what it means.

Mike Evans' Return Timeline Has Changed

The situation looked considerably more encouraging just days ago.

ESPN's Jeremy Fowler reported on August 26 that Evans planned to play in Week 1 and that his groin issue was considered minor barring a change.

There was even optimism from the 49ers on August 31. The team's official website reported that Shanahan said Evans was "ahead of schedule" in his recovery from a groin strain and could potentially practice before San Francisco departed for Australia.

Evans worked separately from the team during Monday's practice rather than participating in the session.

Advertisement

Lynch's September 1 update therefore changes the picture again.

If Evans does not practice until next week, the 33-year-old could have only a limited number of on-field sessions to prepare for his first regular-season game with quarterback Brock Purdy and the 49ers offense.

That doesn't necessarily mean Evans will miss Week 1. But it makes his availability — and how large a workload San Francisco could reasonably give him if he plays — more noteworthy.

Evans Has Dealt With Multiple Injuries in First 49ers Camp

The latest issue has added to an interrupted first training camp in San Francisco for Evans.

Advertisement

Evans initially missed practice in early August because of a quadriceps strain, according to the 49ers. He eventually returned as a full participant on August 15 before later being sidelined by the groin issue.

That lost practice time matters for a player who is learning Shanahan's offense after spending the first 12 seasons of his NFL career with the Tampa Bay Buccaneers.

Evans joined San Francisco after compiling 866 receptions, 13,052 receiving yards and 108 touchdown catches during his Buccaneers career, all Tampa Bay franchise records. He had 30 catches for 368 yards and three touchdowns in eight games during an injury-shortened 2025 season.

The 49ers did not bring Evans in merely to provide veteran depth. He is expected to give Purdy a proven outside target and red-zone weapon, making his availability particularly significant as San Francisco prepares for a divisional opponent in Week 1.

49ers Face Tight Window Before Rams Game in Australia

San Francisco's unusual Week 1 schedule adds another wrinkle.

Advertisement

The 49ers are preparing for an approximately 8,000-mile trip to Melbourne for their September 10 matchup against Los Angeles, forcing the team to account for travel and acclimation while setting its Week 1 roster.

That makes every missed practice more significant than it might be during a normal opening week.

There remains reason for optimism. Evans has not been ruled out against the Rams, and the previous reporting indicated both the player and team expected the injury to be manageable.

But the goalposts have moved.

A week after Shanahan hoped Evans would return to practice during the week of August 31, Lynch is now pointing toward the following week. Until Evans actually gets back onto the practice field, his readiness for the 49ers' opener will remain one of the team's biggest offensive questions heading into Week 1.

text:
The Buffalo Bills have begun preparations for their Sept. 14 opener against the Houston Texans and Joe Brady’s first season as head coach.

After the roster was set, general manager Brandon Beane met with reporters Tuesday to discuss his decisions and several bigger-picture questions.

Hairston, Igbinosun and the No. 2 CB conversation

When training camp began, the starting cornerback job was rightfully wide open.

After all, the Bills’ realistic depth chart consisted of their locked-in top cornerback, Christian Benford, and then some young players with high variability: second-year defender Maxwell Hairston and rookie second-round pick Davison Igbinosun.

Hairston came back on the fly as a rookie from a multi-month injury at training camp and immediately filtered in for defensive reps. While there were flashy moments, the consistency of the performances was altogether uneven. Fast forward to 2026, Hairston has always been viewed as the odds-on favorite to be the starter, though the inconsistencies in camp followed, along with another camp injury — this time a groin ailment.

That, combined with Igbinosun’s steady progress once the pads went on in August, and being a direct improvement over Hairston in dealing with physical receivers and in run support, is presenting extremely logical questions that the Bills have to be pondering inside the building, too. To Hairston’s credit, his ability to turn and run gives him a higher ceiling than Igbinosun.

After the Bills’ preseason finale, Brady said succinctly that Hairston is the starter. Regardless, there is some wiggle room there, as Hairston’s struggles and Igbinosun’s progress bring up the conversation of whether a timeshare is possible in Week 1 — with Hairston being the technical starter.

“We have a lot of confidence in (Hairston),” Beane said. “I think IGB has done a really good job. If we didn’t have confidence in him, we’d just sit him down and throw IGB in. He’s a young player that’s gonna continue to push his way, and Max knows that he’ll have to play at a certain level, or there’s a young man here that’s ready to showcase kind of what he can do.”

Beane also commented on how good of a spring Hairston had, so it appears they want to give him every opportunity to be the guy they hoped for when they used their top pick on him. Still, it’s hard to ignore what has been going on since Hairston returned from the groin injury, which leads back to the possibility of a non-full-time role.

“I don’t really know at this point what we’d do,” Beane said. “I think we’re just kind of taking it one day, one week at a time. I wouldn’t want to put us in a box of saying we would or wouldn’t do. I think anything would be on the table. Whatever we think can help us win. If it’s a platoon, we’ll do it. If it’s just one guy, we will do that.”

It wasn’t a flat-out “no” on the idea, and it’s even more interesting that the Bills aren’t shying away from Hairston needing to prove his spot.

His performance and how the Bills handle that position will be one of the most intriguing parts of their Week 1 showdown in Houston.

Week 1 gamesmanship? Several key starters return

When Beane met with the media on Tuesday, he did so more than an hour before practice began, and it was the first real chance to get injury clarification since the team’s preseason ended. The Bills had a handful of starters and key role players sitting out during last week’s practices, including a pair of key starting defenders — safety C.J. Gardner-Johnson and inside linebacker Terrel Bernard.

Gardner-Johnson has been going through “something different” of an injury than what he did when he injured his calf early in camp. Meanwhile, Bernard’s undisclosed injury kept him out of on-field work last week. In both cases, Beane didn’t give absolute certainty of their Week 1 availability. On Gardner-Johnson, Beane said, “We’ll know more next week,” and on Bernard, they want to get him back to full health. “Hopefully before game one. We’ll see,” Beane said.

The update on both players seemed slightly concerning for Week 1, though when the Bills opened up their doors to practice, Gardner-Johnson and Bernard were going through all individual reps — and they weren’t alone. The Bills also saw the return of defensive lineman Ed Oliver, center Connor McGovern and wide receiver Keon Coleman. In all five cases, returning to practice more than a week before the season opener is an extremely promising sign.

The Bills were without six players from their 53-man roster. Of that group, the biggest name is wide receiver Khalil Shakir, who hasn’t practiced since Aug. 18. Shakir was able to do some jogging around the practice fields while positional work was going on, so there were at least some signs of progress. The other notable absence was backup running back Ty Johnson, who hasn’t practiced since suffering an injury on Aug. 8.

Similarly, Johnson was doing some work along the sideline. It remains to be seen whether either will be available for Week 1, though given Shakir’s usual workload, it may be a case of the team giving him all the rest it can until the first regular-season week arrives.

The other group of non-participants included offensive tackle Jude Bowry, outside linebacker Javon Solomon, nickel cornerback Jordan Hancock and safety Jalon Kilgore.

The Latu surprise

One of the bigger surprises when the Bills unveiled their final roster was that it included a fourth tight end, that being second-year player Keleki Latu, and excluded a fullback. Latu came to the Bills as an undrafted rookie in 2025 and put together an excellent training camp and summer, to the point that they didn’t want to find out if they’d lose him to waivers.

The why is, at the very least, interesting: how the offense will look in 2026 without a fullback. The Bills run a lot of looks with 13 and 12 personnel, so keeping an additional player at the position makes a good degree of sense if he has the right blend of skills, and Latu passed that test in the Bills’ mind.

“He’s come a long way from 12 months ago,” Beane said. “I think the thing that I saw — the passing game was there last year — I think this guy really focused on his play strength and his run blocking, being a more complete tight end. He’s a longer-levered guy, so it’s easier for guys to get up under his pads, but him just getting his leverage, getting his hands, his angles.”

Latu could very well be involved on game days if special teams calls for it, but not having a fullback opens up a lot of possibilities to line up tight ends in places the Bills didn’t traditionally use in 2025. Although it would only be a handful of snaps each game, Jackson Hawes and Dawson Knox likely give them the most versatility in doing just that.

Quarterback Josh Allen said on Tuesday that it could be a way to change some of the defensive rules their opponents have to abide by based on where they’re lined up. The Bills have made a concerted effort to be more unpredictable across the board in 2026, and this is likely another step in that direction.

What’s going on at punt returner?

With the 53-man roster being set for the time being, the Bills really didn’t keep a punt return specialist on their active roster. They unsurprisingly moved on from Mecole Hardman, hoping Ray Davis could take the job and run with it. Still, Davis missing a catch and fumbling a ball to the opponents should rightfully give the team pause heading into the regular season.

Beane mentioned four names for what they could do, and admitted they still haven’t finalized which player will have the role to begin the year. The names consisted of Davis, nickel cornerback Dee Alford, Shakir and newly signed practice squad wide receiver Greg Dortch.

The Bills have been hesitant to use Shakir as a punt returner this summer, suggesting he may be their emergency option. If so, the decision could be between Davis, Alford and Dortch. Alford returned 20 punts in 2023, so he at least has some experience.

Though if the Bills really wanted some pop and real experience, Dortch has returned 92 punts over the last four seasons. The only problem would be finding a gameday spot for him, which could come in the form of someone such as rookie wide receiver Skyler Bell. It might ultimately depend on how much Dortch can learn the offense by the time the Houston game arrives.

Either way, the Bills have to choose between using a major starter in Shakir or Alford, an inconsistent returner in Davis or finding a game-day spot for Dortch, without an easy answer.

Zane Durant injury update

The Bills made one move on injured reserve for fifth-round rookie defensive lineman Zane Durant, who suffered an injury late in the team’s preseason finale. Beane updated the reason behind that decision and said it was a “stinger” type of issue that would take “a little time to resolve itself.” Durant will be out a minimum of four games, but Beane did not rule out a Week 5 return for the rookie.

title: NFL's 11 best comebacks from retirement, ranked ahead of Aaron Donald's Rams return
description:
He’s not the first NFL player to leave the comfort of retirement to put on a pair of shoulder pads again.
Here is a ranking of 11 players who returned to the NFL following significant time away from the league for retirement.
Witten spent the 2019 season back in Dallas, starting all 16 games and catching 63 passes for 529 yards and four touchdowns.
Philip Rivers, QB We start with one of the more fascinating stories from the 2025 NFL season.
Rivers made three starts, throwing for 544 yards and four touchdowns, but eventually the Colts were eliminated from playoff contention.
text:
Aaron Donald is coming out of retirement and returning to the Los Angeles Rams. He’s not the first NFL player to leave the comfort of retirement to put on a pair of shoulder pads again.

He now joins a list of athletes who have returned to their sport after spending some time away from the game. Where Donald will ultimately land on that list of athletes — a list that includes names like Michael Jordan, Mario Lemieux, Magic Johnson, Michael Schumacher, and others — remains to be seen.

But before Donald takes the field, we want to look at some more direct peers. Who are some NFL players who returned to the field after some time away from the game?

Here is a ranking of 11 players who returned to the NFL following significant time away from the league for retirement. For our purposes, we are not considering the brief retirements of Tom Brady and Brett Favre, or time away from the game for legal issues as with Michael Vick.

11. Jason Witten, TE

Jason Witten spent 15 years as a tight end with the Dallas Cowboys, earning 11 Pro Bowl selections and a pair of First-Team All-Pro odds. He retired after the 2017 season, moving to the ESPN booth for a spot on Monday Night Football for the 2018 season.

But his season in the booth was met with mixed reviews, and he decided to return to the field. Witten spent the 2019 season back in Dallas, starting all 16 games and catching 63 passes for 529 yards and four touchdowns. He spent his final NFL season in Las Vegas with the Raiders, starting seven games and playing in all 16, catching 13 passes for 69 yards and a pair of touchdowns.

10. Philip Rivers, QB

We start with one of the more fascinating stories from the 2025 NFL season. Philip Rivers retired from the NFL in 2020, and was named as one of the semifinalists for the 2026 Hall of Fame Class last November.

But that is around the time that Daniel Jones, the starting quarterback for the Indianapolis Colts, was lost for the season with an Achilles tear. With the Colts sitting at 8-5 and clinging to a playoff spot, head coach Shane Steichen — who was Rivers’ quarterbacks coach and offensive coordinator during their time with the Chargers — turned to his former QB to try and save the season.

First, he had to convince the 44-year-old high school coach to come out of retirement.

Rivers made three starts, throwing for 544 yards and four touchdowns, but eventually the Colts were eliminated from playoff contention.

9. Steve DeBerg, QB

Philip Rivers was not the only quarterback to return to the NFL in his mid-40s.

Steve DeBerg first announced his retirement in 1993, after playing 18 years with several teams including the San Francisco 49ers, the Denver Broncos, the Tampa Bay Buccaneers, the Kansas City Chiefs, and the Miami Dolphins.

He started 12 games for the 49ers back in 1978 while their future star, Joe Montana, was still at Notre Dame.

But in 1998 one of his former coaches, Dan Reeves, gave him a call. Reeves was now the head coach of the Atlanta Falcons, and had a need behind starting quarterback Chris Chandler. Mark Rypien, the expected backup quarterback, stepped away from the game after his young son was diagnosed with brain cancer.

DeBerg knew the offensive system, similar to the story with Rivers and the Colts, and made the Falcons roster. He started one game that year and played in eight, completing 30-of-59 passes for 369 yards and three touchdowns. The Falcons advanced to Super Bowl XXXIII, only to lose to none other than the Broncos.

8. Reggie White, DT

Reggie White first walked away from the NFL after the 1998 season, after a first stint in the league that saw him picked for 13 consecutive Pro Bowls from 1986 through 1998. He was the league’s Defensive Player of the Year in both 1987, and 1998, and when he retired he led the league with 192.5 career sacks. The 1998 season, his sixth with the. Green Bay Packers, saw him picked as a First-Team All-Pro for the sixth time in his career.

But after sitting out 1999, he was convinced to come back to the league to play for the Carolina Panthers. In one year with the Panthers, White started all 16 games, recording 5.5 sacks.

7. Eric Weddle, S

Drafted in the second round of the 2007 NFL Draft by the San Diego Chargers, Eric Weddle spent nine years with the organization, securing First-Team All-Pro honors twice. He signed with the Baltimore Ravens ahead of the 2016 season, where he spent the next four years of his career, earning a pair of Pro Bowl nods.

Weddle retired after the 2019 season, but as the 2021 NFL postseason beckoned, the Los Angeles Rams had a need in the secondary. Starting safety Jordan Fuller suffered a season-ending ankle injury in the final week of the season and his backup, Taylor Rapp, was in the concussion protocol. With the Rams set to face the Arizona Cardinals on Wild Card Weekend, Los Angeles convinced Weddle to come out of retirement.

Weddle played in all four of the Rams’ playoff games, making a pair of starts. He even tore a pectoral muscle early in Super Bowl LVI against the Cincinnati Bengals, but stayed in the game to record five tackles as the Rams beat the Bengals by a final score of 23-20.

It was the only Super Bowl appearance of his career.

6. Marshawn Lynch, RB

When it comes to running back Marshawn Lynch, you have two retirements to pick from.

Lynch first stepped away from the NFL the day of Super Bowl 50, posting a photo of his cleats hanging from a telephone wire on social media. He sat out the entire 2016 season, serving as an advisor to players at California, his alma mater.

But Lynch always wanted to play for his hometown team, the Oakland Raiders, and after sitting out the 2016 season he convinced the Seattle Seahawks to trade his rights to the team of his youth. He was officially traded to the Raiders in April of 2017, signing a two-year deal with the team.

He spent two years with the Raiders, starting in 21 games and rushing for 1,267 yards and ten touchdowns. However, a groin injury in October of 2018 ended his second season early, and he again retired.

Yet, he had one more NFL cameo in his future.

Late in the 2019 season, the Seahawks lost three running backs due to injury. He returned to Seattle for Week 17 against the San Francisco 49ers, notching 12 carries for 34 yards and a touchdown in a 26-21 loss. He scored a short touchdown run the following week, as the Seahawks beat the Philadelphia Eagles in the Wild Card Round.

While Seattle’s playoff run ended the following week in a 28-23 loss to the Packers, Lynch scored a pair of touchdowns in the game.

5. Bronko Nagurski, RB/DT

We leave the modern era for a moment to talk about Bronko Nagurski, one of the legends of football’s early days.

Nagurski walked away from professional football after the 1937 season, his eighth year in the game, all with the Chicago Bears. He was a two-way player, serving as a running back on offense and a defensive tackle on the other side of the ball. He even saw time along the offensive line when needed due to injury.

After five years away from the game, and with the Bears having lost several players to the World War II effort, George Halas convinced him to come back to the Bears to help along the defensive line. But with Chicago facing the Chicago Cardinals with a spot in the 1943 NFL Championship Game on the line, Nagurski saw time on offense as well, scoring a touchdown in the 35-24 victory.

Nagurski scored a touchdown against Washington in the title game, as the Bears won 41-21.

After one season coaching in the collegiate ranks, Nagurski walked away from football totally, returning to farming.

4. Ricky Williams, RB

Running back Ricky Williams first walked away from the NFL after the 2003 season, choosing to retire from the Miami Dolphins rather than serve a four-game drug suspension. The running back spent the fall of 2004 at the California College of Ayurveda in Grass Valley, studying the Indian art of holistic medicine.

The Dolphins went 4-12 that year.

Williams returned to Miami the following summer, and after serving that suspension he appeared in 12 games for the Dolphins, making three starts. He ran for 743 yards and six touchdowns, and finished fifth in Comeback Player of the Year voting.

But the following February the league announced a fourth violation of the NFL’s drug policy, and he was suspended for the entire 2006 campaign. He spent that year with the Toronto Argonauts of the CFL, playing 11 games and rushing for 526 yards and a pair of touchdowns.

NFL commissioner Roger Goodell granted Williams’ request for reinstatement in October of 2007, and he returned to the Dolphins that November. But after just six carries in his return, he suffered a torn pectoral muscle, ending his season after just one game.

He played in all 16 games for Miami in each of the next three seasons, including the 2009 campaign where he ran for over 1,000 yards for the first time since the 2003 season. But after the 2010 season, where he ran for 673 yards and a pair of touchdowns, he signed a two-year deal with the Baltimore Ravens.

Williams spent one year in Baltimore, running for 444 yards and a pair of scores. He announced his retirement from the NFL in February of 2012.

3. Deion Sanders, CB

After a remarkable NFL career that spanned 12 seasons, four teams, two sports, and a pair of Super Bowls, Deion Sanders walked away from the league, and the Washington Redskins. Sanders signed a seven-year deal with Washington in the summer of 2000, after the Dallas Cowboys released him in a cost-cutting move.

But Sanders surprisingly retired in the summer of 2001 after just one year in Washington, even forfeiting part of an $8 million bonus he was owed, in an effort to get out of town.

His first attempt at a return came late in the 2002 season. Washington waived him from the reserve/retired list, in an effort to allow Sanders to play with the Raiders in the playoffs. But several other teams put in a waiver claim on him, and the Chargers secured his rights due to their spot in the waiver order. However, he was never activated.

Then came the Baltimore Ravens.

Sanders signed a one-year deal with the Ravens for the 2004 season, picking the number 37 to match his age. He appeared in nine games with a pair of starts, and recorded three interceptions. Sanders returned the first, against the Buffalo Bills in Week 7, for a touchdown, the ninth TD return of his career. He was named AFC Defensive Player of the Week after that performance.

He returned to Baltimore for the 2005 season, playing in every contest for the Ravens. He recorded 30 tackles and a pair of interceptions in that year, while breaking up five passes.

But after a second consecutive season missing the playoffs, Sanders retired again following the 2005 campaign.

2. Rob Gronkowski, TE

Rob Gronkowski spent nine years with the New England Patriots, becoming one of the most dangerous tight ends in league history. Over that stretch he secured four First-Team All-Pro nods, was named the league’s Comeback Player of the Year in 2014 after suffering a significant knee injury the previous year, and helped the Patriots win three Super Bowls during his New England tenure.

But citing the toll the sport was taking on his body and his mental health, Gronkowski retired after the 2018 season.

That retirement lasted a year, until his former quarterback came calling. With Tom Brady now in Tampa Bay with the Buccaneers, the quarterback sold Bruce Arians and the coaching staff on a trade for the tight end.

That first season in Tampa Bay, Gronkowski started all 16 games, catching 45 passes for 623 yards and seven touchdowns. Against the Kansas City Chiefs in Super Bowl LV, Gronkowski caught a pair of touchdowns in a 31-9 romp. He also became the first player in league history to catch a pass in five different Super Bowls.

He returned to Tampa Bay for the 2021 season on a one-year deal. While he endured a rib injury that held him to just 12 games, he actually put up better numbers than the previous season, catching 55 passes for 802 yards and six scores.

Tampa Bay’s season ended in a loss to the Los Angeles Rams in the Divisional Round. Gronkowski caught four passes for 85 yards in that defeat.

He retired again that summer.

1. Randall Cunningham, QB

Randall Cunningham’s NFL career began in 1985 with the Philadelphia Eagles, and spanned 11 seasons in the City of Brotherly Love. But an ACL injury suffered in 1991, as well as some lingering injuries during the 1993 and 1994 season, saw Cunningham retire from the game following the 1995 season.

He started his own marble and granite business in Las Vegas, where he attended UNLV.

But in 1997 Dennis Green called, reaching Cunningham when the former quarterback was on a job site. Green, the head coach of the Minnesota Vikings, had a need for a backup behind Brad Johnson, and Cunningham signed with the team. He appeared in six games, making three starts, and threw for six touchdowns during the 1997 season. During the playoffs that year, Cunningham led a pair of late scoring drives to help the Vikings comeback to beat the New York Giants 23-22 in the Wild Card round.

Then came the 1998 season.

Cunningham played in 15 games that year, making 14 starts, and he led the Vikings to a 13-1 record as a starter. He threw for 3,704 yards and 34 touchdowns, earning the first First-Team All-Pro selection of his career, and he finished second in MVP voting. He led the NFL with a 106.0 NFL Passer Rating, and guided an offense that scored a then-NFL record 556 points.

Minnesota’s season ended with a loss to the Falcons in the NFC Championship Game.

Cunningham lost the starting job early in the 1999 season, when he was benched after throwing nine interceptions in just six games. He spent time with the Dallas Cowboys and Baltimore Ravens over the next few seasons, retiring again after the 2001 campaign.

We’ve reached September.

Real NFL football will be played this month, and fantasy football drafts are reaching the home stretch. Of course, news isn't slowing down just because the season is about to kick off.

In fact, it’s quite the opposite.

San Francisco Hopeful Mike Evans Will Practice Next Week

Evans continues to miss a considerable amount of practice time with multiple injuries, most recently an adductor issue. San Francisco general manager John Lynch is hopeful that Evans will return to practice next week, which sounds both optimistic and worrisome at the same time.

The 49ers play in Australia next Thursday, giving Evans even less time to get on the practice field. This does make his Week 1 status a legitimate question mark. San Francisco could suddenly find themselves very thin at wide receiver to open the season. Ricky Pearsall is already out for the year, while veteran Christian Kirk will begin the season on injured reserve, meaning a potential Evans absence would leave the 49ers with De’Zhaun Stribling, Deebo Samuel and Demarcus Robinson to lead the receiver room.

Jeremiyah Love “50/50” To Play Week 1

Love continues to recover from a high ankle sprain and according to Mike Garafolo of NFL Network, the rookie running back is “50/50” to suit up for Week 1’s contest against the Chargers.

During his preseason debut a few weeks back, Love shined, rushing for 58 yards on 11 carries. The usage was favorable, too, playing alongside Tyler Allgeier during the first two drives of the game, handling 71% of the snaps and 64% of the Cardinals’ rush attempts. He then dominated the snaps on his third and final drive with Gardner Minshew in the game. With James Conner starting the year on injured reserve and Trey Benson no longer part of the equation, Allgeier would be in store for a massive workload if Love isn’t active Week 1. But even if Love is able to play, there’s a good chance Allgeier still sees enough work to warrant FLEX consideration.

Malik Nabers Not A Guarantee For Week 1?

Although the clips of him throughout Giants training camp were promising, Nabers is still noncommittal regarding his Week 1 availability. ESPN’s Jordan Raanan reports that Nabers feels good but still has some hurdles to clear ahead of Week 1. It’s entirely possible this could be some early gamesmanship by the Giants ahead of a matchup with division rival Dallas, especially since all previous signs pointed towards Nabers playing Week 1.

Only time will tell, but this news really doesn’t change my stance on Nabers in fantasy. He remains a high-upside third-round selection with top-six wide receiver upside as long as he’s on the field. Remember, as a rookie, Nabers posted an insane 35% target share, seeing as much volume as anyone in football:

35% target share (1st)

Bengals WRs To Be Limited In Practice

Both Ja’Marr Chase (knee) and Tee Higgins (heel) are expected to be limited in practice this week. Chase hyperextended his knee during practice last week, but stated he’d be able to play if the Bengals had a game. Cincinnati doesn’t seem overly concerned that either injury will keep their star receiver duo on the sidelines for their Week 1 contest against Tampa Bay.

We’ll continue to track the status of both wideouts leading up to Week 1.

text:
I’m ready to rattle off a handful of hot takes, and there’s no better place to do that than in the return of NFL Fact or Fiction.

I’ll focus more on awards and stat leaders because there’s no point in discussing Super Bowl contenders after the NFL dropped off the Lombardi Trophy at the local UPS store to ship to Los Angeles after the Rams signed Aaron Donald on Sunday. I’m kidding, of course. I truly believe it hasn’t gotten to the point where we look at the Super Bowl betting odds and say it’s Rams or the field.

There’s a contender on the other side of the country that’s being slept on despite adding a notable wide receiver in the offseason. And it won’t be a cakewalk for the Rams in the NFC, not when the Lions have just as much firepower on the offensive side.

Let’s kick off this Week 0 edition of NFL Fact or Fiction with Jahmyr Gibbs’s chances of winning MVP this season.

Jahmyr Gibbs will end the 13-year streak of QBs winning MVP

Manzano’s view: Fact

It’s kinda funny how little coach Dan Campbell cares about the backup running back situation after spending the offseason raving about Gibbs.

Campbell should be somewhat worried about Isiah Pacheco possibly not being available for the start of the season due to injury, but when you have a healthy Gibbs, there’s really no point in stressing about the position, even knowing that Jacob Saylors, who only has two career carries, is in line to be the backup running back for next week’s season opener against the Saints.

With how much Campbell has hyped up Gibbs’s first season without splitting carries with David Montgomery, who’s now in Houston, there’s a real possibility Gibbs plays more than 80% of the offensive snaps this season. Last year, Gibbs saw a career-high 67% of the snaps and was on the field less than 60% of the time during his first two seasons. It’s wild how efficient he’s been in his career despite the limited work (at least 1,800 scrimmage yards in each of the past two seasons), and it makes you wonder whether he’s about to deliver a historic season.

I’ll be bold here and say Gibbs ends the 13-year streak of a quarterback winning MVP and becomes the first running to claim the prestigious award since Adrian Peterson in 2012. But he’s going to have to produce a historic season because just rushing for 2,000 yards is no longer enough to win the award—just ask Saquon Barkley, who did it in 2024 and finished third for MVP.

Perhaps Gibbs can flirt with the single-season yards from scrimmage record that currently belongs to Chris Johnson (2,509 yards in 2009).

Myles Garrett will break his sack record playing next to Aaron Donald

Manzano’s view: Fiction

If Garrett can rack up 23 sacks playing for a terrible Browns team that trailed most of last season, it’s certainly possible that he breaks his single-season sack record with all the help he has with the Rams, which now includes playing next to Donald.

But I think the Rams will go with a less-is-more approach for their first season with Garrett and find creative ways to get the others more involved while keeping the star players fresh for when they are needed most. (Conor Orr laid that out perfectly here.)

Also, Garrett hasn’t practiced much this summer (we’ll know more about the injury when the first injury report comes out next week). The Rams will be cautious with the reigning Defensive Player of the Year and jump on opportunities to rest him when possible. Maybe this won’t happen often because it’s still a grueling schedule for the Rams, but they might find themselves up big in a handful of games to allow the veterans to sit for long stretches.

L.A. is all about the Super Bowl this season, not setting records. Still, it wouldn’t be a surprise to see Garrett generate at least 20 sacks in back-to-back seasons.

Not enough people are talking about the Bills adding DJ Moore

Manzano’s view: Fact

I didn’t realize how very little the addition of Moore has been talked about outside of Buffalo until I saw him available in the seventh round of my fantasy football draft last week.

The Bills trading for Moore has gone under-the-radar with the Rams stealing the bulk of the spotlight with all of their acquisitions. In the AFC, the Broncos have generated more hype with the trade for Jaylen Waddle. Even the Bengals have had more attention after the arrival of Dexter Lawrence II and he’s a defensive player.

Now, I’m not only saying this because Moore is now a member of my fantasy team, but I wouldn’t be surprised if Moore plays a key role in the Bills finally getting Josh Allen to a Super Bowl. Too many might be caught up in Moore’s critical mistake that ended the Bears’ playoff run where he appeared to not have gone full speed to prevent Caleb Williams’s costly overtime interception against the Rams.

However, Moore was instrumental in how much Williams improved in his second season. He was the go-to receiver in most clutch situations, and made some sensational touchdowns in the battles against the Packers. The 29-year-old Moore still has plenty to offer for a contender.

Commanders will be able to overcome offensive line challenges

Manzano’s view: Fiction

I try not to get too caught up in training camp storylines, but man, it’s hard not to think the Commanders could be in for a long season with all that has occurred to their offensive line.

Third-year player Brandon Coleman will start the year at left tackle after Laremy Tunsil sustained a torn triceps injury that could keep him out all of 2026. Coleman played guard last season. Meanwhile, the Commanders have limited options at center, perhaps turning to guard Nick Allegretti, who doesn’t have much experience playing the position. As for the cherry on top, reporters recently said the Commanders’ offensive line was a mess during a joint practice with the Ravens.

It’s probably time to panic in Washington. Asking Jayden Daniels to scramble more after dealing with injuries last season and only playing seven games seems like a recipe for disaster.

Anthony Richardson will make at least one start this season

Manzano’s view: Fact

I can’t believe I haven’t fully given up on Richardson and his enticing skill set, but he showed signs of improvement in the preseason and the Colts noticed it too after keeping him on the initial 53-man roster.

Richardson appeared composed in the pocket, displayed better accuracy and showed off his arm strength. With Daniel Jones’s injury history (he hasn’t played more than 13 games in a season since 2022), I’ll bet that Richardson makes at least one start this season.

However, I’ll give myself an out here and say that one start doesn’t have to be with the Colts. There’s a chance the team held on to the 2023 first-round pick in hopes of executing a trade for a quarterback-needy team down the line. And for Richardson to make a start in Indy, he’ll need to leapfrog second-year quarterback Riley Leonard on the depth chart. It seems competition has been good for Richardson this summer.

text:
After trading 2023 second-round draft pick Gervon Dexter and going through a training camp with injuries to key players, Chicago Bears general manager Ryan Poles still views his team as capable of defending the NFC North title.

The major reason is quarterback Caleb Williams' development in his second season under coach Ben Johnson and third year overall.

"I think the first year, he was white-knuckling the whole time, trying to figure it out, trying to do it right," Poles said Tuesday. "He continues to do that, wanting to do it right, but I think you see that joy back in his game where he’s playing free."

Johnson backed that thought about Williams, who threw only five passes in preseason.

"I’ve seen a very composed person every time he steps into the building," Johnson said. "This guy, you know, might have had a little bit of goofy to him a year ago. And I use that term with love.

"And now you just see a more serious player and intent every time I’m around him. And I think his teammates feel that as well."

The Bears may need an explosive offense and more focused QB because their secondary is still in question coming out of training camp despite being an area Poles sees as loaded with versatile players.

Nickel cornerback Kyler Gordon’s injury situation is an issue. He suffered an offseason calf injury and hasn’t practiced all training camp, after missing 14 regular-season games last season with a groin injury.

Poles said he’s still hopeful of Gordon’s return.

"Any time you have an injury and you’re coming back from something, there’s discomfort that you have to push through and that’s what it comes down to," Poles said. "So we haven’t been able to get over that hump and we’re not progressing as fast as we’d like. That’s really all I have to say about that."

Up front on defense, the trade of Dexter for a fifth-round pick and cornerback Clark Phillips III allowed the Bears to set up budding young defensive tackles Jordan van den Berg and Jayden Loving with more potential playing time. They avoided a big pay day next year for a veteran player who hasn’t fit well into defensive coordinator Dennis Allen’s scheme.

"Those young guys started making a push when we got through camp, and along with obviously Grady (Jarrett), (Kentavius) Street and Neville Gallimore)," Poles said. "And we felt like the timing made sense for us. So really, it was about the shape in the room and really how well those young guys were doing, too. So, we feel really good and confident in our talent level at that position."

Phillips could eventually fit their plans to replace Gordon, but he hasn’t played much slot cornerback in the NFL. For now, they’ll use fourth-round rookie Malik Muhammad in the slot. They’ve also considered Josh Blackwell, Xavier Woods, and even first-round rookie safety Dillon Thieneman.

Injuries hit the secondary during camp, starting with Gordon. Safety Coby Bryant is out until at least December. In addition, cornerbacks Tyrique Stevenson and Jaylon Johnson were hurt during a joint practice last week against the Titans, but both returned Tuesday from minor issues to practice.

The injuries were less severe on offense, with only running back Kyle Monangai a real question for the Sept. 13 opener against the Panthers.

The Bears fought through injury and consistency issues at left tackle to settle on Braxton Jones protecting Williams' blind side, possibly until starter Ozzy Trapilo returns from knee surgery. It now appears Trapilo is well ahead of schedule and made it onto the 53-man roster.

"We’re going to be able to operate as an offense and I think we’ll be able to score points," Johnson said. "It’s going to take all 11 of those guys out there in order to get that done."

text:
(2) Poles revealed that the Bears are re-signing linebacker Jack Sanborn and defensive tackle James Lynch and placing safety Coby Bryant and tight end Hayden Large on injured reserve.

Sanborn and Lynch were both released as part of final cuts Sunday.

A valuable reserve and special teams contributor, Sanborn spent his first three NFL seasons with the Bears from 2022-24. After playing for the Cowboys last year, the Lake Zurich native rejoined his hometown team in March.

Lynch, who impressed during training camp and the preseason, signed with the Bears this year after playing his first five NFL seasons with the Vikings (2020-22) and Titans (2024-25). He has appeared in 71 games with four starts, recording 98 tackles, seven tackles-for-loss and 3.5 sacks.

Poles is hopeful that Bryant and Large "can make it back at some point on the back end of the season."

(3) The presence of four solid veterans and two promising rookies at defensive tackle made Gervon Dexter Sr. expendable.

The Bears traded the fourth-year pro to the Falcons Sunday in exchange for cornerback Clark Phillips III and a 2027 fifth-round pick.

The deal came after Poles completely revamped the defensive tackle position during the offseason. He signed free agents Neville Gallimore, Kentavius Street and Lynch to join veteran Grady Jarrett before selecting Jordan van den Berg in the sixth round of the draft and signing Jayden Loving as an undrafted rookie.

"It really has to do with the room," Poles said of trading Dexter. "That room was highly competitive. Those young guys started making a push when we got through camp … and we felt like the timing made sense for us. We feel really good and confident in our talent level at that position."

In Phillips, the Bears are receiving a fourth-year pro who appeared in 28 games with seven starts the past three seasons with the Falcons, compiling 63 tackles, 10 pass breakups and one interception. Phillips spent most of last season on injured reserve, playing only nine snaps, all on special teams, in one game.

"He's definitely going to add depth to our corner room," Poles said. "We like, from the tape that we watched, his man coverage skills. Short-area quickness is really good, speed is really good, [he's] sticky in coverage. We're looking forward to getting him on board and getting him going."

(4) Poles feels that quarterback Caleb Williams is much more comfortable in his second season in coach Ben Johnson's offense.

"I love where he's at," Poles said. "What I see is I see joy. I think the first year [in the system], he was white knuckling the whole time trying to figure it out, trying to do it right. He continues to do that, wanting to do it right, but I think you see that joy back in his game where he's playing free.

"I think he sees and identifies where he comes up short faster than when he did before, and I think that's where him and Ben are continuing to work really well together, trying to get better every single day."

(5) Although the Bears have yet to name a starting left tackle, Poles feels a "little bit better" about the depth at the position than he did last year at this time.

Braxton Jones is healthy after being hampered by injuries the past few years. Theo Benedet is back after starting eight games as a rookie in 2025. And Ozzy Trapilo returned during training camp after initially being expected to miss all or most of the season with a knee injury he sustained in last year's playoff win over the Packers.

"Braxton is way healthier than he was last year," Poles said. "I don't know if he was completely himself last year, so he's in a better place. Theo has a bunch of games under his belt, too, and then when Ozzy's ready, he's started a bunch of big games himself, so we feel good about it."

Trapilo's earlier-than-expected return during camp afforded the Bears an opportunity to involve him in full-contact workouts.

"The big advantage of him coming back when he did, which I still think is amazing, is really the padded practices, team periods, really testing his anchor, mobility, all that stuff," Poles said. "In helmets, or not even helmets, it looks fabulous, or he wouldn't be where he is. But he's playing football.

"There's definitely rust to knock off. I don't know how long that'll take before he's involved with the game plan and starting or a rotational guy or active. It's too early to tell right now. But the beautiful thing is when he got back, one of our big concerns was how many padded practices could he get before [the regular season], because once we get going here, those start to drop off and we've got plenty of short weeks that we've got to deal with here too."

(6) Poles stated that a possible contract extension for running back D'Andre Swift is "something we need to look at."

After establishing career rushing highs with 1,087 yards and nine touchdowns last season, Swift enters the final year of his contract.

"He's done a great job," Poles said. "I love his approach to this offseason. He looks amazing. Second year in the system too … I like where he's at right now.

"This is where this job gets tough, is really trying to figure out how you want to allocate everything, not only for now but into the future. We'll have those conversations and see where we want to go from there. But I love 'Swifty.' I love the way that he's working."

(7) Poles lauded Johnson for how he ran his second training camp as Bears coach.

"I thought Ben did a great job with the schedule," Poles said. "He's got a great feel for where the team is at mentally; when he's got a challenge, when he's got to make it fun, when we've got to take time to spend with each other, like the joint practices we talked about. We had organized position groups going out to dinner together. Food trucks at the hotel in Cincinnati. He's got a great feel for the guys now, and it's really impressive to watch."

(8) Poles provided updates on several injured players.

It has yet to be determined whether defensive end Austin Booker will recover in time from a groin injury to play in the Sept. 13 season opener at Carolina.

"I'm not sure yet," Poles said. "We will get through this week. Week 0 is always good to have. We will get through these next three days and be able to assess and see if he's ready to go."

Defensive back Kyler Gordon, defensive lineman Shemar Turner and linebacker Noah Sewell are all on the physically unable to perform (PUP) list, meaning they will miss at least the first four games of the season.

Asked if he thinks Gordon will play for the Bears this year, Poles said: "I don't know. I hope so. I still have hope there. He's going to have to continue to work hard and get back to playing football again."

Poles added that Turner and Sewell are close to returning.

"We're doing a really good job with our performance team, getting those guys ramped up in shape, ready to go, so that when they play, they're ready to make an impact," Poles said. "Talked to those guys this morning. They're fired up to start that clock and get going."

Poles said that Turner, a 2025 second-round pick who tore his ACL in Week 8 last season, is "trending in a really positive direction."

"He's already doing position work off to the side," said the Bears GM. "We'll simulate some individual- and practice-type things to get him prepared mentally and physically, and his endurance needs to continue to improve. But he's working his butt off. I would imagine him being back at some point here when he gets through this little last phase of his rehab.

"And then from there, these guys will get Weeks 3 and 4 to start practicing before they're actually active, knocking that rust off and becoming a football player, starting to get that short-area quickness and really being able to react and have the instincts come back. Especially playing defensive line, you're getting hit from every different direction. So just knocking the rust off, getting the instincts going, when that happens it'll be great and we'll get him back out there, but I'm not exactly sure of when that all is going to occur."
