LAKE FOREST, Ill. (104.3 The Score) — Bears nickelback Kyler Gordon (calf) will miss at least the first four games of the 2026 regular season after being placed on the physically-unable-to-perform list Sunday. It remains to be seen whether his absence will linger beyond that.

Speaking Tuesday morning, Bears general manager Ryan Poles was noncommittal about Gordon’s health and future with the team. He was also uncertain of where Gordon's injury-plagued career will go next.

"I don't know,” Poles said when asked if Gordon will play again for the Bears. “I would hope so. I still have hope there. He's going to have to continue to work hard and get back to playing football again.”

Gordon, 26, was the first draft selection made by Poles when the Bears selected him at No. 39 overall in the second round of the 2022 NFL Draft. He has played 45 games for the Bears over four NFL seasons amid a career marred by injury.

Gordon played just three games in 2025 while dealing with several different leg injuries. That included a groin injury that he suffered during pregame warmups before a contest against the Packers last December at Lambeau Field.

The Bears’ frustration with Gordon has been clear throughout training camp as he hasn't taken the field. Coach Ben Johnson has been visibly dismayed by questions about Gordon’s status throughout the course of the preseason.

Poles shared insight about how Gordon's rehabilitation process hasn't accelerated as hoped.

“Any time you have an injury and you're coming back from something, there's discomfort that you have to push through,” Poles said. “And that's what it comes down to. We haven't been able to get over that hump, and we're not progressing as fast as we'd like. That's really all I have to say about it."

The Bears signed Gordon to a three-year, $40-million contract extension in early 2025, a deal that keeps him under contract in Chicago through the 2028 season. He's still owed $20 million guaranteed on that deal — $10 million in each of the next two years.

The Bears have pressed forward without Gordon heading into the season. Rookie Malik Muhammad, a fourth-round pick in April, is positioned as the likely starter at the nickelback position with Gordon sidelined.

Gordon hasn't been made available to speak with reporters this season as part of the Bears’ team policy for injured players.

Roster moves

The Bears will sign linebacker Jack Sanborn and defensive lineman James Lynch back to their 53-man roster after they were released Sunday in procedural maneuvers, Poles said. The team will place safety Coby Bryant (knee) and tight end Hayden Large (undisclosed) on injured reserve with the intent for their activations later in the season.

By placing Bryant and Large on injured reserve Tuesday rather than this past Sunday, they'll be eligible for activations later this season. The Bears still have five spots on their practice squad to fill. They signed 11 players to their practice squad Monday.

Following is a look at Detroit's first five games of the 2026 NFL season:

Week 1 vs. New Orleans: Sunday, Sept. 13 at 1 p.m.

Players to watch:

Lions edge rusher Aidan Hutchinson: Coming off an All-Pro season last year, Hutchinson was dominant throughout training camp and looks poised for a monster 2026 season. Hutchinson's 43.0 sacks through his first four seasons are the most in team history.

Saints wide receiver Chris Olave: Olave is the Saints' top receiving option coming off a 100-catch, 1,163-yard season with nine touchdowns in 2025. With wide receiver Jordyn Tyson, New Orleans' first-round pick this year, expected to miss a couple months with a hamstring injury, I expect quarterback Tyler Shough to look Olave's way early and often in this one.

Key matchup: Hutchinson vs. left tackle Kelvin Banks Jr.

Hutchinson ranked top five in the NFL last season in total pressures (100), QB hits (35), sacks (14.5), hurries (64) and forced fumbles (4). Banks was New Orleans' 2025 first-round pick, who started all 17 games and allowed just 4.0 sacks all year.

Important stat: The Saints allowed 49 sacks in 2025, which was seventh-most in the NFL.

Week 2 at Buffalo: Thursday, Sept. 17 at 8:15 p.m.

Players to watch:

Lions quarterback Jared Goff: Goff has had to adjust to a new play caller in Detroit in Drew Petzing, but that transition looked smooth in training camp. Goff, 31, enters his 11th NFL season in the prime of his career with one of the top collections of skill weapons in the league at his disposal.

Bills quarterback Josh Allen: The last time the Lions faced Allen and the Bills was Week 14 of the 2024 season when Allen completed 23-of-34 passes for 362 yards and two touchdowns to go along with 68 rushing yards and two more scores. He's as dynamic a player as there is in this league.

Key matchup: Linebacker Jack Campbell vs. running back James Cook

Cook comes off a monster season that saw him lead the NFL in rushing with 1,621 yards that went along with 12 touchdowns. Campbell is the heart and soul of Detroit's defense. He was second in the NFL last year with 176 tackles and led the league with 44 run stops.

Important stat: Buffalo led the NFL in average rushing yards per game in 2025 with an average of 159.6.

Week 4 at Carolina: Sunday, Oct. 4 at 8:20 p.m.

Players to watch:

Lions wide receiver Amon-Ra St. Brown: Through the first five seasons of a player's Lions career, St. Brown ranks first in receptions (547), receiving yards (6,252) and 100-yard games (24) and is also second in receiving touchdowns (44). He had arguably the best training camp of his career over the last month.

Panthers quarterback Bryce Young: The former No. 1 overall pick in 2023 comes off a 2025 season that saw him reach career highs in completion percentage (63.6), passing yards (3,011), touchdown passes (23) and passer rating (87.8). He led Carolina to an NFC South division title last year.

Key matchup: Guard Tate Ratledge vs. defensive tackle Derrick Brown

Campbell has been very complimentary of the training camp Ratledge had going into his second season. He finished the year ranked in the Top 12 among all NFL guards in run blocking and gave up just one sack and four quarterback hits over his last 12 starts. Important stat: The Panthers' defense was No. 1 in the NFL last year in holding opponents to just a 51.5 passer rating on deep passing attempts that traveled at least 20 yards in the air.

Cardinals tight end Trey McBride: McBride had a monster season in Petzing's offense in Arizona last season, recording 126 receptions for 1,239 yards and 11 touchdowns. He's a matchup nightmare at the position with his size and speed combination.

Key matchup: Tackle Penei Sewell vs. edge rusher Josh Sweat

Sewell made the move to left tackle to protect Goff's blindside. Sewell has developed into one of the best offensive tackles in the game, allowing just one sack in 16 starts in 2025. Sweat's 12.0 sacks last season tied for eighth-most in the NFL. He also added 13 tackles for loss and 17 quarterback hits.

text:
Buffalo Bills general manager Brandon Beane spoke to the local media Tuesday, providing his observations on the state of the team's roster going into the 2026 regular season. Among the topics discussed were injury updates on a number of players.

Here's what we learned:

The Bills placed emerging rookie defensive lineman Zane Durant on injured reserve this week, meaning he will miss at least the first four games of the season. Beane described the injury as a "neck stinger" and the team wants to give Durant time to let the injury "resolve itself".

"I don't think it's out of the question that he could be back when the rules allow, which the earliest would be game five. I don't think that's off the table. I think we're going to need a little more time to kind of see how he progresses," Beane said.

Durant's injury allowed the Bills to keep third-year defensive lineman DeWayne Carter on the 53-man roster. Carter missed the entire 2025 season with an Achilles injury and was one of the players fighting for a roster spot this spring and summer.

"He's a guy I saw get better, was a lot better in week two in the Cleveland game than week one," Beane said. "Knowing the history of that injury, talking to our doctors, you'd like to think he's going to continue to kind of trend up as we work through each week of the season."

Outside linebacker Michael Hoecht got a taste of game action for the first time since his Achilles injury last season. Hoecht played for part of the first half against the Steelers in the final preseason game and now appears on track for the regular season. Beane said he's "hopeful and optimistic" that Hoecht can suit up Week 1 in Houston.

"I think he passed one of those final tests of playing in that Pittsburgh game," Beane said. "We'll see how he gets through this week and next week. But I'm hopeful."

Inside linebacker Terrel Bernard didn't practice Tuesday, with Beane describing Bernard as being "nicked up a little bit".

"Hoping to get him back to full health, hopefully before game one, we'll see," Beane added.

Safety CJ Gardner-Johnson is "getting better" with a lower body injury and was at practice during the media viewing portion on Tuesday.

"I think we'll know more next week, a guy like him, what exactly his status will be for game one," Beane said of Gardner Johnson.

Newly-signed practice squad offensive lineman Jedrick Wills Jr. won't practice with the team for now as he rehabs a back injury. Beane shared that Wills Jr. reached an injury settlement with the Bears, allowing him to be released and join Buffalo's practice squad.

"He had a little tweak of his back there at the end. So we'll ramp him up probably -- this week. I don't know, he's not quite at 100%. But hopefully get him back there soon," Beane said of Wills Jr.

title: Playing tackle football causes brain damage. Why do we keep ignoring the evidence?

text:
A new study showing that at least 1 in 4 people who have played in the NFL will end up with chronic traumatic encephalopathy is just the latest sobering dose of reality for our football-obsessed culture.

The brain disease, known as CTE, is caused by repeated hits to the head, and it is highly prevalent in former NFL players. We’ve learned this by studying the brains of those who have recently died because we still can’t diagnose the disease while someone is alive.

Through building one of the most ambitious brain donation programs in the world at the Boston University CTE Center and the Concussion & CTE Foundation, we proved that 25% to 98% of NFL players who died between 2016 and 2021 had the disease: 878 players died over those six years, 235 brains were studied and 215 (91%) had it. The findings are sobering for NFL players, but they are also concerning for everyone who plays tackle football because we don’t yet know how to cure CTE.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

And the athletes aren’t just statistics — the last person included in the study, Chris Eitzmann, was my roommate and captain when we played football for Harvard University. He passed away at the age of 44 due to heavy drinking that helped him cope with his hidden brain injuries.

It may be hard for many football fans to hear, but we already know how to prevent future cases of CTE. The more hits athletes accumulate, and the harder those hits are, the greater their risk appears to be. And while we cannot erase the hits absorbed by players 30 or 50 years ago, we can reduce them going forward.

First off, we need to stop treating concussion protocols and CTE prevention as the same thing.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

For decades, the sports world has focused on recognizing the symptoms of concussions, removing symptomatic athletes and determining when they can safely return to play. Those efforts are important. But we’ve proven that the number of concussions sustained doesn’t predict who gets CTE. For every concussion a college football player suffers, they take 340 hits that are harder. If we really want to prevent CTE, the goal must be broader: fewer hits to the head. One study estimated that every 1,000 football hits increases someone’s odds of developing the disease by 21%.

The easiest hits to eliminate are the ones suffered by children in youth sports.

In 2024, California came remarkably close to taking an important step. Assembly Bill 734 would have phased in a minimum age for tackle football, ultimately preventing children under 12 from playing.

The bill advanced out of committee and was headed toward a vote in the Assembly. Then Gov. Gavin Newsom announced he would veto the bill if it reached his desk, and it died. Newsom said he was concerned about young athletes’ health but opposed an outright ban, arguing that parents should retain the freedom to decide which sports their children play.

I understand the politics.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

The football establishment and opponents of these reforms have successfully turned youth tackle football into a debate about parental rights — and that’s an extraordinarily powerful political argument.

But there is a fundamental problem with applying that framework to CTE.

A child cannot tell you that tackle football is damaging his brain because they can’t feel their brain being damaged. A parent cannot see their child’s brain being damaged, and a doctor cannot diagnose CTE in that child.

Imagine if an environmental exposure increased a child’s risk of developing a neurodegenerative disease decades later, but the damage could not be detected while the child was being exposed. Would we really say the solution was simply to inform parents and let them decide?

Of course not. We regulate childhood exposures precisely because children cannot meaningfully evaluate long-term risks for themselves.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

When we learned that lead exposure damages the human brain, we banned it from gasoline and house paint. A recent study showed that NFL players who averaged about 15 years of tackle football died with dementia at four times the rate of the general population. For comparison, high levels of lead exposure increase dementia risk two to three times.

None of this means ending football.

I played football. I loved football. I believe football teaches leadership, character and teamwork. Millions of former athletes feel the same way.

The challenge is to preserve what is great about football while removing most of the brain trauma that is destroying the lives of former players.

Children can learn to throw, catch, run routes, read defenses, compete and fall in love with football without repeatedly hitting their heads. For today’s kids, flag football is rapidly growing in popularity, and tackle football will still be there when they get older.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

For those who do play tackle football, we should try to eliminate unnecessary contact in practice, change drills that create repetitive impacts, enforce rules that discourage blows to the head and delay the highest-risk forms of contact for children. At the same time, we must accelerate research that will allow us to diagnose CTE before death and develop effective treatments for athletes already suffering.

Prevention and treatment are not competing goals, and we have a moral obligation to do both.

The sports community likes to say that athletics teaches us courage.

Science is now testing ours.

Their views do not necessarily reflect the opinion of The Chronicle editorial board, which is committed to providing a diversity of ideas to our readership.

Read more about our transparency and ethics policies

We have spent nearly two decades establishing that football can cause CTE and how common the disease might be. The evidence is telling us it is time to move on to the questions that matter most: How many cases can we prevent? How many football players can we cure?

As has been the case in each of the past three years, injuries took their toll on Higgins and turned what would have been a good season into a rather disappointing one. He missed two games with separate concussions. Joe Burrow also spent multiple months on injured reserve with a turf toe injury. His absence briefly tanked the offense, though Joe Flacco eventually saved the day for fantasy managers when he took over for Jake Browning. Higgins finished the year with 59 grabs and 846 yards. Neither of those numbers are particularly close to his best marks, but he did bring down a career-high 11 receiving touchdowns, five of which came from Flacco. Despite the modest year, Higgins is still one of the best No. 2 receivers in the NFL, and fantasy managers will keep him in the WR2 mix when early 2026 drafts come around.

Coming off a triple-crown season in 2024, expectations were sky-high for Chase, with most fantasy managers treating him as the 1.01 in drafts. His and the Bengals’ season, however, was quickly derailed by a turf toe injury to Joe Burrow. Chase totaled 10 catches for 73 yards in Jake Browning’s first two starts of the year. He got on track in Browning’s third start and then kept his foot on the gas after Joe Flacco took over under center. Chase put up his usual video game numbers with Flacco and eventually Burrow on the sticks in the second half of the season. From Week 6 onward, Chase amassed 93 catches for 1,038 yards and five scores. He did, however, miss one game late in the year after being hit with a one-game suspension for spitting on Steelers corner Jalen Ramsey in Week 11. It’s strange to call a 1,400-yard season a disappointment, but Chase could have posted another historic campaign had things gone to plan for Burrow and the team. text:
After he spent most of the offseason in the slog of a grueling recovery process, New York Giants wide receiver Malik Nabers is finally close to making his return from a torn ACL and meniscus in his right knee. But, with just over a week until the season opener, Nabers did not commit to being available against the Dallas Cowboys on the campaign's first edition of "Sunday Night Football."

When asked this week about whether he foresees playing in Week 1, Nabers indicated that he will take a cautious approach and not force his way onto the field if his knee is not ready.

"My mind is focused on playing the regular season, playing whenever that is and playing what team it is," Nabers said after Monday's practice. "I'm gonna be making sure that I'm ready to go out there and I'm healthy enough to play all four quarters; that nobody's gotta make sure I'm not in on every play or they have to make sure I got enough snaps to play or my snaps are limited. That's the main focus, is just trying to be out there as much as I can."

Considering the indications throughout the offseason were that Nabers was behind schedule in his recovery, it was a positive sign that he avoided the physically unable to perform list in training camp. In fact, he progressed to participation in team drills by mid-August.

To bounce back from two knee surgeries in less than a year is a big ask, though. Not only did he have his ACL reconstructed, but Nabers also underwent a full repair of his meniscus, which requires a lengthy and more arduous recovery period. The second procedure was to remove scar tissue which had caused stiffness in his knee.

Although he showed few ill effects in practice, there is still work to be done.

"The outside view, I might look 100%," Nabers said. "I make everything look well. Sometimes I run routes and I look on the internet, and I'm like, 'Dang, I was moving kind of crazy.' But when you're in your body and you're in it, you still have some things that you still gotta work on as a football player. You gotta be like, 'I don't feel right doing this cut,' or 'I don't feel right having been hit.'

"I want to be able to come out there and make no mistakes and just be able to fly around and do what I do. I'm getting there."

Nabers said he "feels good" but that he has not yet checked every box on the recovery to-do list. He was coy about what precisely he needs to prove to the team doctors and training staff before he and they agree that he is ready to suit up on game days, but it is "not really anything too big."

Will Malik Nabers return to elite form in 2026?

The last time Nabers was on the field in regular-season action, he was following up a tremendous rookie season with a strong start to his second campaign as a professional. He exploded for 167 receiving yards and two touchdowns two weeks prior to the injury, which hit in Week 4.

The sample size is still fairly modest at just 19 games, but when he is on the field Nabers is among the best receivers in the NFL. At just 21 years old, the former No. 6 overall pick racked up 1,200 yards and seven touchdowns on a poor Giants offense and earned a Pro Bowl honor as a rookie.

The hope is that the serious knee issue does not disrupt what has been an electric start to Nabers' career. He said he does not view this as a situation in which his momentum has been halted.

"When I get out there, I feel like I'll be better than what I was before," Nabers said. "I put in work. I went through everything that I could just to get to this moment. I thought I would probably never run a route again just how stuff was going, but I made it here. I've been through the hardest stuff. So I feel like there's nothing in my life that I can't overcome. The step that I'm going to take forward is going to be better than before."

Egbuka continues to deal with a minor toe injury. Bowles said in recent weeks that he was optimistic about Egbuka’s status, but also wasn’t sure if he’d be available for Week 1. Now he’s hopeful that the 23-year-old wide receiver will be available. The Buccaneers don’t seem too concerned about the injury at this point, making Egbuka a solid WR2 in fantasy drafts.

He was sidelined for a little over two weeks. McMillan is being treated like an afterthought in drafts, going off the board behind Cooper Kupp in the WR6 ranks. McMillan had a nine-target game last year despite missing most of the season and is still just 24 years old. Even with the Ted Hurst hype coming out of camp, there’s a chance for McMillan to be a useful spot starter in fantasy leagues this year.

This comes just days after it was reported that the Buccaneers “are very optimistic” about Egbuka’s Week 1 availability. The second-year receiver has been dealing with a sprained toe that he suffered on Wednesday and hasn’t practiced since. The Buccaneers are 27 days away from their Week 1 game against the Bengals, which will hopefully give Egbuka plenty of time to heal up. Egbuka profiles as a solid WR2 for this season with Mike Evans now with the 49ers.

Egbuka reportedly underwent more testing with a specialist today, who confirmed Ebuka indeed sprained his toe but determined that the injury is “stable.” This is great to hear. The second-year player is a high-ceiling WR2 candidate this season. The Buccaneers face the Bengals in Week 1, in what should be a fantasy-friendly environment.

As Garafolo notes, Bucky Irving said after practice that he thought Egbuka was okay, so this news shouldn’t come as much of a surprise. Still, it’s good to have that comment confirmed so quickly. For now, expect Egbuka to miss some time in practice while recovering from the issue. That will free up routes for rookie Tedd Hurst, who has already made a good impression at training camp. Fantasy managers can keep drafting Egbuka as a high-ceiling WR2 until further notice.

Egbuka reportedly limped off the practice field Wednesday with the help of Bucs trainers and was examined on the sideline for a while before watching the rest of practice with his cleats off. Though the Bucs are likely being cautious with the second-year stud receiver, Egbuka’s status will be well worth monitoring in the coming days. An Egbuka absence would open up an opportunity for WR Ted Hurst, who has impressed throughout the offseason.

Please don’t let Slivon’s corny phrasing distract you from the fact that Hurst is playing well in the X-receiver role that the team drafted him to fill. While WR Jalen McMillan (knee) sits out, Hurst is reportedly displaying “amazing body control” while making leaping grabs, effectively “using his 6-foot-4 height to his advantage.” The third-round rookie is a no-brainer dice roll as a late-round draft target. He is not guaranteed to be a hit, but reports continue to be positive, and in-season rookie breakouts are always a big fantasy factor down the stretch.

McMillan was one of several Bucs wideouts held out of practice yesterday, but it sounds like the others were largely maintenance days. McMillan, on the other hand, is dealing with a rather mysterious injury, given that we have no timeline for his return. It could ultimately be a minor issue, but his absence in practice will free up reps for rookie Ted Hurst. The two are likely competing for the final starting spot in three-receiver sets. McMillan’s knee issue now has Hurst firmly on the sleeper radar for the remainder of camp.

Fox Sports’ Greg Auman reported the three lead Buccaneers receivers got the day off Tuesday. For Godwin, it is a veteran maintenance day as he aims to open the season fully healthy; expect him to see more maintenance days heading into preseason. Egbuka and McMillan are dealing with lower-body soreness and were held out of practice out of precaution. Ultimately, no major injury concerns as the Bucs play it safe with their top three wideouts in training camp.

HOUSTON -- Texans general manager Nick Caserio set a Week 1 deadline for potentially agreeing to a contract extension with quarterback C.J. Stroud this year.

"If we don't get it figured out before the season starts, then it'll be something we address in the offseason," Caserio said Tuesday.

Throughout the offseason, the Texans and Stroud's camp have had negotiations, but nothing has been imminent toward an agreement, according to league sources. To start camp on July 29, Caserio said there was a "possibility" the team could reach a contract extension. But with the regular season now less than two weeks away, the chance of reaching a deal is gradually shrinking.

The Texans picked up Stroud's fifth-year option for 2027 in April, so they have him under contract for at least two more seasons, which provides flexibility to revisit in the offseason.

Stroud isn't naive to the business aspect, but when he was asked about the contract situation to begin training camp he said he's letting his agent, David Mulugheta, handle it.

"You have to keep the main thing the main thing," Stroud said on July 29. "You have to just focus on one day at a time, one play and the football is what's gotten me to even have the conversation, to be able to get a second contract. I have to focus on football."

After being selected No. 2 overall in 2023, Stroud has compiled 28 regular-season wins (seventh most among NFL QBs during that span), a 54.9 QBR (20th), 10,876 passing yards (ninth), 62 touchdowns passing (tied for 14th) and 25 interceptions (12th fewest among quarterbacks with at least 30 starts). He has led the Texans to two AFC South divisional titles and the playoffs in each of his three seasons at the helm.

After a historic rookie season in 2023 in which he threw for 4,108 yards in 15 games with 23 touchdowns and only five interceptions, Stroud's stats have regressed over each of the past two seasons. In 2024, he had 3,727 passing yards with 20 touchdowns and 12 interceptions in 17 games while being sacked 52 times, the second most in the league during the 2024 campaign.

In 2025, he finished the regular season with 3,041 passing yards, 19 touchdowns and eight interceptions while missing three games with a concussion.

Stroud's recent playoff performance has made negotiations complex. He struggling with ball security (seven total turnovers) in two playoff games, including four first-half interceptions in Houston's divisional round loss to the New England Patriots.

title: These former Wisconsin Badgers and Wisconsinites make NFL rosters - Wausau Pilot & Review
authors: Darren Siewert, Kraemer Funeral Homes & Crematory, Ho-Chunk Gaming Wittenberg
description:

text:
USA TODAY NETWORK

There were no Wisconsin Badgers from the 2026 class who made an initial NFL 53-man roster. But there were still a ton of ex-Badgers from previous teams who made the cut Aug. 30 with an NFL team.

This includes four rookies who were Badgers at some point in their career.

Here’s a look at the players who are on initial 53-man rosters (as well as those with injury designations) who played at the University of Wisconsin:

Braelon Allen, running back, New York Jets

The Fond du Lac High School alumnus only appeared in four games last year after the injury bug bit him, but he had 92 carries as a rookie in 2024.

Zack Baun, linebacker, Philadelphia Eagles

The Super Bowl champion and first-team All-Pro pick two seasons ago had another Pro Bowl season last year, with 3.5 sacks, two interceptions and 123 total tackles.

Skyler Bell, wide receiver, Buffalo Bills

Bell spent three years in the UW program, then transferred to UConn and became a record-setting receiver, selected in the fourth round of the 2026 draft.

Keeanu Benton, defensive tackle, Pittsburgh Steelers

The Janesville native started all 17 games last year for the Steelers (5.5 sacks) and has 40 starts and 51 games in his three-year NFL career.

Tyler Biadasz, offensive line, Los Angeles Chargers

He was placed on season-ending injured reserve after tearing his ACL. He signed a three-year contract worth $30 million in the offseason after Washington cut ties. The Amherst native has been durable in his career, starting at least 15 games each of the past five seasons at center with the Dallas Cowboys and Washington Commanders.

Tanor Bortolini, offensive line, Indianapolis Colts

The center has drawn rave reviews for his play over the past two seasons, and he started 16 games for Indy in his second NFL season last year. He’s from Kewaunee.

Leo Chenal, linebacker, Washington Commanders

After four seasons and two rings with Kansas City, Chenal has landed in a new place on a three-year deal worth $24.75 million. The Grantsburg native primarily made his name on special teams with the Chiefs but has 44 starts and seven career sacks.

Michael Deiter, offensive line, Denver Broncos

He suffered a season-ending quad injury earlier in August and placed on injured reserve. He appeared in only two games in 2025 but has spent seven seasons in the league.

Chimere Dike, wide receiver, Tennessee Titans

The Waukesha North alumnus earned first-team All-Pro recognition as a special-teamer last year in his rookie season, and he also caught 48 passes and four touchdowns. He spent most of his career with the Badgers before transferring to Florida for the final season. The Titans drafted him in the fourth round of the 2025 draft.

David Edwards, offensive line, New Orleans Saints

After four years with the Los Angeles Rams and three with Buffalo, the guard moves on to his third team in eight NFL seasons. He played in all 17 games last year and has started 16 games each of the past two seasons.

T.J. Edwards, linebacker, Chicago Bears

The former undrafted free agent will enter his fourth year with Chicago, where he was limited to 10 games after three consecutive years of playing in all 17 games. It’ll be an eighth NFL season for the 30-year-old.

Jake Ferguson, tight end, Dallas Cowboys

The Madison Memorial graduate and former Badgers standout made his second Pro Bowl in 2025, catching 82 passes for 600 yards and a career-best eight touchdowns. He is Barry Alvarez’s grandson, in case you didn’t know.

Isaac Guerendo, running back, San Francisco 49ers

The speedy back played at Wisconsin for four years, transferred to Louisville and became a fourth-round pick in 2024. He’s opening the season on the reserve/PUP list after suffering a torn pectoral in May.

Matt Henningsen, defensive end, Denver Broncos

In a brutal twist, the Menomonee Falls native suffered a torn Achilles for a second straight preseason, this time in his opposite leg, and will miss a second straight year. He played in 34 games for the Broncos in 2022 and 2023.

Nick Herbig, linebacker, Pittsburgh Steelers

He had a breakout season last year in his third NFL campaign, logging 7.5 sacks, an interception and six starts in 15 games.

Joe Huber, offensive line, Minnesota Vikings

The undrafted guard made the Vikings last year and appeared in 12 NFL games.

Alec Ingold, fullback, Los Angeles Chargers

The Bay Port alumnus and 2023 Pro Bowler will join a new team after three seasons in Las Vegas and four in Miami.

Graham Mertz, quarterback, Houston Texans

The former Badgers top recruit is on injured reserve after tearing his ACL.

Riley Nowakowski, fullback, Pittsburgh Steelers

He finished his career with national-champion Indiana and was a fifth-round pick in the 2026 draft. The Marquette University High School alumnus spent five years in the UW program.

Jonathan Taylor, running back, Indianapolis Colts

The former Badgers star running back signed a new two-year deal this offseason worth $44 million after back-to-back Pro Bowl seasons. He’s been a Pro Bowler three his six years and, last year, he had a league-leading 18 touchdowns and 323 attempts.

James Thompson Jr., defensive lineman, San Francisco 49ers

After four seasons with Wisconsin, he transferred to Illinois and made the 49ers as an undrafted free agent this season.

Joe Tippmann, offensive line, New York Jets

The second-round pick in 2023 has become indispensable for the Jets, playing in 50 games over the past three years and starting 48 of them.

Jordan Turner, linebacker, Denver Broncos

He went undrafted but appeared in seven games last year for Denver. The Michigan native spent three seasons with the Badgers before transferring to Michigan State.

Andrew Van Ginkel, linebacker, Minnesota Vikings

After making the Pro Bowl in 2024, he was limited to 12 games last year but still had seven sacks. He’s up to 35.5 sacks in his seven NFL seasons.

Cole Van Lanen, offensive line, Jacksonville Jaguars

The former Bay Port High School and Wisconsin Badgers alumnus spent his 2021 rookie season in Green Bay before getting traded to the Jags. Last year, he played in all 16 games (10 starts) and heads into his sixth NFL campaign.

T.J. Watt, linebacker, Pittsburgh Steelers

The former Badgers star and Pewaukee native has eight Pro Bowl selections in nine NFL seasons, not to mention a defensive player of the year award and four first-team All-Pro nods. The future Hall of Famer played in 14 games last year for Pittsburgh.

CJ Williams, wide receiver, Jacksonville Jaguars

After two seasons with the Badgers, he finished his career at Stanford and was taken in the sixth round of the 2026 NFL Draft.

Hunter Wohler, safety, Indianapolis Colts

After an injury short-circuited the Muskego native’s rookie season, and he had an impressive preseason to make the roster this time around.

Other Wisconsin connections on 53-man rosters

Nick Bellore, linebacker, Washington Commanders. He’s already announced his retirement but remains on the reserve/retired list with Washington. The 15-year NFL veteran from Whitefish Bay made two Pro Bowls in his career, often working as a special-teams ace.

Ben Bredeson, offensive line, Tampa Bay Buccaneers. The guard out of Arrowhead High School and Michigan has six NFL seasons under his belt, and he’s started every game he’s played over the last three years. This will be his third season with the Bucs after appearing in 11 contests last year.

Max Bredeson, fullback, Minnesota Vikings. The Arrowhead High School alumnus attended Michigan and was taken in the fifth round of the 2026 draft. He is, as you might imagine, Ben’s younger brother.

Mike Caliendo, offensive line, Kansas City Chiefs. The Brookfield East alumnus appeared in all 17 games each of the past two seasons. The undrafted lineman out of Western Michigan heads into his fourth NFL season.

Jon Gaines II, offensive lineman, Arizona Cardinals. The offensive lineman from Marquette University High School and UCLA enters his fourth year in the NFL. After injury slowed the start of his career, he has played in 30 games over the past two seasons, including five starts last year.

Skyler Gill-Howard, defensive tackle, Detroit Lions. The Greenfield High School alumnus was drafted in the sixth round out of Texas Tech.

Luke Goedeke, offensive line, Tampa Bay Buccaneers. The Valders High School alumnus out of Central Michigan heads into his fifth season. Like his teammate Ben Bredeson, he’s started every game he’s played over the last three years, playing at right tackle, including 11 games last year.

Shelby Harris, defensive line, New York Giants. The Homestead High School graduate enters his 12th NFL season in a new home after three seasons with the Browns. He just turned 35.

George Kittle, tight end, San Francisco 49ers. One of the top players at his position for several years, Kittle was born in Madison.

Tanner Koziol, tight end, Jacksonville Jaguars. He never played for Wisconsin but did commit to transfer there before switching gears and heading for Houston instead. The Jaguars made him a fifth-round draft choice in 2026.

JC Latham, offensive line, Tennessee Titans. The Milwaukee-area native began his high school career at Catholic Memorial before the Titans made him the seventh overall pick in 2024 out of Alabama. He has started 30 games over two seasons at tackle.

Hunter Luepke, fullback, Dallas Cowboys. The North Dakota State alumnus hails from Spencer and has started nine games and appeared in 50 overall in three seasons.

Quinn Meinerz, offensive line, Denver Broncos. Having become one of the better offensive linemen in football (and earning first-team All-Pro last year), the Hartford High School and University of Wisconsin-Whitewater alumnus enters his sixth NFL season.

Marcus Mbow, offensive line, New York Giants. The graduate of Purdue University attended Wauwatosa East High School. He appeared in 13 games last year for the Giants, including three starts, after getting taken in the fifth round of the 2025 draft.

Will McDonald, edge rusher, New York Jets. The Waukesha North High School alumnus has 21.5 sacks over three seasons after the Jets made him a first-round pick in 2023.

Max Melton, cornerback, Arizona Cardinals. The third-year cornerback out of Rutgers is the brother of Packers receiver Bo Melton.

Eric Murray, safety, Jacksonville Jaguars. The Milwaukee Riverside alumnus is 32 and entering his second season with the Jaguars and 11th NFL season overall. He started 12 games last year, with an interception and a forced fumble. Murray previously played five years with the Houston Texans.

Billy Schrauth, offensive line, Tampa Bay Buccaneers. From St. Mary’s Springs in Fond du Lac, Schrauth played college football at Notre Dame and was taken in the fifth round of the 2026 draft.

Peter Skoronski, offensive line, Tennessee Titans. The fourth-year offensive lineman, taken 11th overall in the 2023 draft, is the grandson of Packers Hall of Famer Bob Skoronski.

Jack Strand, quarterback, Atlanta Falcons. The Division II All-American who played at Minnesota State-Mankato signed as an undrafted free agent and made the cut for a team that kept a whopping four quarterbacks. Strand is from Bloomer, Wisconsin.

Tress Way, punter, Washington Commanders. The 12-year NFL veteran and three-time Pro Bowler is the brother-in-law of Brewers second baseman Brice Turang.

Payton Wilson, linebacker, Pittsburgh Steelers. The brother of Milwaukee Brewers pitcher Bryse Wilson had two sacks and an interception last year. He has appeared in all 34 games over the past two years.

Practice squad players from the University of Wisconsin

Vinny Anthony, wide receiver, Atlanta Falcons

Ben Barten, defensive line, New York Giants (Stratford High School)

Logan Brown, offensive line, Seattle Seahawks (started at UW, finished at Kansas)

Nyzier Fourqurean, cornerback, Los Angeles Rams

Riley Mahlman, offensive line, Atlanta Falcons

Jack Nelson, offensive line, Minnesota Vikings (Stoughton High School)

Dare Ogunbowale, running back, Las Vegas Raiders (Marquette University High School)

Will Pauling, wide receiver, San Francisco 49ers (started at UW, finished at Notre Dame)

Parker Petersen, defensive tackle, Carolina Panthers

Mason Reiger, linebacker, Philadelphia Eagles

Jay’Viar Suggs, defensive line, New Orleans Saints

Nolan Rucci, offensive tackle, Indianapolis Colts (started at UW, finished at Penn State)

Other practice squad players from the state

Kristian Welch, linebacker, Green Bay Packers (Iola-Scandinavia High School)

Cole Wisniewski, safety, Philadelphia Eagles (Sparta High School)

Did we miss any? Email jr.radcliffe@jrn.com.

title: NFL Injury Report & Analysis: Making Sense of the PUP List and IR | RotoWire
description:
The first thing to understand for is the Physically Unable to Perform (PUP) list.
With training camp over the Active/PUP list is no longer available to teams.
Instead, franchises must now utilize the Reserve/PUP list for these designated players.
If a player is ineligible for the PUP list but becomes injured, teams must now consider using the injured reserve (IR).
IR and PUP list designations may be frustrating, but it does provide a degree of clarity regarding a player's status.
text:
NFL teams have trimmed down their rosters to 53 players, with injuries and health influencing countless decisions around the league. For the first in-season NFL injury report, understanding transactional terms used in the process can be beneficial on draft day especially for opportunistic fantasy managers able to draft a player at a discounted rate.

The first thing to understand for is the Physically Unable to Perform (PUP) list. With training camp over the Active/PUP list is no longer available to teams. Instead, franchises must now utilize the Reserve/PUP list for these designated players. Players placed on the Reserve/PUP do not count toward the team's 53-man roster and cannot appear in the team's first four regular season contests. This season, players can participate in a 21-day practice period while still stashed on the Reserve/PUP list after the team has played in two regular season games. This allows medical teams to better evaluate players in anticipation of their return following the team's fourth game played. If the player is not activated to the 53-man roster during this window, they must sit out the remainder of the year. Notable players starting the year on the Reserve/PUP include Green Bay's Micah Parsons and Seattle running back Zach Charbonnet. Receiver Alec Pierce was activated off the PUP list late last week and is hoping to be ready for Week 1 after undergoing offseason ankle surgery.

If a player is ineligible for the PUP list but becomes injured, teams must now consider using the injured reserve (IR). Like the PUP list, any player placed on the IR must miss a minimum of four weeks. A player can only return from an IR designation twice a season, and each team is granted a total of eight IR-to-return designations for the year. The number grows to 10 if they make the playoffs. Like the PUP list, these players can utilize a three-week window to ramp up their activity level. At the conclusion of the 21 days, the player must be activated, placed on season-ending IR, or be released or traded. Several big names were allotted IR designations entering the regular season including James Conner, Tank Dell, Jordyn Tyson and Christian Kirk.

IR and PUP list designations may be frustrating, but it does provide a degree of clarity regarding a player's status. Once a player is placed on either list, those willing to invest in him know they will have to proceed without the individual for at least four weeks. The use of the IR can also be used as a good indicator of the health of another player on the team's roster. For example, Conner's designation in Arizona suggests the team feels good about Jeremiyah Love's availability for Week 1. The rookie running back is working his way back from a high-ankle sprain suffered August 13 but is "progressing really well" according to head coach Mike LaFleur.

Turf Burns

Emeka Egbuka: The second-year wide receiver has been sidelined since August 12 when he suffered a toe sprain in practice. Toe sprains, particularly those involving the big toe, can be extremely limiting, especially for wideouts. The big toe is crucial in driving the foot off the ground when running or jumping while also withstanding the high amount of stress that comes with weight bearing. Egbuka's Week 1 availability remains in doubt, and I'm moving him down my draft board just a bit.

Puka Nacua: The Rams wideout has been limited by soreness in a specific muscle in his core. Nacua's injury involves the psoas muscle. The psoas sits just under the ribs at the lower spine. Its fibers run down through the pelvis, anchoring to the upper femur. It merges with another muscle, the iliacus, to form the iliopsoas, one of the primary hip flexors. Based on this location, a psoas injury can result in pain in the lower back, groin or hip, and be very limiting. Fortunately, Nacua was able to return to practice Sunday, and it looks like he will avoid any missed time. Look for the Rams to handle him conservatively in the days leading up to Week 1.

Luther Burden: In Chicago, Burden is recovering from a groin injury sustained in the early days of training camp. The timeline suggests Burden's injury was a more moderate strain. He has resumed limited practice, and the team is optimistic he will be in uniform for Week 1.

Chris Olave: Given Olave's checkered NFL injury history, his fans had to hate seeing him leave practice early last week. The team relayed he simply had the wind knocked out of him and it opted to be cautious with his care. He was back at practice the next day and remains the top target in New Orleans.

Wan'Dale Robinson: The Titans receiver appears to have avoided a concussion after taking a hard hit in a joint practice with the Bears. The medical staff will monitor his status for any late developing signs or symptoms, but for now he appears okay.

Zach Charbonnet: We know Charbonnet will miss at least the first four weeks of the regular season as he recovers from the anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) tear sustained in postseason. The timing of his injury made a Week 1 return unlikely, and an exact target date remains uncertain. Rookie Jadarian Price is expected to start for Seattle with George Holani also set for carries. If Price runs well, the Seahawks could opt for an even more cautious approach with Charbonnet's care to ensure his long-term health. As a result, Charbonnet's fantasy value seems tied to the success of Price.

text:
PHILADELPHIA — Philadelphia Eagles general manager Howie Roseman met with reporters Monday afternoon after the franchise cut its roster to 53 players.

The Athletic’s Zach Berman and Brooks Kubena provide their takeaways from the long-time executive’s assessment of the team’s decisions.

Why did the Eagles keep four QBs?

Roseman said the Eagles kept all four quarterbacks — Jalen Hurts, Tanner McKee, Andy Dalton and fifth-round rookie Cole Payton — because it is the “most important position in sports.”

“I feel like all those guys have value for our team,” Roseman said. “Some of them obviously, some is short-term value, some is long-term value — when you think about Cole. So, just as we went through the process here, just thought it was the right thing to do for our football team.”

The Roseman-era Eagles have valued quarterback depth, but that has generally meant securing three. This is the first time they have kept four on their initial roster since at least 2010. One likely reason, although Roseman did not confirm it, is that neither McKee nor Dalton “won” the backup battle. Asked who the QB2 is, Roseman said he’d keep the decision “close to the vest.”

Two other factors: The Eagles wanted to keep Payton for his development or future trade value, a lesson reinforced when the Green Bay Packers flipped former Eagles practice-squad quarterback Kyle McCord for a 2028 sixth-round pick. And Dalton, a vested veteran, could have pursued a roster spot elsewhere rather than sign with Philadelphia’s practice squad.

Dalton did not commit Friday when asked if he’d stay on the practice squad. The Eagles also kept wide receiver Elijah Moore, another vested veteran, while building out a practice squad with youth.

“It’s easy to say, ‘Hey, put this guy on the practice squad, and you’ll get him back, and he’s a vested vet,'” Roseman said. “But understanding that those guys have other options to go other places. And when you say that to a veteran and they say, ‘Hey, I’m going to explore my options,’ and you’ve got 31 other teams, and they say, ‘We’ll give you a 53-man spot,’ now you lose that guy.”

Dalton, a 16-year veteran, offers experience and familiarity with the system. McKee, a 2023 sixth-round pick entering the final year of his contract, struggled in the preseason and likely lost trade value. Payton, who debuted on the punt coverage team in the preseason finale, can develop in the background with the full four years of his rookie contract ahead of him.

“These guys are valuable,” Roseman said. “They take time to develop. At the same time, that position is so valuable to this organization over a long period of time. So, want to be strong there. I think both those guys behind Jalen have value and have shown that over the course of their careers. And we kind of take all the information at our disposal to make all these decisions.” — Kubena

Confidence in Greenard’s return from injury

Roseman pointed out that edge rusher Jonathan Greenard’s inclusion on the 53-man roster, and not the PUP list, “shows that we anticipate him playing sooner rather than later.” Roseman did not disclose a recovery timetable, opting to keep that, too, “close to the vest.” Had the Eagles placed Greenard on the PUP list, he would have had to miss at least four games.

Defensive coordinator Vic Fangio said Greenard will have to learn new things in this defense’s system, namely coverage responsibilities Greenard has yet to experience across six seasons with the Houston Texans and Minnesota Vikings. Roseman acknowledged there will be a learning curve for Greenard, but voiced his confidence in Greenard’s ability to contribute quickly.

“Guy’s a tremendous football player,” Roseman said. “He’s got a tremendous ability to affect the quarterback. He’s gonna come back in tremendous shape. I think that you saw, the D-line’s obviously a position of emphasis for us — always. The guy fits what we do. Yeah, there’ll be some things that will be a little bit different. And we’ll get him up to speed, but we expect him to have a high impact on this team this season. And for all accounts of what he’s done and how he works and how he leads, he’s as advertised.” — Kubena

Why six WRs — plus thoughts on Lemon’s post-injury progress

The Eagles are keeping six wide receivers on their roster for the first time since they hired coach Nick Sirianni in 2021. They enjoyed having both DeVonta Smith and former wide receiver A.J. Brown under contract for four seasons. Roseman had described the overhauled room within an overhauled system as a “basketball squad” of versatility. They traded up to pick Makai Lemon at No. 20, and added veterans Hollywood Brown, Dontayvion Wicks and Moore.

Lemon had a rough debut in the preseason finale after returning from a second hamstring injury that sidelined him for most of training camp. Second-round pick Eli Stowers also missed time in training camp with a hamstring injury. Roseman voiced “tremendous confidence” in both rookies.

“Obviously, they had some setbacks here physically,” Roseman said. “And we looked at that as a staff and a group. Maybe we can figure out some changes here to get those guys going a little bit sooner as from a skill-position perspective. But don’t have any doubt about what they’re going to be in the NFL over time. Still believe that they’re going to contribute to our 2026.”

Moore’s inclusion on the 53-man roster should supplement Lemon’s learning curve. Moore, a sixth-year veteran, offers inside-outside versatility and has been involved in the same sort of motions Lemon took on upon his return. Given Moore’s one-year, $1.3 million contract, which included no guaranteed money, it was perceived that the Eagles could try to move him to their practice squad.

Roseman said Moore’s strong training camp reinforced the impression the Eagles formed during the 2021 pre-draft process. After a disappointing previous season in Buffalo and Denver, Moore consistently created separation and made plays — including two long touchdowns in practice — convincing the Eagles he was too dependable to risk losing. — Kubena

Why the Eagles waived the international players

The Eagles did not keep Uar Bernard and Joshua Weru from the International Player Pathway program on the 53-man roster, but they were able to sign both to the practice squad Monday. Roseman explained there’s never comfort in exposing players to waivers. The front office tries to take a snapshot of what other teams see when deciding who to keep. He recognized that Bernard and Weru have development ahead of them. Vic Fangio previously said they’re “light years away.”

“From our perspective, development is real,” Roseman said. “These guys have tremendous ability to be developed. They want to be developed. They have tools in their body, they’ve got great character, but it’s new to them.”

The point was made that the Eagles kept Jordan Mailata on the roster for two seasons before he played in a game. Roseman said that “nobody’s going to see a Jordan Mailata again.”

“He had just a unique combination of size, strength, athleticism, and pro experience as an athlete. I think sometimes we forget Uar has never played organized sports before,” Roseman said. “It’s a different bar. I think if we’re just judging everyone through the lens of Jordan Mailata, it’s going to be hard to give these guys a fair chance. Still very excited about them, really glad that they did get through. Certainly wasn’t certain about that, but I’m glad they’re back here.” — Berman

Is Zach Ertz next at tight end?

There’s intrigue about whether the Eagles will bring back Zach Ertz, who is almost nine months past a torn ACL suffered last December and has expressed interest in returning to Philadelphia. Ertz spent the first eight years of his career with the Eagles and caught the game-winning touchdown in Super Bowl LII. He’s 10 catches behind Harold Carmichael for the most in franchise history.

“First, I’d say what an unbelievable player, what an unbelievable person,” Roseman said. “Tremendous respect for him. At the same time, love what we have going in our tight end room too. So I would say, I have talked to Zach over a period of time — obviously rehabbing his ACL and the relationship, just like a lot of our former players who’ve been here — but like anything else, we wouldn’t get into any conversations about anything other than from a big-picture perspective.”

The Eagles kept four tight ends: Dallas Goedert, Johnny Mundt, Eli Stowers and E.J. Jenkins. Roseman explained that the decision to keep Jenkins came down to his improvement during his time with the Eagles — he was a member of the Super Bowl roster in 2024 and has bounced between the practice squad and the 53-man roster. A converted wide receiver listed at 6-foot-6 and 245 pounds, Jenkins is now 260 pounds and has developed into a better blocker who can also contribute on special teams, Roseman said.

“You see in this league where the position is going, where it’s trending,” Roseman said. “A lot of similar offensive systems to some of the things that we’re running where these wide tight ends, they’re highly valued in free agency, they’re highly valued in the draft.” — Berman

Youth vs. veterans on bottom of roster

The Eagles had a league-high four players claimed off waivers Monday, a sign of interest in the roster’s young players. The Eagles did not want to risk the chance that some of the vested veterans would choose to sign elsewhere rather than return to the Eagles’ practice squad, which was why Roseman kept them on the roster over developmental players. (Moore, Dalton, Fred Johnson and Jonathan Jones are examples of players who might fit in this category.) Roseman said the practice squad is younger than in previous seasons.

The general manager admitted, though, that the Eagles lost more players than they anticipated to waivers. He said the claim rate is usually 4 percent. In the Eagles’ case, 13.8 percent of the players who were claimed in the NFL were from their roster (tackles Cameron Williams and Myles Hinton; tight end Cameron Latu and defensive back Kapena Gushiken).

“That’s the risk of doing business, and don’t feel good about that,” Roseman said. “Don’t feel good about losing those guys. We lost two draft picks. We lost a special teamer, a tight end who had 10 special teams tackles for us last year and a blocked kick. Don’t feel good about that. We lost a young defensive back that we liked. That goes along with this. You can’t sit here and feel tremendously good when you’re losing players. We’ll do our best to try to replenish that.” — Berman

Two players not on the active roster — tight end Caleb Lohner (injured reserve) and offensive lineman Nick Gargiulo (reserve/PUP list) — continue to rehab from their respective injuries.

Broncos injury report

DNP: WR Marvin Mims (bruise)

Side field: OLB Que Robinson (undisclosed)

text:
Kyle Long walked out of Raymond James Stadium in Tampa on a cool February night in 2021 when the realization hit him.

One year removed from his retirement as an offensive lineman for the Chicago Bears, Long was now building a media career at CBS Sports and had just finished covering his first Super Bowl. He strolled the parking lot with Pro Football Hall of Fame coach Bill Cowher, his now-colleague, the chaos from the day slowly dissipating around them. But there was one aspect of the game Long couldn’t get out of his head.

He turned to Cowher: “Maybe I’m a guy that can help Patrick Mahomes.”

The Tampa Bay Buccaneers battered the Kansas City Chiefs star quarterback in their 31-9 Super Bowl 55 win that day. Behind a makeshift offensive line, Mahomes was sacked three times and was pressured on 29 of his 56 dropbacks, the most of any quarterback in Super Bowl history. For the first time as a pro, Mahomes lost a game by double digits, and his team never scored a touchdown.

Watching this, with a press pass on instead of pads, left Long infuriated. The next day, he sent Mahomes a message.

“There should have been a million offensive linemen that called him and said, whatever you need, I’ll do it in jeans and boots,” Long said in a conversation with The Athletic this summer. “That’s pretty much what the message was that I sent him. And he was like, get a hold of Andy (Reid), let’s make this thing happen.”

One month later, Long signed with the Chiefs. Retirement postponed.

Nothing beats an underdog story. But the story of unretirement comes pretty close, a narrative complete with anticipation, pressure and perseverance. This week, three-time NFL Defensive Player of the Year Aaron Donald announced his return to the Los Angeles Rams more than two years after he retired from football. Donald, 35, makes a Rams roster that was already the Super Bowl favorite look invincible. That is, if he can return to the form that made him a future Hall of Famer in the first place.

Players coming back, despite their ages or injuries, can humanize even the biggest stars. Michael Jordan was already a three-time NBA champion when he retired to try his hand in baseball. Then he said, “I’m back,” and embarked on another NBA three-peat. Michael Phelps won 18 Olympic gold medals when he retired after the 2012 Games; he came back and won five more in 2016.

Some might say these stars should be satisfied. Let them ride off into the sunset and make room for the next generation. But for athletes wired on competitive drive, there comes a time when more than medals, rings or accolades are on the line. It gets personal.

Lindsey Vonn returned to competitive skiing at 40 in the lead-up to the 2026 Winter Olympics, citing a deep love for the sport, speed and competition. She made it to Cortina d’Ampezzo, but crashed during her downhill run and was airlifted out with a devastating injury. This summer, tennis great Serena Williams returned to the singles court at Wimbledon after almost four years away, where she lost in the first round and injured her knee. At 44 years old, she’s set to return to the U.S. Open this month, competing in doubles with her sister Venus, even if Wimbledon didn’t go her way.

In football, returning from retirement comes with added challenges. The physicality of the game puts players on tight timelines, and any extended period away only makes it harder to get back into game shape.

Tight end Rob Gronkowski came out of a one-year retirement to join his old teammate Tom Brady in Tampa Bay in 2020, winning that ring that Long watched from the crowd. Two years later, Brady announced his own retirement, only to backtrack 40 days later and return for one final season at 45 years old, becoming the oldest quarterback to start and win a game.

Quarterback Brett Favre had an even longer grapple with retirement. Favre first retired after the 2007 season with the Green Bay Packers and then following the 2008 season with the New York Jets. He returned to the field both times.

“I don’t know for me if it’s ever easy,” Favre told reporters, announcing his official retirement after the 2010 season with the Minnesota Vikings. “I’m sure throughout this year the comment has been made that, ‘We’ll wait and see in August or September,’ and that’s fine. It’s time. I’m OK with it.”

Just as recently as 2025, the Indianapolis Colts called up 44-year-old Philip Rivers to revitalize their injury-riddled quarterback room, five years removed from Rivers’ last snap.

So, what fuels a comeback? And how does a player prepare for a return to the gridiron? Each athlete’s motivation is unique. But across interviews with multiple NFL players, one thing became clear: a desire to forgo the second-guessing for a second chance, no matter how it ends up.

“I left with a little bit of almost a bad taste in my mouth the first time I retired just because (I thought): Was this the right decision? Was it not? I was just so iffy on it,” said former linebacker Kyle Emanuel, who retired after the 2019 season with the Los Angeles Chargers and rejoined the league one year later. “The fact that I was able to come back, get another year, regardless if it went the way I envisioned or not, I think it was huge for me.”

Tight end Darren Waller was halfway into his 2023 season with the New York Giants when he began to seriously consider retirement. He contemplated his decision in the months following that season, telling The Athletic’s Dan Duggan at the time: “It’s really the idea of signing up for another journey. It’s tough, it’s long, it requires a lot. And if you’re not fully bought into every single thing of the process, it’s going to be tough.”

Multiple athletes shared the same sentiment. Why return to the game if you can’t — mentally, physically, emotionally — give it your all? Reflecting this summer, Waller reiterated the pressure felt during an NFL season.

“The game’s fast. You’re moving from one thing to the next,” he said. “Your nervous system’s always heightened because you’ve got to be ready for so much pressure, stress, pain, high highs. So, it was a big adjustment for me to slow my life down the way that I had to and needed to.”

Waller announced his retirement in June 2023 at 31. Injuries caused him to miss 19 games over his last three years. Waller also battled a drug and alcohol addiction early in his career, and he was suspended the entire 2017 season for violating the NFL’s substance abuse policy. But no factor played a more impactful role in Waller’s decision to step away than his desire to look inward.

“This life that looks good on paper and is — by all means — successful by the common American definition of success. But it’s like, it doesn’t feel right or feel aligned within me,” Waller said. “Everybody would choose my life from the outside looking in, but I am not necessarily choosing my life for myself. So what needs to change? I feel like that required me to remove myself from performing to slow everything down, strip a lot of things away and just walk through that process.”

Emanuel, the linebacker who retired after four seasons with the Chargers, was almost moved to tears sitting at his locker after his team’s 2019 divisional-round loss to the New England Patriots, thinking: “Was that my last game?” For a former fifth-round pick whose contract had just expired, retirement felt like something always lurking in his rearview mirror.

“You hear so much when you’re in the NFL: It’s short-lived. You just never know. Injuries happen. You get cut,” Emanuel said. “I didn’t really know what I wanted to do next. That part of it was always on my mind, actually.”

As Long remembers it, retirement wasn’t a common topic discussed between teammates in the locker room. It silently crept around as what Long called the “Grim Reaper,” usually someone from the scouting or player personnel department, who would ask for certain players to meet the coach in his office during roster decision time, like training camp or the end of a season. But internally, for Long, contemplating retirement came back to a single mantra: “They always say if you don’t recognize yourself on film, that’s the day you should pack your s—.”

“I was so beat up, and I never gave myself time to recover; I was always playing,” Long said. “There’s no void in the calendar where you can just take a breath and take a beat and get your body right.”

Speaking to reporters after announcing his comeback, Donald expressed confidence in his ability to play at a high level. Donald ramped up workouts in the months leading up to his final decision and reconnected with the speed trainer he had worked with since high school. “Once you choose to come back, you’re all the way back in,” he said. “You can’t be halfway in it. You have to be all the way in it.”

Often the biggest, strongest players on the field, linemen take the hardest hits day in and day out. Staying in football-ready shape, at the size and speed of a lineman, is uniquely challenging. Long said he weighed around 330 pounds during his prime days as an NFL player. After spending the 2020 season in retirement, he said he was down to 270 pounds.

That meant that when he decided to come back, there was work to do. He remembers calling one of his former teammates, Taylor Boggs, to train. Long appreciated Boggs’ work ethic, and the two of them worked out around Boggs’ cul-de-sac in Arizona over the summer, pushing sleds and carrying dumbbells. No elite training academy, Long said, “just moving heavy s—.”

“Offensive linemen, we’re different. We’re like Wagyu beef,” Long said. “If you want the best quality beef, if you want the tastiest bite, you got to treat us a little bit and you got to get us big. I’m 300 (pounds) walking around right now. People say, ‘Are you sick? You look skinny.’ I was 330 pounds when I played, and you have to maintain the weight.”

Getting football-ready is also about more than being successful on the field. It’s about avoiding injury.

Center Frank Ragnow attempted to come out of retirement to join the Detroit Lions midway through the 2025 season, five months after he announced his farewell from the game at 29. The return of the four-time Pro Bowler excited the Detroit fan base, until the Lions medical team discovered a Grade 3 hamstring strain during Ragnow’s physical that kept him sidelined.

In June, Ragnow opened up about his comeback attempt at an event in Michigan, telling reporters he was trying to will himself to play, “and my body was telling me otherwise.” The “romantic” comeback story he imagined for himself turned out too good to be true.

“I tried to avoid games, tried to distract myself from it, and then I started watching games, and that’s when I felt guilt,” Ragnow said. “(Quarterback) Jared (Goff’s) getting hit, that’s my guy; those are my guys, and they’re struggling. And then I made a bonehead decision and tried to get ready to play and got hurt. That was tough.”

Mental prep is another key factor. In his year off, Waller said he spent time in therapy. He went on retreats and solo trips across the world, spending time in nature and developing his sound as a musician. He said the time away helped him find validation outside of football — something he struggled with as a young player.

Still, a comeback didn’t cross Waller’s mind until just a few weeks before he signed with the Miami Dolphins in July 2025. Waller said the pieces seemed to fall in place after he watched the Dolphins trade tight end Jonnu Smith to the Pittsburgh Steelers, and his pre-existing relationship with then-offensive coordinator Frank Smith, who was Waller’s tight end coach with the Oakland and Las Vegas Raiders, helped make the Sunshine State feel like a natural fit.

Waller flew in for training camp, embracing his new role as the 33-year-old veteran teammate. And his leadership was tested early after a hip injury during camp sidelined him through the first three games of the season.

“This isn’t the start to my comeback journey that anybody would have written in a storybook. But that’s kind of just how life is,” Waller said. “All of that was worth it for as good as it felt coming back in that first game.”

During his first game, Waller scored two touchdowns and led the Dolphins to their first win of the season.

“I haven’t played in almost two years, and I actually feel like I’m riding a bike and I can still take a game over,” Waller said. “That’s as good as you can ask for as a player.”

Waller played in nine total games for the Dolphins during the 2025 campaign, recording 24 catches, 283 yards and six touchdowns. He spent much of this offseason as a free agent before signing last month with the Carolina Panthers.

“I’ve been training since the day after the Super Bowl. I’m not doing all this for nothing,” Waller said before signing with the Panthers. “I feel like my body is definitely way more calloused than it was going into the Dolphins last year. It has not been two years since I last sprinted. I sprinted today in the house.”

But not every comeback gets adorned with touchdowns and playing time. While second-guessing his retirement decision, Emanuel heard from his agent that a coach had asked about him at the 2020 Scouting Combine. It piqued his interest, and Emanuel decided he would give the league another go, but team visits were a challenge as the COVID-19 pandemic hit its peak.

Eventually, the Raiders flew Emanuel out two weeks into their training camp, and after meeting with then-GM Mike Mayock and head coach Jon Gruden, Emanuel was back on an NFL roster. He described those initial days as a mental grind, learning a new system around teammates who were already familiar with each other and the playbook. But it was in the small moments where Emanuel found what he missed most.

“I knew I would miss the guys in the locker room. I knew I would miss competing on Saturdays or Sundays. I never thought I would miss training camp,” Emanuel said. “I still remember texting one of my buddies in there, calling him and telling him that that was not something I expected.”

Emanuel spent most of his time on the Raiders’ practice squad during the 2020 season. He was traded to the Houston Texans in October, where he played in seven games. He never officially retired again, but he did find his place off the field. Emanuel now works as a color commentator for his alma mater, North Dakota State University, and has a full-time job in construction. He has a more relaxed mindset, knowing his football days are behind him.

“It wasn’t like there were a bunch of teams knocking at my door,” Emanuel said. “I was still open to it, potentially playing again, but it didn’t happen, and I was OK with that.”

For as exciting as a comeback can be, it’s also unpredictable. Injuries and learning curves are part of the game, no matter a player’s experience, success, or motivations.

Long’s comeback in Kansas City was derailed by a knee injury he suffered during OTAs in June. He started the season on the physically unable to perform list. By season’s end, due to the lingering injury and the emergence of rookie Trey Smith, Long did not play a single game snap for Kansas City. So, did his comeback scratch the itch?

“Not quite,” Long said, candidly.

Now back to his analyst gig at CBS, Long said he’s thankful to have found a career that keeps him close to football. And even if his comeback season didn’t come with highlight plays or a Super Bowl ring — he’ll remind you the Chiefs won back-to-back Lombardi trophies in the two years following his second retirement — he knew where he needed to be next.

“I was aware that this was probably the end,” Long said. “I did exit meetings in Kansas City, but coach (Andy) Heck wanted me back, the offensive line coach. They were excited to have me. I let him know, look, I’m going home. I have to be able to shut it off. I’m gonna shut it off. I’m gonna be a dad now.

“Now here we are. It’s four years later. I just sent (center) Creed Humphrey and (right guard) Trey Smith a picture of my 4-year-old, and I was like, ‘Remember when this was a little bump?’”

For Long, it was time for Dad-mode.

For Donald, it’s time for another shot on the field. When he initially retired, Donald said: “I’m complete. I’m full.” He’s not the first to step back and challenge those emotions.

The plot is storybook-worthy: Donald uniting with a roster equipped with quarterback Matthew Stafford, off his first MVP award, and reigning Defensive Player of the Year Myles Garrett, all culminating with the backdrop of Super Bowl 61 in the Rams’ home SoFi Stadium. But the mental clarity of giving it one more go will ultimately define Donald’s return, no matter the successes or failures.

It will be thrilling, yet unpredictable. That’s just how comebacks go.

text:
Chicago Bears general manager Ryan Poles cast doubt on cornerback Kyler Gordon's future with the team.

"I don't know," Poles said Tuesday when asked whether Gordon will play for the Bears again. "I hope so. I still have hope there. He's going to have to continue to work hard and get back to playing football again."

Gordon missed all of spring workouts and training camp with what Poles previously characterized as a "delay" in his recovery from a calf injury. The 2022 second-round pick was placed on the physically unable to perform list on July 28 and remained there as the Bears cut down their roster to 53 players ahead of Sunday's deadline.

After being placed on reserve/PUP, Gordon will have to miss the Bears' first four games. He is eligible to return to practice on Sept. 21.

Poles declined to give specifics about Gordon's injury or what has caused the delay in his rehabilitation process. Gordon has been on site at Halas Hall working with the Bears' training staff and has been seen on the sideline at several training camp practices and Chicago's preseason opener against the Browns.

"Some of these guys they also have other people that they work with too," Poles said. "But yeah, he's working."

The Bears gave Gordon a three-year, $40 million contract extension last offseason but did not see an immediate return on investment after the cornerback missed nearly all of training camp in 2025. He was limited to five games, including both of the Bears' playoff matchups, after two separate stints on injured reserve.

In July, Poles discussed the "frustrations" shared by both the team and Gordon over his struggles to remain healthy. Coach Ben Johnson remained tight-lipped on multiple occasions when asked about Gordon's status, noting on Aug. 18 that he had seen Gordon in the building "rehabbing" and that "there's a plan and he's working toward the plan."

"I really, I wish I had more for you all -- but any time you have an injury and you're coming back from something there's discomfort that you have to push through and that's what it comes down to," Poles said. "So we haven't been able to get over that hump and we're not progressing as fast as we'd like. That's really all I have to say about that."

Chicago turned to fourth-round rookie Malik Muhammad in Gordon's absence during training camp. Muhammad is expected to be Chicago's starting nickel while Clark Phillips III, who came to Chicago along with a 2027 fifth-round pick in exchange for the Bears sending defensive tackle Gervon Dexter Sr. to Atlanta, has experience in both the slot and at outside cornerback.

"He's capable of both, but since he's been in the league, he's been outside, so we'll see where we start him off and go from there," Poles said.

In the meantime, the Bears wait to see if Gordon can make enough progress in his rehab to return to practice.

"We'll see when [Gordon] comes back," Poles said. "I don't have a timetable. We'll see how that goes."
