FLORHAM PARK, N.J. (AP) — Rookie Cade Klubnik will head into the regular season as the New York Jets' backup quarterback behind Geno Smith.

The fourth-rounder out of Clemson received the bulk of the snaps during the three preseason games and had a solid training camp performance, giving the Jets confidence he can step in Smith's place if needed.

"He's our backup quarterback," coach Aaron Glenn said Monday while announcing the decision. “And he'll do a good job.”

Glenn added that the Jets are still likely to add another quarterback to their practice squad. They released Bailey Zappe on Sunday. They also waived Brady Cook, who was claimed Monday by Miami. Cook started the final four games as a rookie last season.

Klubnik started the Jets' preseason opener against Tampa Bay and led New York to scores on his two drives. He came in after one series by Smith the following week at Pittsburgh and then played the first half of the preseason finale against the Giants.

Klubnik was 21 of 34 for 190 yards with no touchdowns and one interception in the three preseason games.

“There’s just a confidence in how he operates and what he’s done in practice, what he’s done in the games,” Glenn said. “I don’t think anybody ever said there weren’t going to be hiccups. I mean, he’s a rookie, but he’s always learning, he’s a very intelligent guy.”

“He's improved over the course of training camp, and he'll continue to improve."

Ossai will be sidelined a few weeks with a foot injury

Edge rusher Joseph Ossai will be “week to week,” according to Glenn, after he ruptured the plantar fascia in one of his feet against the Giants last Friday night.

Ossai, signed to a three-year, $36 million contract in March after five seasons with Cincinnati, began the summer on the physically unable to perform list and made his preseason debut against the Giants. He played 11 snaps and had two tackles and a quarterback pressure before being hurt.

Jets' kicking carousel continues to spin

New York claimed kicker Blake Grupe off waivers from Indianapolis on Monday, adding him to the roster after Jason Sanders — who beat out Cade York for the job — had a shaky performance in the preseason finale during which he was wide left on an extra point and short on a 54-yard field-goal attempt.

Sanders was released by the Jets a few hours after Glenn said the veteran remained on the team for “competition” with Grupe while adding that the roster is still “fluid” as teams continue to make moves in preparation for the regular season. Sanders was later re-signed — but to the practice squad.

New York also claimed former Carolina linebacker Trevin Wallace and waived offensive lineman Kohl Levao.

Grupe spent parts of his first three NFL seasons with New Orleans and finished last year with the Colts, who waived him Sunday after Spencer Shrader won their competition. For his career, Grupe is 86 of 105 on field goals and 96 of 98 on extra points.

“He's a small guy,” the 5-foot-9 Glenn said with a laugh about the 5-7 Grupe. “But he’s a good player. ... Looking forward to him getting out here with us and kicking.”

text:
The grim reaper has taken the NFL by storm throughout August. Players are now hurt, and we must figure out what to do about it. The rankings have shifted, and if you have not yet drafted, changes must account for them. On the other hand, if you have drafted, we have some useful advice to share. Here are the latest injuries to be advised about.

Pat Mahomes

The Chiefs quarterback is going to be a full-go for Week 1. His rushing upside will be limited, but Mahomes does expect to still scramble in low-risk scenarios. He is still a mild risk and is only ranked around QB12 in fantasy football. Draft a backup for safekeeping.

Jeremiyah Love

Love is still about a 50/50 shot to play Week 1. He will have a multi-week ramp-up to full health. Despite the ankle sprain, he is at low risk long-term. I am below consensus, favoring Tyler Allgeier to get 25-30% of the rushing offense, but I do not hate drafting Love in the 4th or 5th round.

Chuba Hubbard

The Panthers are trending towards having Hubbard back for Week 1. While probably not 100%, his playing time should not see much of a dip. Hubbard is expected to have a 60/40 split over Jonathan Brooks. Both are lower-risk draft picks in a run-favoring offense.

Kyle Monangai

D'Andre Swift is going to have the early advantage in Chicago. While Monangai earned his 50/50 split in 2025, early-season woes could give Swift formidable volume well into the season. Monangai is uncertain to play Week 1 and will require a multi-week ramp-up from his knee hyperextension. Monangai sits around RB40 while Swift is around RB20, also with lower injury risk.

Kenneth Walker III

The cited foot issue is not expected to sideline Walker or limit him. He will play Week 1, backed up by Emmett Johnson, who earned the RB2 job and is a prime handcuff.

Ashton Jeanty

It has been reported that Jeanty has a mild high-ankle sprain. Nothing has technically been confirmed on that matter. Suffering last week, Jeanty will truly be on the brink of a return for Week 1. He is in questionable status but hopes to be ready by Week 2 and mostly back to form by Week 4 at the latest. Mike Washington Jr. will be very capable if Jeanty is out; a low-end RB2. I would still draft Jeanty around RB9-12 off the board.

TreVeyon Henderson

Despite an ankle injury, Henderson is expected to play Week 1. He is my low-risk RB24.

Alvin Kamara

The Saints notably kept Kamara off the IR. This means he can return at any time before Week 4. Kamara has been reported missing for about one month. With nearly two weeks until Week 1 and a week removed from injury, a Week 2 or 3 return is most likely.

Breece Hall

Hall's sidelining due to a groin injury has been especially precautionary. He should be a full-go for Week 1.

Zach Charbonnet

My continuous take on Charbonnet has come true. As many fans had hoped for Charbonnet's early-season return, the Seahawks did place him on the IR. Charbonnet should not return until at least October, and would not be close to 100% until the final third of the season.

Alec Pierce

The Colts finally got Pierce back to practice this past week. He appears to look quite good considering his muscle atrophy concerns. It will now be up to Pierce to get in game shape, and if all looks good on the field, Pierce can definitely be a WR2. As of now, he is a low-end WR3 with moderate re-injury risk, so I will not draft Pierce at anything higher than my fourth wide receiver; a high-upside depth piece.

Malik Nabers

Nabers looks fresh, is cutting very well, and is now primed to play Week 1, well ahead of schedule. Nabers can be drafted in the WR12-15 range. There is a mild re-injury risk.

Emeka Egbuka

It is not great to hear Todd Bowles say he is "hopeful" that Egbuka is good for Week 1. Egbuka is projected as my WR26, but I would exercise some caution and wait until the WR30-33 range to pull the trigger. Chris Godwin's stock rises in the meantime; low-risk and high-upside or a great mid-round wide receiver prospect.

Puka Nacua

Nacua is back practicing after his psoas limited him on the field. All reports point towards a full-go Nacua in Week 1, and he is well worth his top-2 wide receiver status. Nacua also avoided the Commissioners Exemption List and is not expected to be suspended.

Ja'Marr Chase

Chase has a bone bruise from knee hyperextension. He will be sidelined for a couple of weeks, but is expected to be quite fine for the Bengals opener. Do not panic at all and make the pick with clarity.

Mike Evans

The 49ers expect Evans to play in Week 1. I am very worried about placing Evans on my fantasy football team. He has continuous issues with his hamstring and groin that will likely persist throughout the season. Evans only played 8 games in 2025.

Luther Burden III

The Bears have always expected his Week 1 return, and with zero setbacks, Burden III is well worth his ADP.

Sam LaPorta

It sounds like LaPorta had a very minor hip bruise. He will be just fine for Week 1, primed for a big comeback season under Drew Petzing. I doubt this is a Trey McBride in the making, but LaPorta is definitely a top-10 tight end with top-6 upside.

Tucker Kraft

Kraft recently retracted statements that he might be on a minor snap count. 2026 should have big things in store for Kraft, who was a TE2 pre-injury in 2025.

Tyler Warren

Warren has been dealing with a minor groin injury, but there is no concern for his Week 1 status.

George Kittle

It is still not clear if Kittle will make the trip to play in Week 1 in Australia. I would lean toward him doing so based on reporting, but I have a backup plan. Personally, I rank Kittle as my TE15 and would not draft him without another member of the supporting cast.

Brosmer started two games for the Vikings last season. After former starter J.J. McCarthy and then-backup Carson Wentz suffered injuries, Minnesota turned to the undrafted rookie from the University of Minnesota earlier than the team had planned. Brosmer began his career with four interceptions against the Seattle Seahawks but contributed to a win at MetLife Stadium against the New York Giants three weeks later.

As of Monday evening, the Vikings still had three quarterbacks on the roster: starter Kyler Murray, Wentz and McCarthy. Coach Kevin O’Connell has not yet clarified the depth chart, though several team sources, speaking on condition of anonymity to discuss internal team matters, said they expect Wentz to become the backup. This leaves McCarthy, a first-round pick in 2024, in a murky situation, especially considering his most recent injury.

The 23-year-old missed Friday’s final preseason game against the Broncos with an ankle injury. At the time, team sources said McCarthy did not feel comfortable playing in the game, but that the injury was “minor.” ESPN’s Adam Schefter told “The Pat McAfee Show” on Monday that he thinks McCarthy’s ankle “is a multi-week injury.”

To this point, the Vikings have not placed McCarthy on injured reserve, a move that could have allowed the team to keep another young talent — like Brosmer — on the roster.

Already dealing with familiar injury volume, the 49ers used both their IR-return slots upon setting their initial 53-man roster Sunday. The team added two more IR-return players today.

Cornerback Nate Hobbs and linebacker Nick Martin are heading to IR, per the team. Safety Ashtyn Davis and punter Corliss Waitman, whom the 49ers released Sunday, are coming back in corresponding moves.

Hobbs is dealing with a groin issue, while Martin suffered a hamstring injury in the 49ers’ second preseason game. Both players are expected to return sometime during the season, according to Matt Maiocco of NBC Sports Bay Area. The 49ers previously gave return designations to wide receiver Christian Kirk and tackle Austen Pleasants. Teams are only allowed to designate eight players to return from IR during the season.

Hobbs put together a 16-game rookie season with the Raiders in 2021, but injuries have been a frequent occurrence since then. He missed between four and six games in each of his last three seasons with the Raiders. Despite that, the Packers gave Hobbs a four-year, $48MM contract in free agency in 2025. It did not go well for the Pack, who saw Hobbs miss six games with knee problems. Over 11 games (five starts) and 358 defensive snaps, Hobbs totaled 27 tackles and a mere two pass breakups.

Green Bay released Hobbs in March, but it only took the 27-year-old two days to land an opportunity in San Francisco. The 49ers guaranteed Hobbs $3.11MM on a one-year, $3.5MM pact, though it looks as if it will be a while before he contributes (if he does). As things stand, Deommodore Lenoir, Renardo Green, Upton Stout, free agent addition Jack Jones and fourth-round rookie Ephesians Prysock make up the 49ers’ top five corners.

Martin, a 2025 third-rounder from Oklahoma State, got into seven games as a rookie and made 11 tackles before a concussion ended his season in December. Martin will continue to miss time at the start of 2026 as a result of his latest injury, but the 49ers are deep enough at linebacker to get by without him. Superstar Fred Warner is healthy again after missing most of last season with an ankle injury, and the team reunited with Dre Greenlaw in free agency. The 49ers have fifth-round rookie/summer standout Jaden Dugger, Tatum Bethune, special teams ace Luke Gifford and Garrett Wallow behind Warner and Greenlaw.

Connor Byrne contributed to this post.

SANTA CLARA — The next three practices for the 49ers are more important than usual.

With the health of several starters hanging in the balance for the team’s season opener in Melbourne, Australia, how they come away from this week’s on-field sessions will determine a lot.

General manager John Lynch and coach Kyle Shanahan spoke to the media after building their initial 53-man roster and were noncommittal regarding the potential of both Nick Bosa and George Kittle being available for the season opener.

“We are going to get them out there in these three days and hope it goes well,” Shanahan said. “With three days before we go, we are balancing it out with both of them. We don’t want them to go three days in a row, so we are going to do a little on some of these days and more on one.

“Both of them are on a little bit different schedule with the three [practices].”

San Francisco has an altered start of the season that includes leaving for Melbourne on Wednesday evening, more than a week before kickoff on Sept. 10 against the Los Angeles Rams. With that in mind, evaluations of player health are on an accelerated schedule.

“We usually have three practices, and then we get three days off and then we kind of settle everything on that bonus Monday of the week,” Shanahan said. “We already had our three days off because of our travel deal.

title: NFL CTE Study and California Brain Injury Claims - San Francisco Legal Examiner
description:
What the NFL CTE Study Could Mean for California Brain Injury Claims This is more than a medical headline.
Why Work With a San Francisco Brain Injury Attorney?
Frequently Asked Questions About CTE and Brain Injury Claims Can CTE be diagnosed while someone is still alive?
What if I was partly at fault for the accident that caused my brain injury?
What compensation can a traumatic brain injury claim recover?
text:
A new study tracked every former NFL player who died over a 14-year period and examined hundreds of donated brains. The findings are the most rigorous evidence yet that repetitive head trauma causes lasting harm, and they raise real questions about how the legal system accounts for damage that, until now, could only be confirmed after death.

Quick Takeaways

What the new NFL CTE study found

What CTE is and why it can't be diagnosed in the living

Why this isn't just a football problem

What the findings mean for your legal rights in California

Warning signs after a head injury

On August 26, 2026, one of the most rigorous studies ever conducted on chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE) was published in The BMJ. Unlike most CTE research before it, this study didn't start with a small group of brains donated by families who already suspected something was wrong. Researchers instead built a complete, fully enumerated list of every former NFL player known to have died between 2008 and 2021 — 1,712 men — and examined the 338 brains that were donated for study. The result was that 93.2% of those donated brains showed neuropathologically confirmed CTE.

As a San Francisco attorney who represents people with traumatic brain injuries, I don't spend most of my time arguing about football. I spend it representing rideshare passengers, delivery drivers, cyclists hit crossing Market Street, construction workers, and people who fell on a cracked sidewalk in the Sunset. But this study matters to every one of them, because it's some of the strongest population-level evidence yet that repetitive trauma to the brain causes real, measurable, sometimes devastating harm. It exposes just how often that harm goes officially unrecorded. Here's what the research found, what CTE actually is, and what it means for your rights if a head injury has touched your life.

What the New NFL CTE Study Found

Most earlier CTE research relied on brains donated to a handful of specialized brain banks — a group that tends to overrepresent players whose families already suspected something was wrong before death, skewing the numbers upward. This study took a different, more defensible approach and started with everyone.

Researchers identified all 1,712 former NFL players known to have died between 2008 and 2021, then examined the 338 brains (about 1 in 5 of that group) that were donated through the UNITE Brain Bank and the University of California, San Francisco Alzheimer's Disease Research Center. Pathologists examined the tissue without being told anything about each player's career or symptoms while alive, to keep the results unbiased.

What they found:

315 of the 338 donated brains (93.2%) showed neuropathologically confirmed CTE.

Accounting for the players whose brains were never examined, and applying the most conservative assumptions possible, researchers calculated that CTE prevalence across the full 1,712-person cohort was at least 18.5% and could be as high as 98.7%.

Among players who died between 2016 and 2021, when brain donation was most common, the confirmed minimum climbed to 24.5% — meaning at least 1 in 4 former players who died in that window had CTE.

104 donors (30.8%) had Stage IV CTE, the most severe classification on the disease's four-stage scale.

Donors with Stage IV CTE had a 44% higher risk of a clinically diagnosed dementia than donors without it, even after researchers statistically corrected for the fact that brain donors aren't a random sample of all players.

Perhaps most relevant to anyone working in personal injury law: only 40.6% of donors whose medical records supported a dementia diagnosis actually had a neurodegenerative disease listed anywhere on their death certificate. The official paperwork missed the diagnosis more often than it caught it.

The researchers were candid about the limits of their own work. Brain donation still wasn't random. CTE prevalence "at death" isn't the same thing as prevalence among all living players. And because this is an observational study, it shows a strong statistical association between severe CTE and dementia — not proof that CTE alone causes it. But the scale of this research, drawn from a complete population rather than a hand-picked sample, makes it one of the most credible pieces of evidence to date that repetitive head trauma leaves lasting, and often unrecorded, damage.

What Is CTE and Why Can’t Doctors Test for It?

Chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE) is a progressive brain disease associated with repeated impacts to the head — not necessarily diagnosed concussions, but the accumulation of blows over years or decades, including subconcussive hits that never produce obvious symptoms at the time they happen.

Here's the frustrating reality this study underscores: CTE can’t currently be diagnosed with certainty in a living person. It can only be confirmed by examining brain tissue after death for a specific pattern of abnormal tau protein around the brain's blood vessels. While someone is alive, doctors can identify probable CTE based on a documented history of head trauma combined with a cluster of symptoms, including memory problems, impaired judgment, mood changes such as depression or irritability, impulsivity, and, in advanced cases, dementia, but they can’t confirm the diagnosis outright.

Researchers classify CTE across four stages. Stage I typically involves mild, often unnoticed symptoms. Stage IV — the stage linked to a 44% higher dementia risk in this study — involves severe cognitive decline that, without a brain autopsy, can be difficult to distinguish from other dementias like Alzheimer's disease.

This diagnostic gap isn't just a medical curiosity. It's one of the central challenges facing anyone trying to hold a person, employer, school, or organization legally accountable for a brain injury's long-term consequences.

Every headline about this study will focus on the NFL, and understandably so, since professional football players sustain an extraordinary number of head impacts over their careers. As I recently discussed in looking at the experiences of Kyle Shanahan and Roger Craig, the long-term effects of brain injury can take very different forms. But repetitive and single-incident traumatic brain injuries reach far beyond the football field, and they make up a significant share of personal injury cases here in the Bay Area:

Car accidents, motorcycle crashes, and rideshare collisions — one of the most common causes of TBI, and among the most common case types we see, where dense San Francisco traffic and sudden stops make head trauma a real risk even in relatively low-speed crashes.

Bicycle accidents and pedestrian crashes — a serious concern in a hilly, densely built city with heavy bike-commuter traffic and some genuinely dangerous intersections.

Slip, trip, and fall accidents — on cracked sidewalks, poorly lit stairwells, wet retail floors, or construction sites.

Workplace injuries, especially in construction, delivery, warehouse, and maritime work.

Youth, high school, and recreational sports — soccer, ice hockey, rugby, cheerleading, and combat sports — all carry a risk of repetitive head impacts, and California schools and athletic leagues have specific legal duties regarding concussion protocols and return-to-play decisions.

Assault and domestic violence, which can produce the same repetitive-impact patterns researchers associate with CTE.

Defective products, including inadequately protective helmets and safety equipment.

Anyone in one of these situations can experience the same category of harm this study describes, and their family can face the exact same problem of proving that harm in a system that, as this research shows, often fails to record it accurately even in official documents like a death certificate.

What the NFL CTE Study Could Mean for California Brain Injury Claims

This is more than a medical headline. It has real, practical implications for how brain injury and wrongful death cases get built and argued.

It strengthens the scientific basis for repetitive-trauma claims. Insurance companies and defense attorneys routinely argue that a single accident, or a history of "minor" impacts, couldn't possibly explain the cognitive or behavioral symptoms someone is experiencing years later. A large, population-based study like this one — free of the selection bias that has limited smaller CTE studies in the past — gives injury attorneys stronger scientific footing to argue that repetitive head trauma causes real, lasting harm.

It shows how badly official records can undercount brain injury. If a death certificate misses a confirmed dementia diagnosis roughly six times out of ten, it's worth asking how often a hospital discharge summary, an insurance claim file, or a police incident report understates the true severity of a living person's brain injury. This is exactly why thorough documentation — neuropsychological testing, brain imaging, treating-physician records, and testimony from people who know the injured person well — matters so much in a TBI claim. The paperwork alone is often not enough.

It raises real questions about timing. In California, most personal injury and wrongful death claims must generally be filed within two years of the injury or death, under Code of Civil Procedure § 335.1. Because CTE can currently only be confirmed after death, and its connection to an earlier head injury may not become apparent until much later, families dealing with a loved one's cognitive decline or death may have a legitimate argument that their claim didn't fully "accrue" until that connection came to light. That's a genuinely complex, fact-specific question — precisely the kind of issue worth raising with an attorney early, rather than assuming too much time has already passed.

Government claims carry a much shorter deadline. If a brain injury occurred on a public road, a public school campus, a transit system, or other government property, California law generally requires that a formal claim be filed with that government entity within just six months — not two years (Government Code § 911.2 and related provisions). Missing that window can permanently bar an otherwise valid claim, which is why anyone with a possible TBI case involving a public entity shouldn't wait to get legal advice.

Wrongful death claims can involve CTE even outside of professional sports. If a loved one's judgment, balance, memory, or behavior declined in ways that contributed to a fatal accident — a fall, a crash, a medication error — and that decline may trace back to an earlier head injury, that connection is worth discussing with an attorney experienced in both traumatic brain injury and wrongful death claims.

Warning Signs After a Head Injury

Whether the injury happened yesterday or years ago, these symptoms deserve prompt medical attention and careful documentation:

Headaches that worsen or won't resolve

Confusion, disorientation, or gaps in memory

Sensitivity to light or noise

Balance problems or dizziness

Sleep that's noticeably disrupted — far more or far less than usual

Noticeable changes in mood, patience, or personality

Difficulty concentrating, planning, or making decisions

Slurred speech or problems with motor coordination

If you notice these signs in yourself or someone you love, especially following any blow to the head, even one that didn't seem serious at the time, see a doctor and keep a record of every visit, symptom, and diagnosis. That documentation protects your health. If someone else's negligence caused the injury, that too protects your legal rights.

Why Work With a San Francisco Brain Injury Attorney?

TBI and CTE-related cases are not standard personal injury claims. They call for an attorney who knows how to work with neurologists, neuropsychologists, and life-care planners; who understands how to document an injury that often doesn't show up cleanly on a CT scan; and who knows San Francisco's hospitals and medical community, including institutions like UCSF, which contributed to the very study discussed above.

At Choulos, Choulos & Wyle, brain injury and CTE-related claims aren't a side practice. They're a central focus of our work. We know how to build a case on real medical evidence rather than paperwork that, as this study shows, is often incomplete.

If you or someone you love has suffered a traumatic brain injury in a car accident, fall, workplace incident, sports injury, or another incident caused by someone else’s negligence, you don’t have to wait until you have every answer before protecting your legal rights.

Contact Choulos, Choulos & Wyle for a free, confidential consultation about your situation and any applicable deadlines. You can reach Claude A. Wyle directly by email at cwyle@ccwlawyers.com or call (415) 432-7290. Claude represents people with traumatic brain injuries, catastrophic injuries, and wrongful death claims throughout San Francisco and the Bay Area.

Frequently Asked Questions About CTE and Brain Injury Claims

Can CTE be diagnosed while someone is still alive?

Not with certainty. Doctors can identify probable or suspected CTE in a living patient based on symptoms and head-injury history, but a definitive diagnosis currently requires examining brain tissue after death.

How long do I have to file a brain injury lawsuit in California?

Generally, two years from the date of the injury or death, under California Code of Civil Procedure § 335.1. If a government entity — a city, county, school district, or transit agency, for example — is involved, you typically must file a formal administrative claim within six months instead.

Does CTE require repeated concussions, or can smaller hits add up?

Current research, including the framework behind this study, points to cumulative exposure to repetitive head impacts — including subconcussive hits that never produce obvious symptoms — rather than any single diagnosed concussion.

Can my family bring a claim if we believe a loved one's death was connected to an old, undiagnosed brain injury?

Potentially. This is a fact-specific and often complex question, particularly in light of how often this study shows death certificates miss a confirmed dementia diagnosis. An attorney can review your loved one's medical and injury history to evaluate whether a claim may still be viable.

Is CTE only a concern for professional athletes?

No. Most public research and media coverage focuses on football, but the same underlying biology applies to anyone with a history of repetitive head trauma, including car accidents, workplace injuries, youth and amateur sports, military service, and domestic violence.

What if I was partly at fault for the accident that caused my brain injury?

California follows a "pure comparative negligence" rule, meaning you can generally still recover compensation even if you were partly at fault. Your award is simply reduced by your percentage of responsibility. Being partially at fault doesn’t automatically disqualify you from a claim.

What compensation can a traumatic brain injury claim recover?

Depending on the facts of your case, compensation may include past and future medical expenses, lost income and diminished earning capacity, the cost of long-term or life-care planning, and pain and suffering. In a wrongful death case, surviving family members may also be able to recover for loss of financial support and companionship. An attorney can evaluate what applies to your specific situation.

title: 2026 NFL Roster Cutdown Day Fantasy Reaction: Josh Jacobs and Jaydon Blue fallout
description:
A handful of teams made some rather surprising moves, on top of a twist in Josh Jacobs’ ongoing legal situation.

The Packers could very reasonably see Jacobs as a net negative for the team given his character concerns.

text:
All 32 squads cut down to their 53-man rosters on Sunday. A handful of teams made some rather surprising moves, on top of a twist in Josh Jacobs’ ongoing legal situation. These are the 10 biggest storylines from roster cutdown day.

🚨🏈 GET YOUR FREE ROTOWORLD FANTASY FOOTBALL DRAFT KIT HERE!

Josh Jacobs placed on the Commissioner’s Exempt List

Jacobs was placed on the Commissioner’s Exempt List and can remain there for as long as the NFL intends to conduct its own investigation into the two misdemeanor offenses he was charged with as the result of an altercation with a woman in May. The league’s standard policy for this type of incident is six games, though it can increase based on aggravating circumstances. According to the collective bargaining agreement, time spent on the commissioner’s exempt list is credited toward any suspension that is later imposed, provided the player “return and shall have no further right to any salary for the games for which he was paid while on the commissioner exempt list that were credited to the suspension.” In layman’s terms, Jacobs could be credited with “time served” if he is on the exempt list during the season and a suspension is later handed out. It would not be shocking for the team to cut him outright either. Jacobs ranked 37th in rush yards over expected last year. He was not efficient. His calling card was reliability, which is now out the window. The Packers could very reasonably see Jacobs as a net negative for the team given his character concerns.

In the meantime, Marshawn Lloyd will serve as the Packers’ starting running back. Lloyd has had an excellent, and more importantly, healthy offseason. Lloyd may be fated to give the starting job back to Jacobs if he does return midseason, but he profiled as a dynamic change-of-pace option coming out of USC. Lloyd only ran the ball 116 times in his final season of college ball, but at 7.1 yards per carry, he turned that workload into 820 yards on the ground. Lloyd also averaged 17.8 yards per catch, going for 232 yards on just 13 grabs. If he succeeds early in the season, it’s hard to imagine the team putting him back on ice even if Jacobs is back.

Packers trade for Kaleb Johnson

Green Bay got out ahead of the Jacobs news by trading for Steelers running back Kaleb Johnson. The team was ready to throw in the towel on the 2024 third-round pick, so the Packers scooped him up for a 2028 sixth-round selection. Johnson was a workhorse in college, posting a 241-1,547-21 rushing line in his junior season. Obviously, none of that production has translated into success in the pros, but a change of scenery could be what the young back needs. He could be in the mix with Lloyd once he gets a grip on the playbook, though redraft managers can hold off on drafting him for now.

Cowboys make a surprise cut

The Cowboys threw in the towel on every slappy’s favorite sleeper Jaydon Blue. The former Texas back barely played as a rookie and drew poor off-field reviews in addition to his non-existent production. Despite earning praise throughout this offseason for turning his career around, Dallas couldn’t find a spot for him on their roster. They also cut Phil Mafah, leaving Malik Davis as the only backup to Javonte Williams. Davis is now one of the better handcuff bets in fantasy drafts and casual leagues may be extremely slow to catch up to such an obscure player. It will be worth watching the transaction wire over the next few days to see if Dallas retains one of Blue or Mafah on their practice squad. That would put a lid on any Davis hype.

Puka Nacua avoids the exempt list

Puka Nacua is not expected to be placed on the Commissioner’s Exempt before Week 1. That doesn’t mean he is out of the woods as far as a potential suspension is concerned, but it takes some risk off the table. He also returned to practice after missing multiple weeks with a groin issue. Nacua currently has an ADP of 4.9 on Yahoo. He out-scored every FLEX player but Christian McCaffrey last year despite missing one week. His per-game average of 23.4 PPR points bested Bijan Robinson by 1.6. With both the injury and suspension risk dying down, Nacua looks more and more like the rightful 1.02 every day.

James Conner lands on injured reserve

James Conner is still recovering from the season-ending ankle injury he suffered early in the 2025 season. He is now looking at a 12-month recovery if he plays the first week he is eligible to return from injured reserve, Week 5. At this point, fantasy managers should not count on him making any impact this year. With Jeremiyah Love also banged up, expect a healthy amount of touches for Tyler Allgeier early in the season. Allgeier made a living taking carries away from a top-10 draft pick in Atlanta. He’s set up to do even more of that in Arizona.

Tank Dell to miss the first four games of the season

Like Conner, Tank Dell is still recovering from a catastrophic injury and will not be eligible to play until Week 5. Dell suffered a multi-ligament knee injury in December of 2024. He’s now 21 months removed from the injury and is still unable to play football. The hope is that he continues to ramp up over the next month and is ready to play early in the season, but fantasy managers can’t count on month No. 22 being the answer. Expect the Texans to roll out Kayshon Boutte and one of Xavier Hutchinson or Jaylin Noel as their starter receivers in Week 1.

As expected, Jordyn Tyson heads to IR

Saints rookie wideout Jordyn Tyson will also miss at least the first four games of the year. Unlike the previous two players, he doesn’t have much of a shot at playing in Week 5. He is expected to miss two months with his never-ending hamstring woes. From the time that was reported, Tyson would be back in Week 6 or 7. The Saints travel overseas for an international game in Week 7 and then get a Week 8 bye. For a player dealing with hamstring issues that date back to his senior season in college, a speedy turnaround shouldn’t be in the cards. A Week 9 return is probably the starting point for Tyson. With Mason Tipton on the PUP list, Bryce Lance appears to be the next man up after Chris Olave and Devaughn Vele. The Saints drafted Lance in the fourth round after a productive pair of seasons at North Dakota State. Lance is a true field-stretcher who scored 25 receiving touchdowns plus two rushing touchdowns in his final two seasons of college ball. At best, his production will be spikey but inconsistent until Tyson returns. That’s a classic “better in Best Ball” profile.

Bucs strong-arm Sean Tucker into a pay cut

Early in the offseason, the Bucs chose not to pick up Sean Tucker’s RFA tender for $3.5 million. They eventually backtracked on that decision and extended him the tender, though it seemed like they regretted that move by the time the preseason rolled around. Tucker split reps with 2025 UDFA Josh Williams during the preseason. He made the roster over Williams, but only after agreeing to a pay cut. His new deal is worth $2.5 million with more money on the table via incentives. This doesn’t seem like the way a team treats a player who they expect to be a meaningful part of the offense. Fantasy managers have been drafting Tucker as if he will be a small part of the Bucs’ backfield-by-committee, especially at the goal line, but that looks less likely after their recent moves.

Emmett Johnson locks up Chiefs’ RB2 gig

The Chiefs gave each of their backup running backs a shot at the RB2 gig during the preseason. Brashard Smith and Emari Demercado took over for Kenneth Walker early in the team’s first and second preseason games. Johnson got the play with some of the starters in their final preseason game because Walker was banged up. After giving everyone a fair shake, Andy Reid watched the tape and landed on the rookie as his guy. Emari Demercado was cut on Sunday and Brashard Smith played deep into the final preseason contest, signaling that he was no longer in the running for the backup job. Johnson profiles as a strong pass-catching complement to Walker. He posted a 46-370-3 receiving line on top of his 251-1,451-12 rushing line as a senior at Nebraska. A landing spot in Kansas City didn’t seem ideal at the time of the draft, but fourth-round capital from a team without a glaring need at running back is a strong vote of confidence from KC’s front office. Johnson’s combination of potential standalone value and sky-high contingent upside makes him one of the better late-round flyers coming out of roster cuts.

Aaron Donald comes out of retirement

text:
Record-setting former University of Kansas running back Devin Neal has been placed on the injured reserve list by the NFL’s New Orleans Saints because of a hamstring injury, the team announced Sunday.

Neal, a 5-foot-11, 215-pound, 23-year-old second-year pro, was placed on IR without a “designated to return” tag, meaning he cannot return for to play for the Saints during the regular season or postseason.

Teams are allowed to use two injured reserve spots on players designated to return during roster cuts made to reach the 53-man roster limit. The Saints used those on receiver Jordyn Tyson and linebacker Jaylan Ford. Those players will miss a minimum of four games and can later return.

According to NOLA.com, it is possible that the Saints could reach an injury settlement with Neal and release him if his injury is not considered season-ending. That injury settlement and release would allow him to sign with another team. That is considered the most realistic path for a player in Neal’s position to enter games this season.

If Neal is not waived by the Saints with an injury designation he will be required to stay on the IR list the entire season and postseason.

“Neal, the Saints’ sixth-rounder from last year’s draft, was considered to be in the mix for a tightly contested spot behind Travis Etienne and Alvin Kamara (at runnin back). But he suffered two separate hamstring injuries during the leadup to the regular season. New Orleans ended up keeping four backs, with the others being Audric Estime and Kendre Miller,” explained Luke Johnson of NOLA.com.

Missing the entire season obviously is a huge setback for Neal, who finished his four-year KU career in 2024 as KU’s all-time leader in rushing yards (4,343), rushing touchdowns (49), total touchdowns (53), 100-yard rushing games (20) and 1,000-yard rushing seasons (3).

The sixth-round draft pick, who attended Lawrence High School as well as KU, had been dealing with hamstring problems throughout training camp. He aggravated the injury on a 4-yard gain in the first quarter of an Aug. 22 game against the Los Angeles Rams.

Neal missed the tail end of his 2025 rookie season with a hamstring injury. For the year he carried 57 times for 206 yards and two touchdowns.

When the Cleveland Browns kicked off training camp this summer, Dawand Jones was running with the first-team offense at left tackle. He was never really considered a legitimate contender to win a job that was earmarked for first-round rookie Spencer Fano, but head coach Todd Monken and offensive line coach George Warhop talked up Jones enough to make it seem like he legitimately remained in the team’s 2026 plans.

That was confirmed Sunday — to an extent — as the Browns and the NFL’s other 31 teams made their initial roster cuts down to the regular-season limit of 53.

It’s been a troubling offseason for Jones, who is coming off a third season-ending injury in as many years. Entering the final year of his rookie contract, he had earned himself a proven performance escalator based on playing time, bumping his $1.1 million base salary up closer to $3.7 million.

The Browns wasted little time restructuring that number, as Jones essentially agreed to a pay cut, reducing his base salary back to its original figure with guarantees added to the deal.

Unfortunately, that was likely the move that cemented Jones’ roster spot, as his trajectory has been in steady decline since the second week of August.

A reworked contract may have done more to secure Dawand Jones' roster spot than his preseason play

Pro Football Focus grades should always be taken with a grain of salt. The site ranked fourth-string quarterback Taylen Green as the Browns’ third-highest-graded offensive player of the preseason despite him playing one half and passing for 27 yards.

PFF’s take on Jones’ preseason performance wasn’t pretty, though. He was the team’s lowest-graded offensive player among those who played at least 60 snaps over the three games.

As usual, he seemed to hold his own in pass protection, especially as the starting left tackle in preseason Game 3 against the New England Patriots. Dillon Gabriel was barely touched in that game as he posted a near-perfect QB rating.

It’s the run blocking that remains a major concern. Jones is a massive human at 6-foot-8 and 374 pounds, but coming off a serious knee injury, he doesn’t appear to be moving well in the ground game. He was the Browns’ worst run blocker of the preseason, per PFF, with a 29.2 grade.

With blossoming rookie Austin Barber now mixing in at right guard, and KT Leveston surprisingly hitting the waiver wire, Jones profiles as the backup left tackle behind Fano to start the season. But Monken and GM Andrew Berry specifically targeted versatility both in free agency and the draft this offseason, and Jones may not be the first player off the bench should a starter go down with an early injury.

Jones has the elite size that NFL front offices covet, but his injury history has capped his upside to the point where the Browns prioritized a contract restructure over a potential trade this offseason.

The former fourth-round pick should still provide Cleveland with some depth on the outside, but the harsh reality here is that he probably wouldn’t be on the Browns’ roster right now had he not agreed to slash his salary back in May.

CLEVELAND, OHIO (TheOBR.com) - Good morning, Cleveland Browns fans!

THE DAILY BLOVIATION

I'm not a suspicious guy. I'm really not. I'm more trusting than naive, assuming people are honest with me until they're proven otherwise or show their true colors. I've gotten burned a few times, which I chalk up to being a useful life experience. I have a lot of "useful life experiences" under my belt.

But even I looked a little askance at Dillon Gabriel's sudden addition to the injured reserve list. Adding one of the quarterbacks to the injury list is something that we joked about last week as an obvious ruse to avoid a difficult decision. I'm not casting doubt on the Browns, but Gabriel's injury seems a bit too convenient to be real.

Adam Schefter says the back problems showed up Thursday against the Patriots. There was tightness Saturday, and Gabriel was held out of the throwing period reporters saw, with a precautionary MRI thrown into the mix. Our understanding is that the building does not view it as long-term. Petrak had him not mentioning it after the game and not throwing Saturday. That is the paper trail.

It doesn't look like a long-term thing, so Gabriel was put in the IR, but a "designated for return list" that makes room for players to come back.

HOW IT WORKS: The Designated for Return list isn't as convenient as it could be. On cutdown day, an NFL club can put two players on reserve and tag them DFR without them counting on the 53. Those two immediately eat two of the eight return designations you get for the season, even if they never come back.

After 4 p.m. ET that day, anyone later moved to IR can still be designated, subject to the same pool. So, Gabriel has to sit four games. Earliest he can play is Week 5. When the club physician clears him to practice, a 21-day clock starts. The team needs to activate him onto the 53, trade him, release him, or leave him on IR for the year within that timeframe. He can practice in that window. He cannot play until they spend the roster spot. Joe Royer is on the same DFR clock, except his list is (a mysterious) non-football illness. Monken would not talk about whether Royer plays in 2026.

HOW THEY "PROVE" IT: As I stated above, the sudden IR designation sure looks convenient. But the Browns need to be able to prove it if called out.

There is no independent NFL doctor for IR, no requirement to make every injury public, and no need to send a bunch of X-rays to the NFL. The club physician certifies. The club files the transaction and sends injury paperwork to the league office. If the commissioner thinks you stashed a healthy player to dodge the 53, he can open the folder after the fact: treatment notes, trainer records, diagnostics, practice video.

That is an audit, not a pre-clear. Concussion return-to-play is the independent-neurologist rule. IR is not. Two cutdown DFRs is explicitly legal. A healthy stash is not. The bar is the club MD plus the paperwork, not a scan they have to post. For this one, the public record is Schefter: hurt Thursday against New England, pain Saturday, MRI, IR-DFR Sunday. That is reporting. We've reported here that the Browns had every intention of keeping Gabriel. Four quarterbacks are still in the building. One of them has to sit four games.

Basically, the Browns file some paperwork, but will get audited if the NFL (or potentially another team complaining to the NFL) thinks they're pulling a fast one.

So, now, it's time for me to be trusting again. Gabriel has a back issue, will sit out four games, and then they'll see how he is. Nothing to see here. I'm sure all the other NFL teams are just as trusting as I am.

Sure.

Have a good one. GO BROWNS!

Cincinnati Reds star shortstop Elly De La Cruz exited Sunday's primetime matchup against the Chicago Cubs with an apparent injury to his left quad muscle. The team announced it officially on social media.

Matt McLain moved to shortstop, and Ivan Johnson replaced him in the lineup and is at second base. He was 2-for-4 with a double and a run scored before exiting.

The Same Injury Effected Him Last Season

Last season, De La Cruz played through nearly the entirety of the second half of the season with the same injury on the same leg, and his numbers dipped mightily. After hitting 18 home runs in the first half of the season in 2025, he hit just four after the All-Star break. His numbers have dipped in a similar fashion this season, but not nearly as drastically. His batting average has dropped 13 points, and he has hit six home runs post-All-Star break this season.

The Reds need De La Cruz to be healthy throughout his career for them to have any real hopes of building a contender while he is under team control. This is the second consecutive season that he has dealt with the same injury. This season was also the first time in his career that he had spent any amount of time on the injured list. He missed nearly the entire month of June after going on the injured list with a hamstring injury.

A Tough Blow

The timing of this injury is also a worst-case scenario and honestly puts a bow on the Reds’ terrible season in 2026. After a tremendous start, winning 20 games at the end of April, fans and media outlets had the Reds as a possible threat to win the division after coming off a 2025 season that saw them make the playoffs for the first time since 2020 and in year one of Terry Francona's regime.

Unfortunately, once the calendar flipped to May, everything fell apart. The bullpen went on one of the worst stretches in recent memory, and the offense can only seem to drive in runs when hitting the ball over the fence. They did show some promise at the end of July, post-All-Star break, but the team is trending back in the direction of what we saw in May and June.

September is going to be one of the toughest stretches of baseball the Reds have faced in a long time. They’ll play the Brewers and Dodgers twice each, along with series against the Cubs, Padres, Braves and Blue Jays. Every one of those teams is either currently in a playoff spot or right in the middle of the postseason race.

For all of the well-deserved ire that social media manages to catch, I will say one thing — it is one of the easiest ways for me to stay up to date with friends and family who don’t live particularly close to me (or play fantasy football).

I still have plenty of friends in high school and college who live in New England, and it isn’t the easiest thing in the world to make time to catch up with everyone. Seeing pictures of kids growing up, job changes, vacation trips — I’ve always enjoyed that aspect of Facebook.

One thing that always tugs at my heartstrings is the “Remember this day, 10 years ago?” pictures that pop up in my feed. Time is a thief, and in the blink of an eye, I’m somehow a decade older. My children went from being in strollers and car seats to learning to drive. How on Earth did that happen?

Time somehow seems to speed up the older I get — perhaps it is my faulty memory or a cramped schedule blending; who knows. The other day, I was convinced it was still early August, rather than the end of the month. Days fly by.

Just like that, the NFL preseason has nearly concluded. Training camps are behind us, Labor Day is right around the corner, and so is the official start of the 2026 NFL season.

The NFL preseason gives coaches time to evaluate where their team stands. It lets them hash out positional battles and evaluate roster deficiencies before the season gets underway. Most superstars generally sit out the entirety of it — there is no reason for them to be placed in a situation of unnecessary risk, especially now that there are only three preseason games instead of four.

Time is limited, and reps are precious. Thus, the list of who fell flat this preseason will consist of lesser-known options, rather than top-tier talent. Baltimore’s Joe Fagnano leads all quarterbacks with 509 passing yards. Arizona’s Evan Hull leads the league in rushing yards with 189. I seriously doubt either makes an impact this season. At least, I hope not, since that would mean the injury bug was hungry.

Which players failed to take advantage of their opportunity to shine? Here are a few options that I was hoping to see more from in August.

Quarterback

Fernando Mendoza (QB – LV)

The odds that Fernando Mendoza would immediately seize the job from veteran Kirk Cousins were always low, but when given the limelight, Mendoza’s luster seemed to fade. In three preseason appearances, Mendoza completed just 55.6% of his pass attempts, throwing one touchdown with two interceptions for a quarterback rating of 59.5.

It is hardly fair to view this as a failure — most rookie quarterbacks need to adjust to the speed of the NFL, and it takes time to adapt to more complex blitz schemes, defenders barreling down on you and progressing through reads in a new system. Still, Mendoza was the first overall selection for a reason, and expectations are high that he will contribute in short order.

A traditional pocket passer whose calling card was picking apart defenses with precision passing, Mendoza drew comparisons to Matt Ryan early on in the draft process. It is clear he needs more time to develop, and Las Vegas needs to keep surrounding him with weapons, especially in the passing game.

A healthy Ashton Jeanty behind him will do wonders, but Mendoza will need to speed up his mental process and deliver more accurate passes in order to usurp Kirk Cousins on the depth chart any time soon.

Tua Tagovailoa (QB – ATL)

Tua Tagovailoa was signed by Atlanta as a seasoned mentor to Michael Penix Jr., giving him additional time to recover from his left ACL tear sustained in November.

With Penix still working his way back from the injury and unable to take the field this preseason, Tagovailoa was given an opportunity to shine. Instead, he fell flat on his face. Tagovailoa was simply an extension of what we saw previously in Miami — a quarterback who is afraid to push the ball downfield and relies on short throws to move the ball downfield instead.

Backup Jack Strand performed much better, with a higher completion rate (66.7)% and quarterback rating (90.7). There was also a striking difference in average depth of target (aDOT) — 9.3 vs. 2.3. Yes, you read that right: Tagovailoa’s aDOT was 2.3.

Tagovailoa fumbled an exchange with the center in the team’s final preseason game and seems gun-shy of contact, not allowing plays to develop downfield and instead immediately getting the ball out of his hands.

Borrowing a statistic from Warren Sharp, Tagovailoa had zero pass attempts this preseason that traveled more than six air yards. Of his 95 passing yards in Week 3 of the preseason, 68 came after the catch. I’ve rarely seen a quarterback who plays things so conservatively.

Wide Receiver

Darius Slayton (WR – NYG)

Giants general manager Joe Schoen was rightly given plenty of criticism for his curious decision to reward Darius Slayton with a three-year, $36 million contract in March of 2025.

Though he had occasionally provided spurts of fantasy relevance as New York’s primary receiving threat in the wake of Malik Nabers‘ injury, Slayton’s propensity for drops in key situations and inability to ever expand his route tree were notable.

Initially, I thought Slayton’s bloated contract would save him from being cut, even after New York inked Darnell Mooney to a deal in the offseason and drafted Malachi Fields from Notre Dame.

Now? That might not be the case. Slayton started the third preseason game opposite Odell Beckham Jr. on Friday and failed to register one look in his direction all game from either Jameis Winston, Brandon Allen or Jake Haener.

New York Post beat reporter Paul Schwartz made the point that “financial considerations are not going to save Slayton” at this point. If he can’t fit into this new offensive scheme, he will be cut as New York attempts to reach the 53-man roster limit. The longest-tenured player on the team could be shown the door.

Makai Lemon (WR – PHI)

I’ve mentioned it several times in earlier articles, but it is worth reiterating — fantasy managers were incredibly spoiled by the offensive-rich class from 2025, and should seriously temper their expectations this season for the incoming rookie class. I’ve listed Makai Lemon’s name here, but I could have just as easily gone with Carnell Tate or Jordyn Tyson.

Lemon finally managed to take the field for Philadelphia’s third preseason game after nursing a hamstring injury for the last several weeks, and his first start was underwhelming, to say the least. Primarily playing out of the slot and “Z” position, Lemon saw five targets, securing three passes for three yards, including a dropped pass that led to an interception.

I’m willing to admit that this was Lemon shaking off the rust. Still, he looked tentative and appears to be listed behind Dontayvion Wicks and Marquise Brown on the Eagles’ depth chart.

Pivoting to Tate, he failed to register a reception in the first two preseason games, despite being healthy. Titans offensive coordinator Brian Daboll has already come under criticism for the team’s inept downfield passing attack and quarterback Cam Ward‘s shaky preseason. The hope is that Tate can move around the formation to become a focal point, but there is cause for concern early.

New Orleans chose Tyson as the second receiver off the board in April, with the eighth overall selection. A mix of tantalizing upside and lengthy injury history, Tyson is expected to miss a large part of the regular season while nursing a lingering hamstring strain. The hope was that he would provide a stable complementary piece opposite Chris Olave in the passing game — who knows if that will ever come to fruition.

Running Back

Kaleb Johnson (RB – GB)

I’ll fully admit I was very high on Kaleb Johnson coming out of the 2025 NFL Draft, and he has been one of the more disappointing running backs in recent memory.

After a career season in 2024 with the University of Iowa, Johnson was a mid-third-round selection by Pittsburgh, which had a clear hole to fill opposite Jaylen Warren, following the departure of Najee Harris. Rather than seize the opportunity, Johnson was immediately placed into Mike Tomlin’s doghouse and hardly saw the light of day last season, handling just 28 carries total.

My hope was that Johnson would be given another shot following Tomlin’s departure, but that never came to fruition. Instead, seventh-round selection Eli Heidenreich played ahead of Johnson in the preseason and claimed the team’s RB3 role.

Perhaps Johnson will ultimately find greener pastures in Green Bay following his trade to the Packers, but it was disheartening to see this once-promising player derailed before he ever got a real chance.

Trevor Etienne (RB – CAR)

Trevor Etienne was a depth piece I had an eye on entering 2026 as a potential contributor, given the struggles we saw from Chuba Hubbard last season. The younger brother of New Orleans’ Travis Etienne Jr., Trevor was selected by Carolina in the fourth round of the 2025 NFL Draft, and he caught my eye as a featured local player out of Georgia.

In college, Etienne was incredibly elusive in the open field, an adept receiver and dangerous on screen passes. Listed at a diminutive 5-foot-9 and 198 pounds., Etienne’s calling card was burst and acceleration, rather than a power-running style. Sadly, he was rolled up by another player during Carolina’s recent preseason game and had to be helped off the field.

Head coach Dave Canales said Etienne is being evaluated and will undergo imaging to determine the extent of the injury — not the news I was hoping to read about his prospects this season. He might return in short order and assuage my fears, but I was hoping Etienne would shine this preseason for a team in desperate need of playmakers.

Dexter did not travel with the Bears to Tennessee for their final preseason game because of a hamstring injury.

Dexter's departure clears the way for defensive tackle Jordan van den Berg to take on a more prominent role after an impressive training camp. Van den Berg was a sixth-round pick in April.

Phillips joins a secondary hit hard by injuries. Safety Coby Bryant had surgery on his left knee on Aug. 7. Cornerback Kyler Gordon is working his way back from a calf issue.

Three players landed on what amounts to the “suspended with pay” list on Sunday, but Pelissero reports Nacua isn’t one of them. That does not necessarily mean Nacua is out of the woods for all time with the NFL, but his situation did not rise to the level of Josh Jacobs’ in the eyes of the shield. Now the main Week 1 question mark for Nacua is his groin injury, but it is not expected to keep him out of the Rams’ Australian opener vs. the 49ers.

We try not to go daily with training camp injuries, but Nacua has now missed the Rams’ entire slate of Saints sessions. Coach Sean McVay had previously said he would return this week. That still does not suggest anything other than standard summer caution, but it’s of course worth noting. For now there is no reason to alter course when it comes to selecting Nacua in the first round of fantasy drafts.

Nacua is entering the final year of his contract. Atkins writes that it is only a matter of time before “Nacua lands a monstrous extension,” but whether it comes from the Rams or another team, presumably via free agency or a trade, remains a question. Both the team and player reportedly “hope” that Nacua remains a Ram long term, and the team is “encouraged by some of the steps he’s taken this offseason.” The superstar wide receiver still has a civil suit that must be dealt with and the league has not yet clarified whether it intends to suspend him. For now, Nacua is a member of the Rams’ explosive offense and can be treated as a locked-in WR1, albeit with some suspension risk.

Nacua suffered a groin injury nearly a week ago and is still dealing with soreness. McVay said last week that he expects Nacua to return sometime this week, but the starting receiver was not on the field during Monday’s practice. McVay didn’t say which day he expects Nacua to be back, noting that the team prefers to “err on the side of caution” with soft-tissue injuries.

McVay was helpfully forthcoming with information today, telling reporters that Nacua’s absence is specifically due to soreness in his psoas muscle. Nacua does not seem to be at risk of missing any time in the regular season, and should return with more than enough time to ramp up for Week 1. He is deservedly a top-five pick in fantasy drafts.

This is mostly just for bookkeeping purposes, though it’s now been three days since Nacua was able to practice in full. NFL Network’s Ian Rapoport has reported Nacua is dealing with “minor soreness,” but “minor soreness” has a way of spiraling when teams aren’t required to actually be honest with their injury reports during training camp. The most important thing is, there has been zero indication Nacua’s Week 1 status is in doubt. We will let you know if that changes.

Nacua left practice with a trainer early on Tuesday. Head coach Sean McVay initially was unsure on what Nacua was dealing with, but Rapoport now reports the 25-year-old is managing groin soreness. The Rams are being cautious with a minor injury but no reason for fantasy managers to fret; Nacua may miss some preseason time but there is no indication he is in danger of missing any regular season games.

Same. We’ll monitor this, but there’s not any actionable advice to hand out until we get a more detailed report. A non-minor Nacua injury, of course, would be stratospheric news in the fantasy community.

Nacua has had a civil lawsuit filed against him for biting a woman and making an “unprovoked antisemtic sentiment.” The star receiver checked in to a luxury treatment center this past offseason. Schefter confirmed that the NFL is still discussing potential discipline for Nacua and Rams LT Alaric Jackson. This probably isn’t something to be overly concerned about in fantasy drafts — we suspect any suspension for Nacua would be short-term — but Schefter believes it’s possible that Nacua is suspended for the Rams opener against the 49ers.

Lloyd is a no-brainer top-100 pick, even if he's a fill-in starter for the first month or so, but he has a pathway to being the Packers' starter all year long if things continue to turn for the worst. The Packers notably said they expect Jacobs to remain a Packer, however. Most teams take the suspension at face value and place a player back into the lineup after their return.

Advertisement

Cowboys waived RB Jaydon Blue

It's never a good sign when a former coach cites the current staff when calling a player "lazy", but that's what happened last summer when Blue was brought up. He never earned the trust of the coaching staff and was waived on cutdown day, despite some buzz that he could be Javonte Williams' backup. Blue never had that skillset. Malik Davis is the current RB2, and he has the early-down skills to be Williams' insurance. Expect Dallas to add more help here. That could simply be by signing Blue and Phil Mafah to the practice squad again. For now, Davis is a great last pick in deep leagues. Williams' doubters would struggle to make a convincing case against him at the Round 3/4 turn.

Raiders kept RB Ashton Jeanty off of IR

Jeanty's mysterious ankle sprain is now officially not that serious. If the Raiders knew he'd be out for the first four games, then he would've ended up on IR, but that did not happen. We should fully expect him back early on. Their season opener is against the lowly Dolphins, and Jeanty was only wearing a sleeve on his ankle when he rolled into the preseason finale in street clothes. I'd expect him to miss 0-2 games. The injury still has setback and efficiency risks. Mike Washington Jr. remains a quality late-round pick in fantasy but shouldn't be drafted inside the top 100 anymore.

Advertisement

Saints kept RB Alvin Kamara off of IR

Kamara's knee injury had a timeline of about a month, but the Saints expect him to be back before Week 4 at this point, if not earlier. The Saints have Travis Etienne Jr., Kamara, Audric Estime and Kendre Miller on the active roster. One of them will likely be a scratch each week.

Seahawks placed RB Zach Charbonnet on PUP

Not surprising. He had ACL surgery on Feb. 20 of this year. It was shocking to see so many reports suggesting he could be so far ahead of schedule that he would dodge PUP, but GM John Schneider said it wasn't a consideration to take him off PUP. If we follow the typical nine-month timeline, then Charbonnet will be back between Halloween and Thanksgiving. First-round rookie RB Jadarian Price will have plenty of time to establish himself before we see Charbonnet. He'll miss at least the first four games of the season.

Cardinals placed RB James Conner on IR

Conner hasn't been able to practice with a foot injury. He wasn't going to be heavily involved on the Cardinals most likely, but Conner was oft-cited as a potential fill-in for other teams on cut day. That won't happen now. It'll be Jeremiyah Love, Tyler Allgeier and Bam Knight for Arizona to start the season.

Advertisement

Bucs RB Sean Tucker remains on team, took paycut

There was beat reporter speculation that the Bucs could release Tucker, as his $3.5M salary was non-guaranteed. Instead, Tucker is staying on the team but needed to drop his salary to a fully-guaranteed $2.5M. That's equivalent to low-end RB2 veterans like Brian Robinson Jr., Rachaad White, Isiah Pacheco and Samaje Perine. He won't be the Bucs' RB2 with Kenny Gainwell complementing starter Bucky Irving, but Tucker could have a miniature role as the RB3 in particular situations. Last year, Tucker led the team in inside the five-yard line carries from Week 13 on when Irving was back from injury. He is the biggest back, by far, on the depth chart, and it's unclear if he'll mix in on short-yardage, or if Irving will be an early-down bellcow while Gainwell plays on passing downs. I would've moved Irving up if Tucker had been released.

Chiefs released RB Emari Demercado

This was the analysis from long-time Chiefs reporter Pete Sweeney: "Moving on from Emari Demercado speaks to a couple things: the Chiefs see Ken Walker as a three-down back, and they love what Emmett Johnson has showed. Brashard Smith is a wild card Andy Reid can move around on offense, and he's KR2. Best return in a while for KC on Friday night."

Advertisement

I have Walker as a first-round fantasy pick and am fully confident in Johnson being a draftable player in the last rounds of drafts after seeing him in preseason.

Quick notes

Jaguars RB3 LeQuint Allen Jr. is on the 53-man roster. We don't have to pretend Bhayshul Tuten is gaining this pass-down role anymore. It's a minor injury.

Bills RB3 Ty Johnson (calf) is on the 53-man roster.

Dolphins released RB Jarquez Hunter right after trading for him. He's a practice squad candidate as he competes with Jaylen Wright and Ollie Gordon II.

The Lions have more RBs (5) than WRs (4) right now. One could read into this being Isiah Pacheco's injury could end up resulting in a stint on IR.

Ravens rookie RB Adam Randall was placed on IR, allowing Rasheen Ali to be the early-down backup to Derrick Henry, while Justice Hill is the rotational pass catcher.

Commanders rookie RB Kaytron Allen makes the team with Jeremy McNichols (quad) injured. He probably would've made it regardless but it wasn't a guarantee.

Colts RB3 DJ Giddens sneaks onto the roster. He's been behind RB2 Seth McGowan in camp.

The Texans "RB3" is just the fullback. That alone makes Woody Marks an interesting insurance play in fantasy.

Steelers rookie Eli Heidenreich is on the 53-man active roster, listed as a RB/WR. He's as much of a slot receiver as pass-down RB to me, but it's notable the Steelers don't have a "real" RB3. It's Jaylen Warren, Rico Dowdle, Heidenreich and a fullback.

Wide Receivers

Colts WR Keenan Allen arrested for DWI

Allen was arrested in downtown Indianapolis early on Sunday and was released later in the day. Typically, DWIs take more than just a few months to clear through the courts, and typically, the NFL doesn't suspend players for DWI until after the case is cleared. I wouldn't expect the Colts to release him for this, so the most likely scenario remains Allen just plays this year without a suspension.

Advertisement

text:
The Minnesota Vikings will be without one of their up-and-coming defenders for the season.

Outside linebacker Tyler Batty suffered a torn ACL during Minnesota's preseason finale on Friday, according to Netflix's Tom Pelissero. The former BYU Cougars standout was placed on injured reserve and ruled out for the 2026 season.

Advertisement

Batty was signed by the Vikings as an undrafted free agent last year. He appeared in 12 games as a rookie, racking up 12 total tackles (two for loss). Most of his time on the field came on special teams. The focus for Batty will be getting healthy for the 2027 season.

This news comes after Batty was having an outstanding training camp ahead of the upcoming season. Analysts around the leagues were starting to take notice of his play for the Vikings. Somewhat rare for an undrafted free agent to make a splash early in his career. He was expected to be one of Minnesota's main rotational pass rushers behind Dallas Turner and Andrew Van Ginkel.

"Tyler Batty has had a nice start to camp, and he'll help in that area, along with second-round pick Jake Golday, who has the versatility and athleticism to play on and off the line," SI's Albert Breer wrote.

The 6-foot-6, 270-pounder spent his entire collegiate career at BYU. He recorded 224 tackles (33.5 for loss) with 16.5 sacks, two fumble recoveries, three forced fumbles, two PDUs and two INTs in 53 games. He earned All-Big 12 honors two straight years. First Team in 2024 and Second Team in 2023.

Advertisement

He led BYU in tackles-for-loss and quarterback hurries in his final three seasons. He was a team captain and leader of the defense in the Cougars' 11-2 campaign during his final season. BYU dominated Colorado led by Shedeur Sanders and Heisman Trophy winner Travis Hunter in the 2024 Alamo Bowl.

Batty was able to stay consistent throughout a defensive coordinator change in Provo. He was part of Ilaisa Tuiaki's three-man rush approach before Jay Hill took over in 2023. This increased his production due to the aggressive pass rush concepts. However, Batty had great talent around him, which allowed for others to be double-teamed.

Minnesota will have to find a replacement for Batty ahead of the upcoming season.

The Vikings open the 2026 season at home against the NFC North rival Green Bay Packers on Sunday, Sept. 13. Kickoff from U.S. Bank Stadium in Minneapolis will be at 4:25 p.m. ET on CBS.

description:
