Specialists (3) On the Initial 53: Long snapper Andrew DePaola; Kicker Will Reichard; Punter Brett Thorson Released: Punter Johnny Hekker (Aug. 30) DePaola, 39, has been a First- or Second-Team All-Pro every year dating to 2022.
text:
Scroll below for positional and historical breakdowns and more at each position.

Positional Breakdowns

Note: Players listed first at each position correspond with starters on the most recent unofficial depth chart, which will be updated for Week 1.

Quarterbacks (4)

On the Initial 53: Kyler Murray; J.J. McCarthy; Carson Wentz; Max Brosmer

Minnesota kept four quarterbacks on its initial roster for the first time in at least a decade. Murray is entering Year 8 in the NFL and will make his Vikings debut Sept. 13, starting at home in Week 1 against Green Bay, whose defense is coordinated by Murray's former head coach with the Cardinals (and a Vikings assistant from 2014-17), Jonathan Gannon. McCarthy was held out of the team's final exhibition due to an ankle injury and enters his third season with 10 starts in 2025 under his belt. Wentz returns to Minnesota with 99 career starts, including five last season. Each QB was drafted in the Top 10: Murray (1st in 2019), Wentz (2nd in '16) and McCarthy (10th in '24). Brosmer is the outlier as a developmental 2025 UDFA but is valued by the organization.

Running backs (3)

On the Initial 53: Aaron Jones, Sr., OR Jordan Mason; Demond Claiborne

Waived: Zavier Scott (Aug. 30)

Waived/Injured: Jermar Jefferson (Aug. 30)

Mason and Jones accounted for 809 and 747 scrimmage yards, respectively, in 2025, and look poised for even larger production this season playing within a revamped run scheme influenced by new Assistant Head Coach Frank Smith (formerly Dolphins Offensive Coordinator) and Keith Carter, who was promoted to offensive line coach. Both veteran backs had fantastic camps. They will help bring along Claiborne, a sixth-round rookie who has tantalizing and unteachable speed.

Fullback (1)

On the Initial 53: Max Bredeson

The Vikings begin the post-C.J. Ham era with another hammer in Bredeson, who was drafted in the fifth round out of Michigan. Bredeson quickly impacted the offense in spring and summer as a lane creator and reliable receiving outlet in the flats. He's got an old-school toughness to him.

Receivers (6)

On the Initial 53: Justin Jefferson, Jordan Addison and Jauan Jennings; Tai Felton and Myles Price; Dillon Bell

Waived: Michael Briscoe, Terrill Davis, Trayvon Rudolph and Marcus Sanders, Jr. (Aug. 30)

Waived/Injured: Dontae Fleming (Aug. 30)

Placed on Reserve/Suspended list: Jeshaun Jones (Aug. 30)

Unlike the past two training camps when he was hampered by a hamstring injury, "Jets" was full-go this year and really started to click with Murray in recent practices. He and Addison are in the same boat, attempting to bounce back from "down" seasons by their lofty standards. The main addition to the group is Jennings, who has 1,618 receiving yards and 15 touchdowns since 2024. Felton and Price are both entering Year 2 and both flashed in camp. Bell, undrafted out of Georgia, possesses a notable run/catch skill set and the physicality to break tackles — and block.

Tight ends (4)

On the Initial 53: T.J. Hockenson; Josh Oliver; Ben Yurosek; Gavin Bartholomew

Waived: Marshall Lang and Matt Lauter (Aug. 30)

Waived/Injured: Bryson Nesbit (Aug. 30)

Hock' sported a new, shorter haircut this summer, and appeared like his old self in several camp practices, boxing out defenders in the red zone and threatening coverages down the seams. Oliver still is a gigantic human capable of acting as an extra offensive lineman in the run game or a "Sears Tower"-sized target. Yurosek will look to elevate his receiving/blocking role in Year 2 — after making the team as an undrafted player last year — and figures to be used on special teams. Bartholomew was a summer standout after missing his rookie season with a back injury.

Offensive line (8)

On the Initial 53: LT Christian Darrisaw; LG Donovan Jackson; C Blake Brandel; RG Will Fries; RT Brian O'Neill; T Ryan Van Demark; T Caleb Tiernan; G Joe Huber

Placed on Injured Reserve-Designated for Return: Michael Jurgens (Aug. 30)

Traded: OL Walter Rouse (Aug. 30)

Waived: G Henry Byrd, C Gavin Gerhardt, G Joshua Gray, G Vershon Lee, OL Tristan Leigh, OL Delby Lemieux and OL Tomas Rimac (Aug. 30)

Brandel is locked in as the club's starting center after committing to the position full-time in the offseason, following part-time duties in a pinch last year. He's flanked to his left by Darrisaw and Jackson — Vikings first-rounders in 2021 and 2025 — and Fries and O'Neill to his right, the latter of whom signed a contract extension in July. Darrisaw and Fries came back from serious injuries (suffered in 2024) in 2025 and have great expectations this season. Huber offers interior depth at three spots, and the third-round rook Tiernan and veteran Van Demark are backups at tackle.

Defensive line (6)

On the Initial 53: Tyrion Ingram-Dawkins, Jalen Redmond and Levi Drake Rodriguez; Caleb Banks, Domonique Orange and Elijah Williams

Released: Jonathan Harris and Isaiahh Loudermilk (Aug. 30)

Waived: Jahvaree Ritzie and Smith Vilbert (Aug. 30)

Redmond, 27, is the "old head," so to speak, in the DL room now. He first emerged in 2024 and proved himself as a dogged two-phase player against the run and pass in 2025. "L.D.R." has come a long way from his seventh-round roots and had a fantastic training camp, often lining up as the starting nose tackle. Ingram-Dawkins is a quasi-edge defender thanks to his inside-outside flexibility and is primed for a much bigger role in his second season. Banks, Orange and Williams round out the youth movement up front. The former two were drafted 18th and 82nd overall this year and could buddy up as future game-wreckers. Williams tried out for the team in 2025 and has been undeniable ever since, with a motor that is bound to find the field in some capacity.

Outside linebackers (4)

On the Initial 53: Dallas Turner and Andrew Van Ginkel; Bo Richter; Chaz Chambliss

Placed on Injured Reserve: Tyler Batty (season-ending)

Waived: OLB Cam'Ron Stewart (Aug. 30)

Waived/Injured: Kenny Dyson, Jr. (Aug. 30)

Turner is taking over the "rush" role previously occupied by Jonathan Greenard, and there is palpable buzz surrounding him after a solid camp that included two days of feasting off the edge in joint practices versus Baltimore. Van Ginkel, most importantly, is healthy, which means he's fully capable of vying for accolades. Richter and Chambliss were 2024 and 2025 UDFAs who are gritty and will contribute to special teams. Chambliss also is getting work as the backup fullback.

Inside linebackers (4)

On the Initial 53: Blake Cashman and Eric Wilson; Jake Golday and Ivan Pace, Jr.

Waived: Bangally Kamara and Josh Ross (Aug. 30)

Cashman and Wilson will aim to replicate their 2025 excellence in tandem as outstanding blitzers and instinctive playmakers. Pace, another great blitzer, is the longest-tenured Viking in the LB room and poses to spell those two whenever they need it, and also dynamically impact special teams. Golday is the ultimate understudy. The second-round rookie will eventually take snaps as an off-ball 'backer, as well as an edge rusher. Golday is big, fast and good in space.

Cornerbacks (5)

On the Initial 53: Byron Murphy, Jr., and Isaiah Rodgers; Chuck Demmings and James Pierre; Zemaiah Vaughn

Waived: Tre Hawkins, Bryce Phillips and Jarod Washington (Aug. 30)

Waived/Injured: Marcus Allen (Aug. 30)

Murphy and Rodgers — and the whole defense, of course — should benefit from quality reinforcements at cornerback this season. That veteran duo, plus Pierre, who had a career year in 2025 on the Steelers, will be mentors to Demmings, who's seamlessly made the jump so far from the FCS to the NFL, and Vaughn, who only started playing corner in college and has great length for the position. Murph', especially, was picking off passes left and right in training camp.

Safeties (5)

On the Initial 53: Joshua Metellus and Jay Ward; Theo Jackson and Jakobe Thomas; Jacob Thomas

Released: Tavierre Thomas (Aug. 30)

Waived: Kahlef Hailassie (Aug. 30)

The glaring omission, obviously, is Harrison Smith, who may or may not rejoin the Vikings at some point this season. Either way, Metellus is streamlining communication in the secondary, and he's got a supporting cast with upside. Jackson and Ward have familiarity in Brian Flores' scheme, and the rookie Thomases (Jakobe, a third-round pick; Jacob, an undrafted addition) are equipped with strong skills compatible with Flo's assignments.

Specialists (3)

On the Initial 53: Long snapper Andrew DePaola; Kicker Will Reichard; Punter Brett Thorson

Released: Punter Johnny Hekker (Aug. 30)

DePaola, 39, has been a First- or Second-Team All-Pro every year dating to 2022. Reichard may very well be an All-Pro every year from now until he's 39. And, Thorson is the reigning Ray Guy Award winner (college football's best punter), who beat out the NFL's All-Decade punter of the 2010s (Hekker). In other words, it's a special trio under Special Teams Coordinator Matt Daniels.

title: Browns roster breakdown: Lots of youth, complicated decisions and 1 surprise - The Athletic
description:
Roster remains fluid There were no trades involving the Browns over the weekend — at least there haven’t been any yet.
Ten practice squad spots must go to players with two or fewer years of experience.
Last year, the Browns traded quarterback Kenny Pickett and acquired offensive lineman KT Leveston just ahead of the roster deadline.
Leveston was waived on Sunday but could return via the practice squad.
The Browns kept only five linebackers, a sign they’ll add at least two to the practice squad this week.
text:
The Cleveland Browns prepared for the possibility of going with four quarterbacks on their 53-man roster, but Sunday’s league-wide cuts came with a surprise.

Dillon Gabriel will begin the season on injured reserve due to a back injury. He will be eligible to potentially return after four games, but he’s not on the initial active roster. The Browns will open the season with Deshaun Watson as the starting quarterback, Shedeur Sanders next in line and rookie Taylen Green as the No. 3 passer.

Green likely will be a game day inactive and the emergency quarterback early in the season, but he could eventually be used as a short-yardage runner and gadget player.

The Browns still have four quarterbacks in the mix, and there’s no real guarantee any of them will be in the team’s plans after this season. New Browns coach Todd Monken has insisted that Watson is the starter and that it’s not a week-to-week situation, but the Browns have had at least three starting quarterbacks in each of the last three years.

Gabriel might have been available via trade had he been healthy, but the Browns were never going to give him away. Gabriel and Sanders are on their standard rookie contracts through the 2028 season.

Green didn’t get many competitive reps this spring or summer and is viewed as a long-term developmental option, but because of his rare combination of size and athleticism, the Browns likely were going to be hesitant to let him hit the waiver wire on Monday, even if Gabriel was healthy. Unless another quarterback addition is made via the practice squad, the Browns will prepare for their Sept. 13 season opener in Jacksonville with Green as their scout-team quarterback.

Roster remains fluid

There were no trades involving the Browns over the weekend — at least there haven’t been any yet. They figure to be seeking upgrades at tight end, cornerback and along the defensive line in the coming days.

The first run of the waiver wire is Monday afternoon, after which teams can officially begin building their 16-man practice squads. Ten practice squad spots must go to players with two or fewer years of experience.

Trades have often been a part of general manager Andrew Berry’s late-August decision-making process. Last year, the Browns traded quarterback Kenny Pickett and acquired offensive lineman KT Leveston just ahead of the roster deadline. Leveston was waived on Sunday but could return via the practice squad.

The Browns chose to keep Luke Wypler and Zak Zinter as interior backups. Leveston started training camp competing for the starting right guard job but later moved back to tackle, where he made seven emergency starts last season. His versatility should help him retain an NFL job — on some level — for the season ahead.

Wypler might be the backup center for now and one of the players whose roster spot could be in jeopardy as the Browns continue to shuffle things in the days ahead. Rookie center Parker Brailsford missed almost all of training camp with a thumb injury on his right (snapping) hand but was back to practice on a limited basis last week.

Rookie Austin Barber is making a push to potentially take over the starting right guard job, which means Dawand Jones is the top backup tackle for now. If the Browns lost one of their starting tackles to injury, Barber could move back outside. He spent the spring and the first three weeks of training camp working mostly as a right tackle.

Ins, outs and maybes

The Browns waived local product and preseason hero Luke Floriea despite him having three receiving touchdowns over the final two preseason games. The sixth wide receiver spot went to Malachi Corley, a move that says the Browns view Corley as a core special teams contributor.

Outside of the Gabriel injured-reserve designation, it’s hard to say there were really any major surprises. Some of the decisions were complicated.

Brailsford, fullback Michael Burton and defensive tackle Kalia Davis are on the initial 53-man roster despite missing almost all of training camp due to injury. Brailsford was a roster lock, but it was tough to project the other spots.

The Browns chose to waive both of their undrafted rookie defensive ends, Khordae Sydnor and Logan Fano. At least for now, Burton and rookie tight end/fullback Carsen Ryan are on the roster.

As expected, this is a young roster, with 23 of the 53 players having no more than one previous year of NFL experience. Only one undrafted rookie, cornerback Michael Coats Jr., made the initial 53.

Nine of the team’s 10 2026 draft picks are on the active roster, with tight end Joe Royer, who’s been placed on the non-football illness list, the lone exception. Royer did not participate in any of the full-squad training camp practices and has been away from the team since July for undisclosed personal reasons, but he’ll be eligible to potentially play later this season.

There are seven players 30 or older, so the Browns may not end up as the league’s youngest team by average age. But this is going to be a young team that will likely look to add youth in its obvious areas of need. Age probably won’t matter as the team seeks immediate help from a blocking-first tight end, but it figures to look for developmental players across the defense as Berry examines waiver and external practice squad options.

Floriea, Leveston, Fano, Sydnor, running back Davon Booth, defensive tackle Tyreak Sapp and linebacker Nathaniel Watson are likely practice squad candidates, assuming they clear waivers and want to return to the team. The Browns kept only five linebackers, a sign they’ll add at least two to the practice squad this week.

The full list

Here are the moves the Browns made Sunday to trim their roster to 53.

Placed on reserve/injured: Dillon Gabriel, QB

Placed on reserve/non-football illness: Joe Royer, TE

Contract terminated (3): Myles Bryant, CB; Sam Kamara, DT; D’Angelo Ross, CB

title: Gut Reaction: Broncos' Most Surprising Cuts and What They Mean - Sports Illustrated
description:
It's a necessary evil, though, as the Broncos' prime directive is to land on the right 53-man roster.
As always, there were some shocking cuts and a few surprise players to make the Broncos' 53-man roster.
And while there's always a need for an emergency quarterback on game day, that doesn't mean he needs to be on the 53-man roster.
He needs more time to ripen on the vine, and he'll likely get it on the practice squad.
Meanwhile, the Broncos released fullback Adam Prentice with the full intention of re-signing him to the practice squad.
text:
For the Denver Broncos, the hard part is in the rear-view.

There are still 17 tough regular-season games to play, but the painful process of cutting nearly 40 players over a two-day period is one the Broncos' coaching staff and front office dread each year. It's a necessary evil, though, as the Broncos' prime directive is to land on the right 53-man roster.

As always, there were some shocking cuts and a few surprise players to make the Broncos' 53-man roster. There are many implications, so let's break down the biggest takeaways from the roster cut-down process.

Broncos Can't Quit Sam Ehlinger

The Broncos opted to keep three quarterbacks out of training camp, with Ehlinger joining Bo Nix and Jarrett Stidham on the 53-man roster. Ehlinger outplayed Stidham for most of the summer and punctuated his preseason with an impressive three-touchdown showing in the finale on Friday, but it wasn't enough to bump Stidham off the roster or leapfrog him on the depth chart.

Why do the Broncos feel compelled to keep three quarterbacks? It's hard to say, because at first blush, it seems like a wasted roster spot when the Broncos cut so many surprise players and three rookie draft picks.

We know the Broncos love their quarterback room; we've heard head coach Sean Payton and GM George Paton mention it often over the past two years. And while there's always a need for an emergency quarterback on game day, that doesn't mean he needs to be on the 53-man roster.

The silver lining is that the Broncos will have plenty of quarterback depth entering a season in which Nix is coming off a serious injury. The Broncos believe Nix is as good as new, and he certainly looked like it in camp and his one preseason performance, but perhaps the team has adopted the "it's better to have and not need than to need and not have" philosophy at quarterback.

A Tough Roster to Crack

Again, three of the Broncos' seven draft picks did not make the initial roster out of camp. One came as a moderate surprise, and the other as a shocker.

Fifth-round tight end Justin Joly was waived after a very uneven rookie training camp. He struggled throughout camp and didn't seem to take to his NFL coaching well. His 88-yard touchdown reception in the finale (busted coverage) didn't save him from the consequences of his lackluster summer.

What makes Joly a moderate surprise is that he was a fifth-round pick the Broncos traded up to select, and we knew he was going to take some time to develop. He still may get that time, by the way, if he passes through waivers. The Broncos could re-sign him to the practice squad, but if he gets claimed by another team, he'll end up being a colossal waste of two draft picks.

The big shocker was linebacker Red Murdock. This year's "Mr. Irrelvant" distinguished himself well the second half of camp, and played at a relatively high level in the preseason, leading the Broncos in tackles.

Alas, the Broncos prioritized Jordan Turner's special teams acumen over Murdock, and now there's a good chance Red will be gone on waivers. If Murdock goes unclaimed, he's a sure-fire practice squad addition, but that's a big if.

The Murdock cut is a short-sighted move. The Broncos have lacked youthful depth at inside linebacker — a candidate to offer future starter potential for life after Alex Singleton and Justin Strnad — and while Karene Reid played well in the preseason, Murdock has more of the long-term markers. I hope this decision doesn't blow up in Denver's face.

The third rookie to be waived was seventh-round safety Miles Scott. He needs more time to ripen on the vine, and he'll likely get it on the practice squad.

The rookies to make the Broncos' 53-man roster out of camp were:

Tyler Onyedim | OL | Third Round

Jonah Coleman | RB | Fourth Round

Kage Casey | OL | Fourth Round

Dallen Bentley | TE | Seventh Round

No Undrafted Rookie Makes the Cut

For just the second time in the past 23 years, no undrafted rookie made the 53-man roster out of camp. There were some rookies who got close, like wideouts Kolbe Katsis and Cameron Ross, both of whom will be re-signed to the practice squad if they clear waivers; linebacker Taurean York; offensive lineman Gavin Ortega; and long snapper Luke Basso.

Again, it's a tough roster to crack.

Long Snapper Shenanigans

The Broncos released veteran long snapper Mitchell Fraboni, which means, I suppose, that Basso won the competition this summer, even though he had a few cringe moments, including a bad snap that led to a botched field-goal attempt in the preseason.

It's not clear yet if there will be any roster shenanigans with Fraboni, but it appears the Broncos might be willing to lean on Basso as a practice squad elevation for the first three games. We'll have to wait to hear what GM George Paton says on the matter this evening.

Update: Paton explained that Fraboni will be re-signed to the practice squad, not Basso, where the Broncos plan to elevate him to the game-day roster initially.

“Yes, Mitch is going to be on our practice squad," Paton said on Sunday evening. "He’ll be a practice-squad veteran. They don’t have to clear waivers. It just provides flexibility within the roster throughout the season when they start here, and so that’s all it was.”

Cody Schrader Gets Robbed

The Broncos kept four running backs, but Schrader wasn't one of them, despite performing at such a high level in the preseason. The Broncos said goodbye to Jaleel McLaughlin, too, who's been with the team since 2023 and chose to re-sign back in March.

Instead, the Broncos are rolling with Tyler Badie as the fourth and final running back behind J.K. Dobbins, RJ Harvey, and Coleman. The Broncos value Badie for his blocking ability on third down, his pass-catching skills, and his verastility as a special teams returner.

Unless the plan is to make Coleman a healthy scratch, though, Badie will be unlikely to suit up in many games this season, so the utility of having that well-rounded skill set won't avail the Broncos unless there's an injury ahead of him on the depth chart. Then again, the team could plan to dress Badie and not Coleman initially, though that would be a crime.

Hopefully, Schrader clears waivers and can be re-signed to the practice squad, but I doubt it. He earned a 53-man roster spot somewhere, in all likelihood.

Meanwhile, the Broncos released fullback Adam Prentice with the full intention of re-signing him to the practice squad. He'll be part of this team and contribute throughout the season.

Goodbye, Drew Sanders

The Broncos waived Sanders with an injury designation, ending his troubled tenure in Denver. The 2023 third-round pick is a talented player, but the injury bug claimed each of his past two seasons, and just when he was building up a head of steam this summer, he suffered an injury in the first preseason game that sidelined him the rest of the way.

It's a bummer, for sure, but hopefully Sanders can get healthy and continue on with his NFL career. If anyone could use a fresh start somewhere else, it's him.

Calvin Throckmorton Doesn't Survive

Despite stepping up in the face of the Broncos' injury crisis at center and playing exceedingly well in the preseason, Throckmorton was released. Now, he could choose to re-sign with the practice squad, since he's a vested veteran, but I wouldn't be surprised if he finds an active roster spot elsewhere.

The Broncos kept Alex Forsyth instead, a 2023 sixth-round pick, despite missing the entire preseason with an injury. Forsyth is also entering a contract year, so I'm not sure what the upside is to retaining him, especially when Throckmorton played so well and offers the versatility to play any of the three spots on the interior offensive line.

Hopefully, this isn't the last we see of Throckmorton in the Orange and Blue.

Lil'Jordan Humphrey Makes the Cut

After months of speculation, the Broncos indeed kept six wide receivers, with Humphrey as the last guy. His special-teams acumen made the difference, although he's not a returner.

Humphrey has rolled with the punches as a Bronco, going back and forth from the practice squad to the active roster, and he had an excellent camp, though he didn't stand out in the preseason. He's the Broncos best blocking receiver, which is another big reason he was kept.

Jonathon Cooper Hits the Commissioner's Exempt List

Cooper will miss two to six games on the commissioner's exempt list after he was arrested twice during the summer and charged with felony assault. His first court date is on Monday, August 31, when he's scheduled to be arraigned.

The Broncos knew this was coming, and thankfully, they're deep at outside linebacker. Because Cooper won't count toward the 53-man roster while he's on the commissioner's exempt list, the Broncos were able to go deep at quarterback and wide receiver.

Cooper could miss up to six games, but time will tell. Meanwhile, expect Jonah Elliss to take over Cooper's starting job in the interim. Time will tell whether Cooper gets it back upon his return.

Tycen Anderson Makes the Team

Anderson made the 53-man roster by the skin of his teeth. The Broncos' plan was to have Taylor Rapp on the roster, but less than a week after signing him, they released him due to personal issues he's dealing with off the field, though they hope to have him back once they're resolved.

So JL Skinner made it on the heels of a strong camp and preseason, and Anderson. The Broncos waived Scott and undrafted rookie Parker Robertson. The top three safeties are Talanoa Hufanga, Brandon Jones, and Devon Key, with Skinner and Anderson as key special teams contributors.

Key is a special teams All-Pro, too, so expect him to continue contributing in the third phase.

The Injured Ones

The Broncos placed tight end Caleb Lohner and offensive tackle Frank Crum on injured reserve to open the season, while offensive guard Nick Gargiulo will start the year on the Physically Unable to Perform list. Gargiulo's injury came a year ago, an ACL tear, and he's yet to return to the field, but as a recent sixth-round pick, the Broncos want to keep him around.

Lohner underwent a knee clean-up procedure early in the summer, missing all of camp and the preseason. Crum was injured during the preseason.

The NFL’s cutdown day has come and gone, meaning the Las Vegas Raiders have their initial 53-man roster set. One player who isn’t on it is rookie third-round pick Keyron Crawford.

Crawford was placed on injured reserve after suffering an ankle injury in the Raiders’ final preseason game against the San Francisco 49ers this past Thursday night. The defensive end had to be carted off the field, and while the full extent of his injury is still unknown, the fact that Las Vegas didn’t use one of its two return designations on the Auburn product means it’s significant. The Raiders did designate tight end Carter Runyon to return from IR after Runyon missed the majority of training camp with an undisclosed injury.

Crawford likely wasn’t going to get much playing time behind Maxx Crosby, Kwity Paye and Malcolm Koonce in year one, anyway. Of course, practice reps are valuable for a young player’s development down the line, but the rookie being out will have a minimal impact on this year’s defense.

Meanwhile, Crawford’s injury likely was the final boost Patrick Johnson needed to make the team. The 28-year-old was arguably the Silver and Black’s best top performer during the preseason, collecting 11 tackles, two sacks and four TFLs over the three games. Baring another move/waiver wire pickup on Monday, the Silver and Black will roll into the 2026 season with Crosby, Paye, Koonce and Crawford at edge defender.

title: The 53: Breaking Down the Jaguars Roster
description:
The Jaguars waived rookie J'Mari Taylor and released veteran DeeJay Dallas Sunday, with Taylor a strong possibility for the practice squad.
Wide receivers (6) Projected starters: Jakobi Meyers (eighth NFL season), Parker Washington (fourth), Brian Thomas Jr. (third NFL season).
Williams and Cameron, both of whom were selected in the sixth round of the 2026 NFL Draft, impressed in training camp.
The Jaguars waived/injured Keivie Rose Sunday, and waived Tommy Akingbesote, T.J. Bollers and Jalen Hunt Sunday.
The Jaguars waived Jabbar Muhammed and Preston Hodge Sunday, releasing Corey Ballentine.
text:
Running backs (4)

Projected starters: Bhayshul Tuten (second NFL season), Chris Rodriguez Jr. (fourth). Others on roster: LeQuint Allen Jr. (second), Ameer Abdullah (12th).

The Jaguars will enter the 2026 season with four running backs on the roster for a second consecutive season, with the position undergoing significant change since the end of last season. Tuten, who rushed for 307 yards and five touchdowns as a Jaguars rookie last season, and Rodriguez – who signed with the Jaguars as a restricted free agent after rushing for 500 yards and six touchdowns with the Washington Commanders last season – have been listed as co-starters on the depth chart throughout the preseason. Allen finished preseason not playing because of a soft-tissue injury, and Abdullah impressed offensively and on special teams throughout training camp. The Jaguars waived rookie J'Mari Taylor and released veteran DeeJay Dallas Sunday, with Taylor a strong possibility for the practice squad.

Wide receivers (6)

Projected starters: Jakobi Meyers (eighth NFL season), Parker Washington (fourth), Brian Thomas Jr. (third NFL season). Others on roster: Travis Hunter (second), CJ Williams (rookie), Josh Cameron (rookie).

This has become a position of strength in the past year – with Meyers, Washington and Thomas a strong, versatile and balanced core trio. Hunter, the No. 2 overall selection in the 2025 NFL Draft, focused mainly on defense late in training camp and preseason but is expected to play a significant role offensively. Williams and Cameron, both of whom were selected in the sixth round of the 2026 NFL Draft, impressed in training camp. The Jaguars released veterans Tim Jones and Austin Trammell Sunday and waived Trebor Peña, Chandler Brayboy, Michael Wortham and Brady Boyd. Jones, Peña, Wortham and Trammell seem candidates for the practice squad.

Tight ends (4)

Projected starter(s): Brenton Strange (fourth NFL season). Others on the roster: Nate Boerkircher (rookie), Tanner Koziol (rookie), Quintin Morris (fifth).

This is a strong, intriguing position with the Jaguars talking throughout the offseason about playing more multiple tight-end formations in 2026 than they did in 2025. Strange, who signed a contract extension in the offseason, emerged as one of the NFL's top tight ends last season. The Jaguars selected Boerkircher in the second round of the 2026 NFL Draft and Koziol in Round 5, marking the first time in franchise history they selected two tight ends in the same draft. Morris is a solid blocker who the team re-signed in the offseason. The Jaguars traded Hunter Long to the Arizona Cardinals Sunday and waived Patrick Herbert, with Herbert seemingly a practice-squad possibility.

Offensive linemen (9)

Projected starters: Left tackle Anton Harrison (fourth NFL season), left guard Emmanuel Pregnon (rookie), center Robert Hainsey (sixth), right guard Ezra Cleveland (seventh), right tackle Cole Van Lanen (fourth). Others on roster: Walker Little (sixth), Jonah Monheim (second), Wyatt Milum (second), Daniel Faalele (fifth).

This is a deep position that underwent change as it dealt with injuries during 2026 Training Camp, with Harrison moving to the left side after starting at right tackle in 2022-2024 and Van Lanen moving to the right side after finishing 2025 starting at left tackle. Pregnon, a third-round selection in the 2026 NFL Draft, worked with the starters much of the last two weeks of training camp, with Cleveland – a starter at left guard last season – moving to the right side. Monheim had a strong camp, as did Little. The Jaguars acquired Faalale in a training camp trade with the New York Giants. They released Chuma Edoga, a veteran who started two games for the Jaguars last season, and Geron Christian Jr. and Sam Mustipher Sunday. They waived Jerome Carvin, Jimbo Obidegwu, Sam Mustipher, Jerome Carvin, Ricky Lee, Kilian Zierer and Timothy McKay Sunday – with multiple players from that group practice-squad possibilities.

Defensive ends (6)

Projected starters: Josh Hines-Allen (eighth NFL season), Travon Walker (fifth). Others on roster: B.J. Green II (second), Danny Striggow (second), Wesley Williams (rookie), Bryan Thomas Jr. (rookie).

This is a talented position that finished the 2026 preseason feeling potentially deep as the Jaguars leaned fully into acquiring young players – and developing them – behind Hines-Allen and Walker. That duo forms one of the NFL's best end combinations, with Hines-Allen a two-time Pro Bowl selection and Walker one of the best run defenders who also had double-digit sacks in 2023 and 2024. Green had an impressive training camp, with Striggow a strong run defender. The Jaguars selected Williams in the fourth round of the 2026 NFL Draft, and Thomas – who signed with the Jaguars as a collegiate free agent following the '26 draft – registered 3.5 sacks in three preseason games. The Jaguars waived Quindarius Dunnigan Sunday and placed rookie seventh-round selection Zach Durfee on injured reserve designated to return.

Defensive tackles (5)

Projected starters: DaVon Hamilton (seventh NFL season), Arik Armstead (12th). Others on roster: Matt Dickerson (seventh), Ruke Orhorhoro (third), Albert Regis (rookie).

This a strong position, particularly against the run, with Hamilton emerging last season as one of the NFL's top nose tackles and Dickerson emerging as a front-line player in the Jaguars' defensive line rotation. Armstead has been a quality pass rusher when healthy, and the Jaguars acquired Orhorhoro in an offseason trade with the Atlanta Falcons. Regis, a third-round selection in the 2026 NFL Draft, flashed at times in the preseason and had a sack against the New Orleans Saints in the preseason opener. The Jaguars waived/injured Keivie Rose Sunday, and waived Tommy Akingbesote, T.J. Bollers and Jalen Hunt Sunday. Bollers and Hunt seem strong practice-squad possibilities.

Linebackers (5)

Projected starters: Foyesade Oluokun (ninth NFL season), Ventrell Miller (fourth) or Branson Combs (second), Dennis Gardeck (ninth). Others on the roster: Jahlani Tavai (eight).

This was an area of focus during '26 preseason and training camp, with Miller and Combs competing at weakside linebacker alongside Oluokun and Gardeck. Oluokun, a starter the past four seasons since joining the Jaguars as an unrestricted free agent, remains a consistent key to the defense and Gardeck is a reliable pass rusher/strong-side linebacker. The Jaguars waived three former draft selection at this position Sunday – Yasir Abdullah (Round 6, 2023), Jalen McLeod (Round 6, 2025) and Jack Kiser (Round 4, 2025) – and waived Amari Burney and released Baylon Spector Sunday.

Cornerbacks (5)

Projected starters: Montaric Brown (fifth), Travis Hunter (second), Jourdan Lewis (10th). Others on the roster: Jarrian Jones (third), Christian Braswell (third).

The Jaguars have transformed this position in the last year, with Hunter – the No. 2 overall selection in the 2025 NFL Draft – expected to move permanently into a starting position opposite Brown, who emerged as a starter last season before signing a contract extension in March. Lewis remains critical to the secondary, as does Jones – who proved solid in multiple positions late last season with Lewis out with a foot injury. The Jaguars waived Jabbar Muhammed and Preston Hodge Sunday, releasing Corey Ballentine. Muhammed seems a strong practice squad possibility.

Safeties (5)

This position has transformed in the last year, largely because Johnson has emerged as one of the team's top defensive players after beginning the 2025 season as a reserve. Murray, who signed with the Jaguars as an unrestricted free agent in the 2025 offseason, remains a reliable veteran and Lane is one of the team's top special teams players. Ransaw and Huskey each played extensively throughout the preseason, with Ransaw – a third-round selection in the 2025 NFL Draft – missing his rookie season with a foot injury. The Jaguars waived Cam'Ron Silmon-Craig, Trevian Thomas and Devin Neal Jr. Sunday.

Specialists (3)

Kicker Cam Little (third NFL season), punter Logan Cooke (ninth), long snapper Ross Matiscik (seventh).

text:
With three NFL preseason games in the books and training camp starting to wrap up, the Las Vegas Raiders got their roster down to the required 53 players on Sunday, setting the stage for Week 1 against the Miami Dolphins on Sept. 13 at Allegiant Stadium.

Advertisement

Although there were some surprise cuts and moves ahead of the Sunday deadline, with players like defensive end Cian Slone getting waived and Patrick Johnson making the final roster, the team is finally set, and the real countdown to the season opener can begin.

Ashton Jeanty Won't Start 2026 NFL Season on IR

One of the major question marks for the Raiders heading into Sunday was whether star running back Ashton Jeanty would be put on the injured reserve list, which would cost the second-year back at least the first four games of the 2026 NFL season.

Fortunately for Jeanty and first-year head coach Klint Kubiak, the team's lead back won't be put on IR to begin the season, meaning the Raiders are confident he'll be back on the field sooner rather than later, according to Sam Warren of The Athletic.

"The Raiders did not place Ashton Jeanty on IR to begin the season," Warren wrote. "Shows that the team is confident he'll return from his injury within four games."

Advertisement

Obviously, this is great news for the Raiders ahead of Week 1 against the Dolphins, though it remains unclear when Jeanty will be ready to return to the field. Las Vegas can be confident that the run game likely won't miss a beat, especially with rookie Mike Washington Jr. ready to shoulder the load as the starter if Jeanty misses time right out of the gate.

Washington has been impressive, to say the least, during the preseason and training camp, earning him a significant role on this team moving forward. Dylan Laube will likely serve as Washington's backup if Jeanty can't go in Week 1 against Miami.

Raiders Keep 3 Quarterbacks to Start 2026 Campaign

Along with the good news on the running back situation, the Raiders have decided to begin the 2026 campaign with three quarterbacks on the roster, which is a little surprising.

text:
The Browns officially announced their initial 53-man roster heading into the 2026 season. The 53-man roster showcases young players in prominent roles on offense and defense, as well as key veterans to anchor units on all three sides of the ball.

Offensively, the Browns are rostering three quarterbacks in Taylen Green, Shedeur Sanders and Deshaun Watson, with Sanders to serve as the backup quarterback to Watson as the starter. The Browns also placed Dillon Gabriel on injured reserve.

Their quarterbacks will have a number of pass-catching threats, as their roster carries six receivers and three tight ends. Harold Fannin Jr. leads the tight end room as he enters his second season with the Browns, one that features rookie Carsen Ryan and veteran Blake Whiteheart. Cleveland drafted Ryan in the seventh round of the 2026 NFL Draft.

The receiving corps is anchored by veterans in Jerry Jeudy and Tylan Wallace, and features two standout rookies in Denzel Boston and KC Concepcion. Boston and Concepcion demonstrated their abilities to impact the offense throughout training camp to hold prominent roles in the offense. Isaiah Bond and Malachi Corley add to key depth players to receiver room.

The running back room combines youth and talent, as Quinshon Judkins and Dylan Sampson enter their second seasons in Cleveland. Rounding out the room is Raheim Sanders and fullback Michael Burton.

The offensive line consists of a majority of new faces – whether in veterans who joined the Browns during free agency or rookies drafted in the 2026 NFL Draft. Ninth overall pick Spencer Fano is joined by fellow rookies Austin Barber and Parker Brailsford. Their veteran leaders on the starting offensive line feature Tytus Howard, Elgton Jenkins, Teven Jenkins and Zion Johnson. Returning young players like Dawand Jones, Luke Wypler and Zak Zinter round out the depth in the room.

Defensively, the Browns' attacking front is built with a mix of young players and veterans.

Jared Verse, Isaiah McGuire and Derek Barnett anchor the edge, while Maliek Collins and Mason Graham hold down the interior. They also have key depth players in Kalia Davis, Mike Hall Jr., Adin Huntington and Julian Okwara who can fill in at positions across the line.

Their linebacker room features both returning players and new additions, as the reigning Defensive Rookie of the Year Carson Schwesinger is in his second season in Cleveland, while the addition of Quincy Williams brings veteran presence to the room. Easton Mascarenas-Arnold earns a key role in his second season with the Browns, while rookie Justin Jefferson and third-year Winston Reid add necessary depth to the room.

The defensive backs return six players from the 2025 season in CB Tyson Campbell, S Grant Delpit, CB Myles Harden, S Ronnie Hickman, CB Denzel Ward and Donovan McMillon. They made key additions during the offseason by drafting S Emmanuel McNeil-Warren and bringing in Daniel Thomas and Mekhi Blackmon. Michael Coats Jr., who signed with Cleveland as an undrafted free agent, earns a chance to be a depth piece in the secondary.

Their specials return for the second consecutive year with P Corey Bojorquez, LS Rex Sunahara and K Andre Szmyt.

The Browns can make additional roster moves in the coming days via waiver claims and free agent signings. They will also look to construct a 16-man practice squad, a group of players that play a vital role throughout the season and serve as an additional layer of depth in the event of injuries on the active roster.

text:
With the NFL cutdown day off to a fast start, there have been plenty of trades, surprise cuts, and even a future Hall of Famer coming out of retirement. Sunday provided much-needed news in a truly eventful fashion.

Three-time Defensive Player of the Year Aaron Donald is coming out of retirement for one last championship run on a one-year deal with the Los Angeles Rams. Meanwhile, Odell Beckham Jr. made the New York Giants' 53-man roster, continuing his story right where it began.

Running back Josh Jacobs went on the Commissioner's Exempt list, which prompted the Green Bay Packers to acquire running back Kaleb Johnson from the Pittsburgh Steelers. In Minnesota, the Vikings kept J.J. McCarthy, while the Titans moved on from quarterback Will Levis.

Here’s the latest NFL news that took place on Sunday.

After months of speculation, the payoff finally arrived. The Los Angeles Rams lured three-time Defensive Player of the Year Aaron Donald out of retirement on a one-year, $20 million deal, ESPN first reported on Sunday afternoon.

The deal can reach as much as $30 million with incentives, assuming he plays up to expectations this season. Donald joins one of the league’s top defenses, forming a dominant front alongside Myles Garrett and pairing two of the greatest defensive linemen in NFL history.

"I think this is a complete team with me here or without me here," Donald told reporters about re-joining the Rams. "I already thought it was a stacked D-line with Verse … then you bring a guy like Myles Garrett, a generational talent, and it's like, that could be fun, right?

After Donald last suited up for the Rams in 2023 and announced his retirement in March 2024 at the age of 32, the Rams posted back-to-back winning seasons. Now, after continuing to strengthen their defense, they welcome the legend back.

With Donald back in action, he’s expected to make his long-awaited debut in Week 1 when the Rams take on the San Francisco 49ers at Melbourne Cricket Ground in Melbourne, Australia.

After years of injuries, Beckham is back on a Week 1 roster – and it's a familiar one for him. He earned a spot on the Giants' 53-man roster, completing a full-circle journey that lands him back where his career started.

After weeks of speculation, Beckham has officially made the cut. This marks the first time he'll be on the Giants' Week 1 roster since 2018 and with Malik Nabers working his way back from injury.

"I never wanted to leave; I wanted to win," Beckham told reporters after the Giants' preseason win over the Jets. "All I ever wanted was for the Giants organization was win a championship. All I ever wanted to do was be great, and those things still very much matter to me."

Adding depth with an experienced player like Beckham was a must for head coach John Harbaugh. Now, with Beckham set to make the roster, the Giants have improved the receiver room from last season for second-year quarterback Jaxson Dart.

Beckham was selected No. 12 overall in the 2014 NFL Draft and he put up staggering numbers during his Giants tenure. In 59 games, he recorded 390 catches, 5,476 yards, and 44 touchdowns before he was traded to the Cleveland Browns in 2019

With Nabers returning, Beckham joins a Giants receiver room alongside Darnell Mooney, Darius Slayton, and Notre Dame third-round pick Malachi Fields. Beckham offers depth while Nabers, Fields, and Mooney absorb most early snaps.

The Green Bay Packers officially placed edge rusher Micah Parsons on the Reserve/Physically Unable to Perform (PUP) list Sunday, ruling him out for at least the first four games of the regular season.

Parsons continues to recover from a torn ACL and meniscus damage sustained last December against the Denver Broncos.

Under NFL regulations, placement on the Reserve/PUP list requires a minimum four-game absence, sidelining Parsons for matchups against the Minnesota Vikings, New York Jets, Atlanta Falcons, and Tampa Bay Buccaneers. He remains on track for a potential October return, making a Week 6 matchup against his former team, the Dallas Cowboys, a possible target.

In a separate move, running back Josh Jacobs was placed on the commissioner's exempt list on Sunday, which prevents him from practicing or playing while the league continues its review.

The decision follows a May arrest in Wisconsin, where initial domestic abuse charges were reduced Thursday to two misdemeanors: misdemeanor battery and criminal damage to property.

Packers general manager Brian Gutekunst acknowledged earlier in the week that the organization was "preparing" for a potential league suspension. To address backfield depth with Jacobs unavailable, Green Bay acquired running back Kaleb Johnson in a trade with the Pittsburgh Steelers.

The Packers also made two trades on Sunday.

To address backfield depth with Jacobs unavailable, Green Bay acquired running back Kaleb Johnson in a trade with the Pittsburgh Steelers. The Packers addressed their backfield depth by acquiring running back Kaleb Johnson from the Pittsburgh Steelers.

Johnson, a 2025 third-round draft choice out of Iowa, saw limited action in Pittsburgh behind Jaylen Warren and Rico Dowdle, logging 28 carries for 69 yards across 10 games as a rookie.

He joins a Packers running back room that includes MarShawn Lloyd and Chris Brooks as Green Bay prepares for the regular season with starter Josh Jacobs on the commissioner's exempt list. During his final season at Iowa, Johnson rushed for 1,537 yards and 21 touchdowns.

The Green Bay Packers traded second-year quarterback Kyle McCord to the Miami Dolphins on Sunday in exchange for a 2028 sixth-round draft pick.

McCord, 23, is positioned to serve as the primary backup to starting quarterback Malik Willis in Miami. The trade follows a strong preseason finale performance by McCord, who completed 22 of 35 passes for 226 yards and four touchdowns against the Arizona Cardinals.

With Tyrod Taylor serving as Jordan Love's backup in Green Bay, McCord was slated for third-string duties. Miami created roster availability over the weekend by trading quarterback Quinn Ewers to the Jacksonville Jaguars and releasing backup quarterbacks Cam Miller and Mark Gronowski.

After weeks of speculation regarding J.J. McCarthy's future with the Minnesota Vikings, his future (at least in the short term) is now set. The second-year quarterback from Michigan is expected to make the Vikings' final 53-man roster, as first reported by ESPN.

General manager Nolan Teasley has the final say over the Vikings' 53-man roster, and he decided that the Vikings will carry quarterbacks Murray, McCarthy, Carson Wentz and Max Brosmer on their roster heading into the regular season. That could change in the two weeks before the Vikings' regular-season opener, but O’Connell now has a strong mix of experience and development in the room.

After missing his entire rookie season with a meniscus tear, McCarthy underwhelmed in his first year as a starter in 2025. He completed just 57.6% of his passes for 1,632 yards, totaling 15 touchdowns against 12 interceptions.

Minnesota went 6-4 in the 10 games McCarthy started as he battled ankle and hand injuries, as well as a concussion. Still, those results weren't enough to fully convince O’Connell and his staff that he is the long-term franchise quarterback.

All eyes now shift to the coming week to see if McCarthy remains on the active roster or if a trade partner finally emerges for the former 2024 first-round pick.

The Tennessee Titans released quarterback Will Levis on Sunday as part of their final 53-man roster cutdowns. The decision solidifies veteran Mitchell Trubisky as the primary backup behind 2025 No. 1 overall pick Cam Ward heading into the regular season.

Levis completed 53.8% of his passes for 200 yards across three preseason appearances this summer before the team made the move.

Originally selected by Tennessee with the 33rd overall pick in the 2023 NFL Draft, Levis started nine games as a rookie before earning the starting job in 2024.

He struggled through a 2-10 record as a starter that season, throwing 13 touchdowns and 12 interceptions while battling shoulder issues.

After the Titans selected Ward with the top overall pick in the 2025 NFL Draft, Levis missed the entire 2025 campaign following season-ending shoulder surgery in July.

The Detroit Lions have placed veteran center Cade Mays on injured reserve with a designation to return.

Mays, who suffered a wrist injury that's set to have him miss "significant" time, according to coach Dan Campbell, will now be forced to miss at least the first four games of the 2026 regular season. The Lions are allowed two players with an "IR-to-return" designation; when a player is given one of these designations, he does not count against the 53-man roster limit.

The move doesn't come as a surprise, but it does add a bit of finality to a situation that seemed somewhat fluid after NFL Network's Ian Rapoport reported on Aug. 10 that the injury could keep him out for "roughly 8-10 weeks."

The reported timeline would give him a chance to return in Weeks 4 through 6, but Mays' addition to the list would allow him to come back in Week 5 at the earliest.

Detroit has a bye in Week 6, which could prompt the Lions to delay his return to the lineup to maximize his recovery, even if it goes well.

In the meantime, the Lions appear set to deploy Juice Scruggs, an offseason addition who was acquired via the Houston Texans in the trade for running back David Montgomery, as the starting center in Week 1.

title: NFC North Preview: A Rebound Year for the Lions? - The Ringer
description:
Detroit Lions What’s at Stake for the Lions Is their championship window still open?
Murray has finished from 12th to 21st in EPA per pass play every single season he’s been healthy.
I think Minnesota will finish in second place in the NFC North and sneak into the playoffs as a wild-card team.
The Bears offense finished ninth in EPA per drive after finishing 26th the previous season.
How I See It As is the case with all of these NFC North teams, the ceiling here is high.
text:
Over the next week, The Ringer will be going deep on each division as the start of the 2026 NFL season approaches. So far, we have covered the NFC East and the AFC East. Now we’re on to the NFC North. Has the Lions’ window closed? Are the Bears primed to make the leap to Super Bowl contender? Is the Kyler Murray experiment in Minnesota going to work? And is everyone sleeping on the usually reliable Packers? Let’s talk about it!

Detroit Lions

What’s at Stake for the Lions

Is their championship window still open? Or did they miss their chance during the 2023 and 2024 seasons, when they went 12-5 and 15-2, respectively, in the regular season but didn’t make a Super Bowl? It’s possible that the Lions will settle into a stretch where they’re a decent, competitive team but not an actual title contender. But there are also plenty of reasons to think this team is primed for a bounce-back in 2026.

Reasons for Optimism

There are quite a few! Let’s start out by pointing out that last season—a year in which it felt like nothing went their way—wasn’t really that bad. The Lions finished 9-8, but they were third in DVOA (I know, hang the banner!). According to the advanced stats, only the Seahawks and Rams were better during the regular season. Detroit was 2-5 in games decided by seven points or fewer, and only the Cardinals had worse injury luck, according to FTN’s adjusted games lost metric. Bottom line: By all accounts, this was a team that wasn’t quite as bad as its record indicated.

OK, so why will 2026 be different? First, I still believe that they have a top-five roster. And second, I think they have a reliable offense. The transition from the Ben Johnson era was not a smooth one. Dan Campbell hired John Morton to be the offensive coordinator in 2025 and then took over play calling duties in November. While it certainly felt like the Lions had taken a big step back, they still finished sixth in expected points added per drive, and they were better statistically than offenses like the 49ers, Bears, and Jaguars.

In the offseason, Campbell hired Drew Petzing as his offensive coordinator. I’m not going to sit here and tell you that Petzing is Bill Walsh, but I do think he can be an upgrade from last year’s situation. The most important factor here is talent. Quarterback Jared Goff has finished from third to seventh in EPA per pass play for four consecutive seasons. He’s surrounded by a loaded skill group that includes Jahmyr Gibbs, Amon-Ra St. Brown, Jameson Williams, and Sam LaPorta. You want playmakers who will keep opposing defensive coordinators up at night. The Lions have that.

Oh, and one more thing: The Lions have the second-easiest schedule in the NFL. There’s a scenario where they pile up wins even as they’re trying to figure out some of the potential problem areas on the roster.

Reasons for Concern

You may notice that I haven’t mentioned the defense yet. The Lions finished ninth in defensive DVOA last year despite having the most injured unit in the NFL. That’s pretty impressive. The problem? Those injuries are lingering into 2026. Safeties Brian Branch and Kerby Joseph—both of whom are among the team’s best defensive players—are expected to miss time at the start of the season. And the Lions released cornerback Terrion Arnold amid troubling legal issues. The Lions played a lot of man coverage last year, but their personnel wasn’t good enough, and they gave up too many explosive plays. They need to be quicker to adjust in 2026.

The other potential area of concern is the offensive line. Brandon Thorn ranks Detroit’s O-line as a mediocre unit. They’re starting a rookie, Blake Miller, at right tackle, and they’ll be without starting center Cade Mays for a chunk of the season because of a wrist injury. When Goff is kept clean, he can carve up defenses. But when he’s pressured, it can get ugly. If the O-line has issues, this offense could take a step back.

How I See It

The Lions look like a sneaky Super Bowl contender to me. Their winning formula is simple: talented roster plus efficient offense plus easy schedule. It’s possible that their secondary just isn’t good enough and will put a cap on the Lions’ ceiling. But I choose to hold out some hope that they can get healthy by mid-October and that they’ll feel some urgency to be active at the trade deadline (Maxx Crosby, anyone???) if they sense that they have a real chance to compete for a Super Bowl this season.

Detroit is 45-23 over the past four seasons. In the NFC, only the Eagles have posted a better winning percentage in that span. I’ll always take my chances with a team that has a lot of talented, young players and a coach who won’t turtle in big moments.

Projected record: 11-6

Minnesota Vikings

What’s at Stake for the Vikings

Kevin O’Connell’s reputation? Kyler Murray’s career?? Another offseason reset??? It feels like there’s quite a lot at stake for the 2026 Vikings! Just think about the past four years. At quarterback, they went from Kirk Cousins to Sam Darnold to J.J. McCarthy to Murray. They fired general manager Kwesi Adofo-Mensah. And they have failed to win a playoff game in that time. We could be talking about a lot of the main characters here differently depending on what happens over the next five months.

Reasons for Optimism

I have never been the biggest Murray fan, but I think the pendulum has swung too far in the direction of “You can’t win with this dude as your quarterback.” The week-to-week Murray experience feels high-variance. But when we look at where he usually ends up, it’s a relatively narrow range of outcomes.

Murray has finished from 12th to 21st in EPA per pass play every single season he’s been healthy. He’s had months when he’s looked like a top-10 guy, but he has not had full seasons in which he’s been a top-10 guy. Most importantly for the Vikings, though, he sets a floor of at least mediocrity (or competency, if we want to be nicer about it). That’s something the Vikings did not have last season. With McCarthy, Carson Wentz, and Max Brosmer, the Vikings finished 28th in passing DVOA. If Murray simply plays to his career average—nothing more, nothing less—it’ll be a huge upgrade over what Minnesota had last season. Given that the offensive line should be solid and the Vikings have a good group of pass catchers—Justin Jefferson, Jordan Addison, Jauan Jennings, T.J. Hockenson—around Murray, producing a respectable offense seems realistic.

On the defensive side of the ball, the case for hope starts and ends with Brian Flores. There aren’t a lot of coordinators to whom I give the benefit of the doubt, but Flores is one of them. The Vikings are coming off of back-to-back top-five defensive performances. Flores’s creativity is unmatched. I just trust that he’ll look at his personnel and eventually figure it out.

Reasons for Concern

There’s a chance that O’Connell has gotten too much credit and Flores too little. If we’re talking just offensive acumen, look at where the Vikings have ranked over the past four seasons.

O’Connell has coached a few mediocre offenses and one terrible offense. Look at it this way: If your favorite offensive coach—Kyle Shanahan, Sean McVay, Sean Payton, whoever—had the Vikings’ group of talent on offense, would they be able to produce a top-10 to top-12 offense? I think the answer is yes. O’Connell has to show this season that he can get the Vikings to that range.

And despite what I said about Flores above, there are concerns with the defense. The talent here is below average. I have questions about their pass rush, their safety group, and their overall depth. It will be on Flores to once again do more with less. He’s shown in the past that he’s capable, but there are limits to what any coach can do if the talent is simply not good enough.

How I See It

The Vikings started McCarthy, Wentz, and Brosmer last year. They ranked 29th in EPA on turnovers. They didn’t have a single offensive line combination play more than 25 percent of the snaps, according to the FTN Football Almanac. And they still went 9-8. The defense could easily take a step back this season, but I think the offense will be competent, which is a huge leap from where it was last season. I’m holding on to my O’Connell stock. I think Minnesota will finish in second place in the NFC North and sneak into the playoffs as a wild-card team.

Projected record: 10-7

Chicago Bears

What’s at Stake for the Bears

There’s a chance that by the end of the season, we’ll look at the Ben Johnson–Caleb Williams duo as the best coach-quarterback combination in the entire NFL. Seriously. That’s a thing that can realistically happen. That’s the ceiling that this team has. But as we see often in the NFL, success and development are not linear. Johnson himself has acknowledged that a lot of things went the Bears’ way last year that might not go their way this season. The wide range of outcomes (from missing the playoffs to winning the Super Bowl) makes Chicago one of the toughest teams to project.

Reasons for Optimism

Johnson is millennial Sean Payton. It feels like he thinks he’s God’s gift to coaching. It also might be true that he’s kind of God’s gift to coaching. In a league where coaches and general managers often like to preach (whine about?) patience, Johnson went to Chicago and won 11 games in his first season. He was the no. 1 reason for its turnaround. He schemed up a run game out of nowhere and created an environment where Williams could succeed. The Bears offense finished ninth in EPA per drive after finishing 26th the previous season. Going back to his Detroit days, Johnson has now coached a top-10 offense for four straight seasons.

Last year’s Bears passing game was successful because Johnson provided Williams answers and Williams leaned into his one-of-one talent as a playmaker. Only Bo Nix threw into tight windows at a lower rate than Williams, and Williams did a great job of avoiding negative plays. Pro Football Focus measures how often a quarterback’s pressures turn into sacks. Williams had the third-lowest rate among starters.

The Bears have a promising supporting cast around Williams. They are expecting big things from wide receivers Rome Odunze and Luther Burden III, and it’d be no surprise to see tight end Colston Loveland emerge as an All-Pro. But really, the optimism comes down to the coach and the quarterback. We might leave this season assuming that we should just pencil Johnson in for 10-plus wins every year, and we might view Williams as a perennial MVP candidate.

Reasons for Concern

There’s a reason why Johnson called the Bears the no. 1 regression candidate. Chicago had nearly unprecedented turnover luck last season. Its EPA on turnovers was the second highest of any team in the last 10 years! That’s not the type of thing that is sustainable year to year. The turnover luck is also at least part of the reason why the Bears won seven games decided by seven points or fewer—the third most of any team.

Roster-wise, the big concern is that this might end up being a bottom-quartile defense. Last year, Chicago ranked 30th in defensive success rate, and it allowed explosive passes at the highest rate of any defense. When it wasn’t forcing turnovers, this was one of the NFL’s worst units. And it’s hard to make the case that the talent is significantly better this season. Their big free agent signing was safety Coby Bryant, but he’s expected to miss most of the season with a knee injury. On paper, the Bears’ pass rush looks like it will be one of the NFL’s worst. It’s possible that some of the guys who missed time last year will stay healthy and play well, but there are just a lot of question marks with this group.

Offensively, left tackle remains a concern. And while Williams’s talent is undeniable, his game still lacks consistency—specifically when it comes to accuracy. Last season, according to PFF, Williams ranked 34th out of 38 quarterbacks in adjusted completion percentage. Only Marcus Mariota, Cam Ward, Shedeur Sanders, and Dillon Gabriel were worse. We know that Williams can make the high-degree-of-difficulty plays. The next step in his development is to make all the layups.

How I See It

I flip-flopped on the Bears roughly 700 times this summer. I really do think that there’s a world in which Johnson and Williams are crowned the new kings of the NFL. And I certainly don’t want to bet against a coach who pounds six cups of coffee plus a cold brew every day. But ultimately, I just have too many questions about Chicago’s defense—both the pass rush and the secondary. I think the Bears will have a top-10 offense, but I’m not sure they’ll have an elite unit that can make up for the defensive deficiencies. This looks to me like a good team that will indeed regress a bit.

Projected record: 9-8

Green Bay Packers

What’s at Stake for the Packers

It felt like the heat—both locally and nationally—was turned up on Matt LaFleur last season, but the Packers ended up signing him to a contract extension in the offseason. Now the Packers are trying to transition from being a good, competitive team to a Super Bowl contender. When they got to the divisional round in Jordan Love’s first year as a full-time starter in 2023, it felt like they’d be near the top of the NFC every season. But the Packers have failed to win a playoff game in each of the past two seasons. Given the coach-quarterback combo and the fact that Green Bay went all in for Micah Parsons last summer, there should be an expectation that the Packers can compete for a Super Bowl right now.

Reasons for Optimism

LaFleur flat out has one of the NFL’s most impressive track records as an offensive schemer and play caller. Look at how the Packers have performed in seven seasons under his direction.

His offenses have been top 10 in six of seven seasons, and even at their worst, they were still in the top half of the league. That’s been with different quarterbacks and different offensive personnel. The Packers have just been extremely reliable in the regular season with LaFleur, regardless of variables.

Love has become a polarizing quarterback, and I think I know why. From a statistical perspective, the case is overwhelming that he’s really, really good. Love ranked first in EPA per pass play last season. Want to zoom out for a bigger sample? Sure. Over the past three years (45 starts), he’s second. The problem is: When Love makes a mistake, it’s often of the “What the $%&! happened there? Did his brain just short-circuit?” variety. It’s not the number of mistakes he’s making, because that is relatively low. (Love was tied for the eighth-lowest turnover-worthy play percentage, as tracked by PFF, and he had the fourth-lowest pressure-to-sack rate last season.) It’s the type of mistakes.

If the Packers’ skill group can stay healthy, the sky’s the limit for this offense. It could legitimately be the best group in the NFL. On paper, Christian Watson, Matthew Golden, and Jayden Reed should complement one another well. And before he got injured last year, I thought Tucker Kraft was the best tight end in the NFL.

Bottom line here: LaFleur and Love offer a high floor. And everyone else will determine the ceiling.

Reasons for Concern

Let’s start on defense. At coordinator, the Packers went from Jeff Hafley to Jonathan Gannon. The book on Gannon is straightforward: When his unit has a distinct talent advantage, he can coach a good defense. When he doesn’t have great talent to work with, he gets exposed. Here’s how Gannon’s defenses have performed over the past five seasons (two years as the Eagles’ coordinator and three years as the Cardinals’ head coach).

In Philadelphia, Gannon ran a vanilla scheme that was dominant against bad quarterbacks and got exposed by competent (or better) quarterbacks. As a play calling head coach in Arizona, he got more creative, but look at the results. Nothing really worked (to be fair, the Cardinals had bad injury luck and faced a tough schedule). I just have not seen him be a “do more with less” defensive coach, and that’s what it’ll take to be successful with a Packers defense that is expected to be without Parsons for at least the first four to six weeks of the season. Green Bay has a below-average defensive depth chart with questions both up front and in the secondary.

Offensively, the main concern is the offensive line. It feels like the Packers usually figure it out, but Thorn has them as the 29th-ranked unit in his preseason projections. The issue here is that Love had a little Jared Goff in him last year when it came to performing under pressure. Love ranked first in EPA per pass play when kept clean but was 13th when under pressure. If the offensive line takes a step back, there very well could be a domino effect.

And the final concern here is with the Packers’ run game. Green Bay ran the ball on early downs at the third-highest rate last season. If you’re a Love critic, it’s fair to point out that his own coach doesn’t want to put the ball in his hands more often. And the Packers had an average rushing attack last season, ranking 18th in DVOA. In terms of personnel, running back Josh Jacobs has been charged with two misdemeanor counts of battery and criminal damage to property stemming from an offseason arrest related to domestic abuse. Jacobs has been placed on the commissioner’s exempt list, meaning he’s on paid leave while the legal process plays out and the NFL conducts its investigation.

How I See It

As is the case with all of these NFC North teams, the ceiling here is high. The Packers could produce the NFL’s best offense, and the defense could level up the second that Parsons steps back on the field. He’s that kind of transformational player. If the 2026 season unfolds in that specific (and realistic) way, Green Bay can absolutely contend for a Super Bowl.

I am usually higher on the Packers than consensus because I believe in the LaFleur-Love duo. But I have too many questions this season. I don’t trust Gannon to keep up against good quarterbacks and offensive coordinators. And I have questions about Green Bay’s offensive line and defensive personnel. I don’t see a whole lot separating these four teams, but ultimately, somebody has to finish last in this loaded division, and I’ve got the Packers.

text:
The San Francisco 49ers have officially set their initial 53-man roster, but the work is far from over. The team anticipates further moves, including potential trades and re-signings, as they navigate a landscape dotted with injuries and strategic roster construction.

Several players are currently sidelined, with head coach Kyle Shanahan indicating that many could be ready to return to practice soon. Among the notable names dealing with injuries are cornerback Renardo Green (hamstring), wide receiver Mike Evans (groin), safety Malik Mustapha (hamstring strain), wide receiver Jacob Cowing (groin), tight end Brayden Willis (concussion), quarterback Kurtis Rourke (ribs), nickel back Upton Stout (hip flexor), nickel back Nate Hobbs (groin), cornerback Ephesians Prysock (shoulder), fullback Kyle Juszczyk (finger), linebacker Nick Martin (hamstring), linebacker Luke Gifford (hamstring), offensive tackle Vederian Lowe (ankle), guard Dominick Puni (concussion), defensive tackle Gracen Halton (ankle), defensive end Romello Height (ankle), and defensive end Nick Bosa (soreness). Bosa, in particular, is expected to rejoin practice if his tendinitis improves.

The defensive tackle position saw decisions made regarding players like Keith Washington and Gracen Halton. Washington, an undrafted free agent, impressed with his ability to move defenders, while Halton, a fourth-round pick, also had a strong camp. The team is opting to carry five defensive tackles.

On the offensive line, the 49ers reportedly acquired depth through a trade. Veteran center Jake Patterson, who has experience at both center and guard, joins the team. Patterson's recent performance with the Texans showed a 1.5% blown block rate, with particular strength in pass protection, though his run blocking metrics were slightly below average.

The team also faces decisions regarding vested veterans. Players with four or more years of service cannot be placed on waivers. A common strategy involves releasing such players before the deadline and then re-signing them shortly after, often to make space for players returning from injury or to accommodate other roster adjustments. Only two players can be designated for return from injured reserve on cutdown day.

In positive injury news, tight end George Kittle is reportedly on track to practice this week and has a legitimate chance to play in the season opener. He has not experienced any setbacks in his recovery from a torn Achilles.
